ex: The deed describes the venue, scilicet the parish of Westminster, with unusual care.

def: Used in pleadings and formal writing to introduce particulars of something already referred to.
ex: The claim alleged three breaches, videlicet late delivery, defective goods and short weight.

def: In the first place, used especially to introduce the first item in a will or list.
ex: Imprimis, the testator commended his soul to God before turning to his lands.

def: The operative part of a deed, beginning with words such as now this deed witnesses, that effects the transaction.
ex: The recitals explained the background, but the testatum actually conveyed the property.

def: A historical offence of asserting papal or foreign jurisdiction in England against the authority of the Crown.
ex: Wolsey was charged under praemunire for exercising his powers as papal legate.

def: A formal discharge or release from a debt, duty or office.
ex: Once the final accounts were approved, the executor received his quietus.

def: A historical writ issued on the fiction that a defendant was hiding, used to bring civil cases into the King's Bench.
ex: By means of the latitat, the King's Bench drew lucrative business away from the Common Pleas.

def: The acquisition of ownership of property through continuous, uninterrupted possession for a period fixed by law.
ex: After decades of open occupation, the farmer acquired the meadow by usucapion.

def: The mixing of liquids or other substances belonging to different owners so that they cannot be separated, creating co-ownership.
ex: When the two merchants' oils were poured into one vat, confusio made them joint owners.

def: The transfer of ownership of property by physical delivery from one person to another.
ex: In civilian systems, a valid sale of goods is completed by traditio rather than mere agreement.

def: A formal Roman ceremony for transferring ownership of important property in the presence of witnesses and a scale holder.
ex: Land and cattle could pass only by mancipatio in early Roman law.

def: The male head of a Roman household, holding legal authority over its members and property.
ex: No son could own property in his own right while his paterfamilias was alive.

def: The thing or property that forms the subject matter of a legal right, action or trust.
ex: A trust fails for uncertainty if the res cannot be clearly identified.

def: Conducted between national governments, with each state keeping its own authority rather than handing power to a common body.
ex: Defence policy remains largely intergovernmental, so any single capital can block a joint mission.

def: Opposition to, or deep doubt about, the powers and further integration of the European Union.
ex: Rising Euroscepticism in rural constituencies reshaped the party's manifesto.

def: A treaty clause allowing EU decision-making to switch from unanimity to majority voting without a formal treaty amendment.
ex: Several ministers urged the Council to activate the passerelle on foreign policy votes.

def: The removal or relaxation of government rules governing an industry or market.
ex: Airline deregulation in the 1990s opened European skies to budget carriers.

def: The process by which economies or legal systems become increasingly similar in their standards and performance.
ex: Candidate states had to meet strict criteria on inflation and debt before joining the single currency, a test of economic convergence.

def: The policy aim of reducing economic and social disparities between regions, typically through targeted funding.
ex: Cohesion money paid for the new motorway linking the port to the interior.

def: The process by which national laws, institutions and policies adapt to the influence of European integration.
ex: Scholars trace the Europeanisation of environmental law in the member state's courts.

def: A theory holding that cooperation in one economic sector creates pressure for integration in neighbouring sectors.
ex: Her lecture used neofunctionalism to explain how coal and steel cooperation grew into a customs union.

def: The transfer of a policy area from intergovernmental cooperation to the ordinary decision-making of the EU institutions.
ex: The communitarisation of asylum rules gave the Court jurisdiction over national practice.

def: The pooling of debts or risks so that they are shared jointly by a group of states.
ex: Northern governments resisted any mutualisation of sovereign debt across the eurozone.

def: The policy of shielding domestic industries from foreign competition through tariffs, quotas or other barriers.
ex: The Commission warned that subsidising national champions risked a slide into protectionism.

def: The process by which rules or standards in different jurisdictions grow apart over time.
ex: Exporters feared that regulatory divergence after withdrawal would mean duplicate testing.

def: The bringing of a country's laws or policies into conformity with those of another body.
ex: Dynamic alignment with single market rules was the price of frictionless trade.

def: The setting of common technical specifications so that products are compatible and comparable across markets.
ex: European standardisation of phone chargers ended the drawer full of tangled cables.

def: The ability to track a product or ingredient through every stage of production and distribution.
ex: Strict beef traceability let inspectors identify the contaminated farm within hours.

def: Describing an approach that permits protective measures where a risk is plausible even before scientific certainty is reached.
ex: Regulators took a precautionary line and suspended the pesticide pending further studies.

def: An official classification system defining which economic activities count as environmentally sustainable.
ex: Investors scrutinised whether gas plants would be included in the green taxonomy.

def: The making of misleading claims that a product or company is more environmentally friendly than it really is.
ex: The new directive bans vague labels such as eco-friendly to curb greenwashing.

def: An official ban on trade or a particular commercial activity with a specified country.
ex: The Council extended the arms embargo for another twelve months.

def: The quality of an institution or decision being accepted as rightful and properly authorised by those it governs.
ex: Critics argued that unelected officials lacked the legitimacy to impose such cuts.

def: Government or control by technical experts rather than elected politicians.
ex: Opponents painted the Brussels machinery as a remote technocracy deaf to voters.

def: A technical expert who holds significant political or administrative power.
ex: A former central banker, the new prime minister was hailed as a steady technocrat.

def: An official working in the administration of the European Union, often used disparagingly.
ex: The tabloid blamed a faceless Eurocrat for the rule on banana curvature.

def: A person paid to influence legislators or officials on behalf of a particular interest.
ex: Every lobbyist meeting a commissioner must now appear on the public register.

def: A department of an administration responsible for a specific policy area.
ex: The competition directorate opened a formal investigation into the merger.

def: A group of three institutions or leaders acting jointly, especially those overseeing a financial rescue.
ex: Inspectors from the troika arrived in Athens to review the austerity programme.

def: Describing an arrangement in which some states integrate faster and further than others.
ex: A multispeed Europe would let a core group press ahead on defence.

def: The taking back by a state of people who entered or stayed in another country without authorisation.
ex: The bloc offered visa concessions in exchange for a readmission agreement.

def: A supporter of a political system in which power is shared between a central authority and constituent states.
ex: As a committed federalist, she called for a directly elected Commission president.

def: The export of goods at a price below their normal value in the home market, harming foreign producers.
ex: Steelmakers petitioned for duties to counter the dumping of cheap imports.

def: Financial support given by a government to a business or sector to keep prices low or output high.
ex: The tax break was treated as an unlawful subsidy that distorted competition.

def: The act of meeting the requirements of a law, rule or regulatory standard.
ex: The bank hired forty extra staff to manage compliance with the new data rules.

def: The permanent administrative office of an organisation, supporting its work and meetings.
ex: The Council secretariat circulated a compromise text late on Thursday.

def: A fixed limit on the quantity of something that may be produced, caught or imported.
ex: Fishermen protested that the new cod quota would bankrupt the harbour.

def: A member of a governing commission who holds responsibility for a particular policy portfolio.
ex: The trade commissioner flew to Washington to defuse the tariff row.

def: A member of a parliament, especially one experienced in its procedures.
ex: A veteran parliamentarian, he knew exactly how to stall the amendment in committee.

def: A union of sovereign states that delegate limited powers to a central body while retaining most authority.
ex: Some historians describe the early Community as closer to a confederation than a state.

def: The practice of coordinating policy among several states through shared institutions and rules.
ex: The summit communique reaffirmed a commitment to multilateralism and the rules-based order.

def: The pursuit of policy by one state acting alone, without consulting or agreeing with partners.
ex: Allies condemned the sudden border closures as reckless unilateralism.

def: The body with the power to make, amend and repeal laws.
ex: The regional legislature voted to challenge the directive before the Court.

def: A powerful political entity formed by the union of several states, often used critically of centralised integration.
ex: Campaigners warned that the new treaty was a step towards a European superstate.

def: The concentration of power and decision-making in a single central authority.
ex: Regional leaders resisted the centralisation of banking supervision in Frankfurt.

def: The transfer of authority from a central government to regional or local bodies.
ex: Decentralisation of competition enforcement put national authorities in the front line.

def: A person who strongly dislikes or fears the European Union and European integration.
ex: Even the most ardent Europhobe in the cabinet admitted the trade deal brought jobs.

def: A person who advocates closer political and economic union between states.
ex: An unrepentant integrationist, the minister proposed a common budget for the eurozone.

def: To organise a political system on federal lines, sharing power between a centre and constituent units.
ex: Some delegates wanted to federalise fiscal policy as well as monetary policy.

def: To remove or reduce government controls over an industry or activity.
ex: The government moved to deregulate the energy market and invite foreign suppliers.

def: To open a market or sector to competition by relaxing state restrictions.
ex: The directive required member states to liberalise postal services by 2011.

def: The reduction of carbon dioxide emissions from an economy, industry or activity.
ex: Funding for decarbonisation was ring-fenced in the recovery plan.

def: The gradual erosion of democratic standards or the rule of law by a government.
ex: The Commission froze funds in response to judicial backsliding in the capital.

def: A form of governance that keeps elections but curbs judicial independence, media freedom and civil liberties.
ex: MEPs debated how the bloc should respond to illiberalism within its own borders.

def: A body of officials responsible for checking that rules and standards are being followed.
ex: The food safety inspectorate audited the slaughterhouse without notice.

def: A public body that supervises a sector and enforces the rules that govern it.
ex: The telecoms regulator capped roaming charges across the single market.

def: A semicircular debating chamber, particularly the main assembly hall of the European Parliament.
ex: Applause rang around the hemicycle as the result flashed on the screens.

def: A standing executive committee that directs the business of a larger assembly or convention.
ex: The convention's presidium drafted the text before it went to the full membership.

def: A temporary trade measure, or legal protection, that a state may invoke to prevent serious harm.
ex: Brussels imposed a steel safeguard after imports surged by a third.

def: A rule-of-origin principle allowing materials from partner countries to count as local content for preferential tariffs.
ex: Diagonal cumulation lets the factory use fabric from Turkey and still qualify for duty-free access.

def: The conduct of diplomacy through meetings of heads of government.
ex: Weary officials joked that crisis summitry had become a monthly ritual.

def: Involving a group of several countries, but not all members of a wider organisation.
ex: Frustrated by deadlock, the bloc pursued a plurilateral deal on digital trade.

def: Relating to government by experts, often implying detachment from popular politics.
ex: The technocratic tone of the report did little to reassure anxious farmers.

def: A school of economic thought holding that the state should set firm legal rules to ensure fair competition and stable money.
ex: Ordoliberalism shaped the strict deficit rules written into the monetary treaty.

def: A policy of sharp cuts in public spending and tax rises intended to reduce government deficits.
ex: Years of austerity left hospitals short of staff and equipment.

def: Involving authority shared across local, regional, national and supranational tiers of government.
ex: Water policy is a textbook case of multilevel governance in Europe.

def: The former term for financial orders made on divorce, covering maintenance, property adjustment and lump sums.
ex: Older precedents on ancillary relief still guide how the court approaches a fair division of assets.

def: An order directing a pension scheme to pay part of a member's pension or lump sum to the former spouse when benefits become payable.
ex: Because the husband was close to retirement, the wife's counsel sought a pension attachment order rather than an immediate share.

def: An order postponing the sale of the family home until a trigger event, typically the youngest child finishing education, after which the proceeds are divided.
ex: The judge made a Mesher order so the children could stay in the house until the youngest turned eighteen.

def: An order allowing one spouse to live in the former matrimonial home for life or until remarriage or cohabitation, with sale and division deferred until then.
ex: Given the wife's age and lack of income, a Martin order secured her housing without extinguishing the husband's share.

def: An agreement between spouses or intended spouses regulating how their assets will be dealt with if the marriage ends.
ex: Following Radmacher, the court will give effect to a freely entered nuptial agreement unless it would be unfair to do so.

def: The interim divorce order in England and Wales confirming entitlement to divorce, which replaced the decree nisi in 2022.
ex: The parties must wait six weeks after the conditional order before applying to make it final.

def: A court order appointing a person, often a relative, to exercise parental responsibility for a child to the exclusion of the parents without severing the legal parental link.
ex: The grandmother applied for special guardianship so she could make day-to-day decisions without pursuing adoption.

def: The capacity of a child under sixteen to consent to their own medical treatment where they have sufficient understanding and intelligence.
ex: The clinician recorded her assessment of the fifteen-year-old's Gillick competence before prescribing without parental involvement.

def: An order placing a child in the care of a local authority, which then shares parental responsibility with the parents.
ex: After repeated neglect findings, the council applied for a care order in respect of all three children.

def: An order requiring a local authority to advise, assist and befriend a child who remains living at home, without acquiring parental responsibility.
ex: The court considered a supervision order sufficient because the mother had engaged well with support services.

def: The statutory conditions that must be proved before a care or supervision order can be made, namely that the child is suffering or likely to suffer significant harm.
ex: The parents conceded that the threshold criteria were met but disputed that removal was proportionate.

def: An order authorising a local authority to place a child for adoption with any prospective adopters it chooses.
ex: Because the placement order dispensed with parental consent, the mother sought leave to oppose the adoption.

def: The jurisdiction under which the High Court takes a child into its guardianship so that no important step in the child's life may be taken without the court's consent.
ex: Fearing the child would be taken abroad for marriage, the family's solicitor applied urgently for wardship.

def: The residual power of the High Court to protect children and vulnerable adults where no statutory remedy is available.
ex: The judge invoked the inherent jurisdiction to authorise the teenager's deprivation of liberty in a secure unit.

def: The place where a person, especially a child, has a degree of integration in a social and family environment, used to determine jurisdiction.
ex: The case turned on whether the child's habitual residence had shifted to Spain during the eight months there.

def: Keeping a child in another country beyond an agreed period in breach of the other parent's rights of custody under the Hague Convention.
ex: When the father failed to return the boy after the summer visit, the mother alleged wrongful retention and sought a summary return.

def: Court permission for a parent to take a child permanently out of the jurisdiction without the other parent's consent.
ex: The mother's application for leave to remove to Canada was refused because it would sever the children's bond with their father.

def: Assets generated or acquired during the marriage through the parties' joint endeavour, which are presumptively subject to equal sharing.
ex: The husband argued that the inherited farm was not matrimonial property and should be ring-fenced.

def: The principle that matrimonial property should normally be divided equally between spouses unless there is good reason to depart from equality.
ex: Applying the sharing principle, the court split the marital assets fifty-fifty despite the husband's higher earnings.

def: The notional reattribution to a spouse of assets they have wantonly dissipated, so that the loss is borne by them in the division.
ex: Counsel sought an add-back of the gambling losses incurred after separation.

def: An unforeseeable supervening event shortly after a financial order that invalidates its fundamental basis and may justify setting it aside.
ex: The sudden collapse of the company months after the order was argued to be a Barder event.

def: The second court appointment in financial remedy proceedings, at which a judge gives an indication of likely outcome to encourage settlement.
ex: The parties settled on the day of the financial dispute resolution hearing after the judge's robust indication.

def: An order transferring legal parenthood from a surrogate to the intended parents after a surrogacy arrangement.
ex: The couple applied for a parental order within six months of the baby's birth abroad.

def: Relationship by blood descent, which within prohibited degrees bars a valid marriage.
ex: The registrar refused the notice of marriage because the parties were within the prohibited degrees of consanguinity.

def: Interim periodical payments ordered to support a spouse until the final financial order is made.
ex: Pending the final hearing, the wife obtained maintenance pending suit to cover her rent and legal fees.

def: A court decree relieving spouses of the obligation to live together without dissolving the marriage.
ex: For religious reasons, she sought judicial separation rather than divorce.

def: An order obtained in a foreign court replicating the terms of an English order so that it is enforceable in that jurisdiction.
ex: Before allowing the holiday to Dubai, the judge required the father to obtain a mirror order there.

def: The rule that a court should not make an order about a child unless doing so would be better for the child than making none.
ex: Since the parents had agreed contact amicably, the judge applied the no order principle and dismissed the application.

def: A short-term order authorising the immediate removal of a child, or their retention in a safe place, where they are at risk of significant harm.
ex: Social workers obtained an emergency protection order overnight after the infant was found with unexplained fractures.

def: Permission granted to a person already in the UK to stay for a specified period or indefinitely.
ex: Her leave to remain as a student expires in March, so she must switch routes before then.

def: Immigration permission to stay in the UK with no time limit, commonly a step towards naturalisation.
ex: After five years on the skilled worker route, he applied for indefinite leave to remain.

def: Indefinite leave granted under the EU Settlement Scheme to EEA nationals with five years' continuous residence in the UK.
ex: Once she obtained settled status, her right to reside no longer depended on exercising Treaty rights.

def: Limited leave under the EU Settlement Scheme for EEA nationals with less than five years' continuous residence.
ex: The client holds pre-settled status and will become eligible for settled status next spring.

def: Formal directions specifying the date, flight and destination for removing a person from the UK.
ex: Removal directions were set for Thursday, prompting an urgent application for an injunction.

def: The enforced departure of a person who has no leave to be in the UK, carried out without a deportation order.
ex: As an overstayer with no pending application, she was liable to administrative removal.

def: Protection granted to a person who does not qualify as a refugee but faces a real risk of serious harm if returned.
ex: Although his fear was not linked to a Convention reason, he was granted humanitarian protection.

def: The core element of the refugee definition, requiring both a subjective fear and an objectively reasonable likelihood of persecution.
ex: The tribunal accepted she had a well-founded fear of persecution owing to her political opinion.

def: The principle that protection may be refused if the claimant could safely and reasonably relocate to another part of their home country.
ex: The Home Office argued internal relocation to the capital was reasonable, but the judge found it unduly harsh for a lone woman.

def: A country other than the claimant's own through which they passed and to which they may be returned to have their asylum claim decided.
ex: His claim was treated as inadmissible because he had transited through a safe third country.

def: Further submissions after a refused claim that are significantly different from previous material and create a realistic prospect of success.
ex: New medical evidence of torture allowed her representatives to lodge a fresh claim.

def: A certification that a protection or human rights claim is bound to fail, which removes the right to an in-country appeal.
ex: The Secretary of State certified the claim as clearly unfounded, so judicial review was the only route.

def: Home Office permission allowing an employer or institution to sponsor migrants under the points-based system.
ex: The startup had to obtain a sponsor licence before it could hire the overseas engineer.

def: A unique electronic reference assigned by a licensed sponsor confirming the job offer on which a work visa application relies.
ex: Her visa application stalled because the certificate of sponsorship listed the wrong occupation code.

def: A prescribed verification an employer must carry out to confirm a worker's lawful entitlement to work, giving a defence to a civil penalty.
ex: The restaurant faced a civil penalty because no right to work check had been recorded for two kitchen staff.

def: Release from immigration detention, or freedom from it, subject to conditions such as reporting and residence.
ex: The First-tier Tribunal granted immigration bail on condition that he report weekly.

def: Permission obtained from abroad before travelling to the UK, usually in the form of a visa.
ex: The spouse's application for entry clearance was refused for failing the financial requirement.

def: A national of a country listed in the Immigration Rules who must obtain entry clearance before travelling to the UK for any purpose.
ex: Because she is a visa national, even a two-day business trip requires a visitor visa.

def: Leave granted on a discretionary basis where the Immigration Rules are not met but compelling compassionate factors exist.
ex: Her lawyers sought leave outside the rules given her role as sole carer for a terminally ill parent.

def: A form of limited leave granted on exceptional grounds to people who do not qualify for asylum or humanitarian protection.
ex: He was granted thirty months' discretionary leave on medical grounds.

def: The elevated threshold for showing that a foreign criminal's deportation would affect a qualifying partner or child to an extent beyond the ordinary consequences.
ex: The tribunal found that separating the autistic son from his father would be unduly harsh.

def: The demanding test a serious foreign offender must satisfy, over and above the statutory exceptions, to resist deportation on Article 8 grounds.
ex: With a sentence exceeding four years, he had to establish very compelling circumstances to defeat deportation.

def: The statutory extension of existing leave while an in-time application or resulting appeal remains pending.
ex: Because she applied before her visa expired, she continued to work lawfully on section 3C leave.

def: A route to settlement based on ten years' continuous lawful residence in the UK.
ex: A three-month gap in his leave threatened his long residence application.

def: The route allowing the pre-flight spouse, partner and minor children of a refugee to join them in the host country.
ex: Once granted asylum, he applied for family reunion so his wife and daughters could join him.

def: Upper Tribunal decisions designated as authoritative on conditions in a particular country, binding in later cases unless strong new evidence emerges.
ex: The judge followed the current country guidance on returns to Baghdad.

def: A right of residence that arises not in a person's own name but from their relationship to another, such as the primary carer of a citizen child.
ex: As sole carer of a British child, the mother claimed a derivative right of residence.

def: A condition attached to leave that prevents the holder from accessing most welfare benefits and housing assistance.
ex: The family applied to lift the no recourse to public funds condition after the father lost his job.

def: A mandatory fee paid by many visa applicants for access to the NHS during their leave.
ex: The immigration health surcharge for the whole family added several thousand pounds to the application.

def: A historic exception, abolished in England in 1995, under which a buyer in good faith in an open market acquired good title even from a non-owner.
ex: Counsel noted that, since market overt was abolished, the antique dealer could no longer rely on the open-market sale to defeat the true owner.

def: A buyer who has obtained goods with the seller's consent before property passes and can pass good title to a good-faith sub-purchaser.
ex: The finance house lost its claim because the dealer had acquired the cars as a buyer in possession and resold them.

def: An agent who in the customary course of business has authority to sell or buy goods, and who may pass good title to a purchaser in good faith.
ex: The owner left the car with a mercantile agent, so the innocent buyer obtained good title despite the unauthorised sale.

def: A self-employed intermediary with continuing authority to negotiate the sale or purchase of goods on behalf of a principal, protected by statutory rights.
ex: Because she qualified as a commercial agent, the principal could not terminate without paying compensation.

def: A principal whose very existence is unknown to the third party dealing with the agent, but who may nonetheless sue and be sued on the contract.
ex: When the supplier discovered the buyer was acting for an undisclosed principal, it sued the principal directly for the price.

def: The authority an agent in a particular position or trade would ordinarily be expected to have to perform acts incidental to that role.
ex: The court held that ordering stock fell within the usual authority of a general manager.

def: The implied term that goods supplied in the course of business meet the standard a reasonable person would regard as satisfactory.
ex: The buyer rejected the machinery because recurring faults showed it was not of satisfactory quality.

def: A sale in which the goods are identified by words describing them, giving rise to an implied condition that they correspond with that description.
ex: Since the timber was sold as seasoned oak, delivery of green pine breached the terms of a sale by description.

def: Goods defined only by description and not identified and agreed upon at the time of contract, in which property cannot pass until they are ascertained.
ex: The wheat remained unascertained goods in a bulk cargo, so title had not passed when the seller became insolvent.

def: The transfer of ownership in goods from seller to buyer, which occurs when the parties intend it to and may differ from delivery.
ex: The dispute turned on the passing of property, since the goods were destroyed before delivery but after payment.

def: A seller who has not received the whole price and so enjoys statutory real remedies against the goods, such as lien and resale.
ex: As an unpaid seller, the manufacturer kept the consignment in its warehouse until the balance was paid.

def: The right of an unpaid seller to recover possession of goods still with a carrier when the buyer becomes insolvent.
ex: Learning of the buyer's administration, the seller instructed the carrier to halt delivery, exercising its right of stoppage in transit.

def: A bank's undertaking to pay the seller on presentation of specified conforming documents, such as a bill of lading and invoice.
ex: The exporter insisted on payment by documentary credit because it had never traded with the buyer before.

def: The rule that a letter of credit or demand guarantee is independent of the underlying sale contract, so disputes under that contract do not affect payment.
ex: Under the autonomy principle, the bank had to pay against conforming documents despite the buyer's complaints about the goods.

def: The doctrine that a bank need pay under a documentary credit only if the documents presented conform precisely to its terms.
ex: Applying strict compliance, the bank rejected the presentation because the invoice misdescribed the vessel's name.

def: A bank, usually in the seller's country, that adds its own independent payment undertaking to a letter of credit issued by another bank.
ex: Worried about the issuing bank's credit risk, the exporter required a London confirming bank.

def: A credit that operates as a guarantee, payable only if the applicant defaults on its underlying obligation.
ex: The landlord accepted a standby letter of credit in place of a cash rent deposit.

def: A guarantee payable on the beneficiary's written demand without proof of the principal's default, subject only to the fraud exception.
ex: The employer called the demand guarantee in full, leaving the contractor to dispute the default in arbitration.

def: A security, typically issued by a bank or surety, protecting an employer against a contractor's failure to perform.
ex: The tender required a performance bond for ten per cent of the contract price.

def: An unconditional written order by one person requiring another to pay a sum on demand or at a fixed future date to a named person or bearer.
ex: The importer accepted a bill of exchange payable ninety days after sight.

def: A person who takes a negotiable instrument for value, in good faith and without notice of defects, and so acquires it free of prior equities.
ex: As a holder in due course, the discounting bank could enforce the bill despite the drawer's dispute with the payee.

def: The formal certification by a notary that a foreign bill of exchange has been dishonoured, preserving recourse against prior parties.
ex: The bank arranged noting and protesting of the dishonoured bill so it could pursue the drawer abroad.

def: A form of receivables finance in which a lender advances funds against unpaid invoices while the business continues to collect its own debts.
ex: The manufacturer used confidential invoice discounting so its customers would not learn of the facility.

def: A transfer of a chose in action that does not satisfy the statutory formalities, so the assignee generally must join the assignor in proceedings.
ex: Because no written notice reached the debtor, the transfer took effect only as an equitable assignment.

def: A contractual term prohibiting or restricting a party from transferring its rights under the contract without consent.
ex: The anti-assignment clause rendered the purported transfer of receivables ineffective against the customer.

def: A sale under which the price is paid by instalments and property remains with the seller until specified conditions, usually full payment, are met.
ex: The van was supplied on conditional sale, so the dealer retained title until the final instalment.

def: Under the former consumer credit regime, a credit agreement requiring grossly exorbitant payments or grossly contravening fair dealing, which the court could reopen.
ex: The borrower's barrister argued the loan was an extortionate credit bargain given its annual rate of several hundred per cent.

def: A distribution system in which a supplier sells only to resellers chosen against specified criteria, who may not resell to unauthorised dealers.
ex: The luxury brand's selective distribution network barred retailers from selling to discount websites.

def: The approach in a battle of the forms under which the contract is usually concluded on the terms of the last set of standard terms sent before performance.
ex: Applying the last shot doctrine, the court held that the buyer's terms on its delivery note governed the contract.

def: Standardised trade terms published by the International Chamber of Commerce that allocate delivery, risk and cost between buyer and seller.
ex: The contract incorporated Incoterms 2020, so the meaning of FCA was not open to argument.

def: The doctrine that a power conferred on a minister may lawfully be exercised by a suitably senior civil servant in the minister's name.
ex: The claimant argued the deportation decision was invalid, but the court applied the Carltona principle because a senior official had signed it.

def: Proven partiality or prejudgment by a decision-maker, as distinct from the mere appearance of bias.
ex: Lacking evidence of actual bias, the claimant relied instead on the fair-minded observer test.

def: A body bound by the Human Rights Act only when performing functions of a public nature, but not when carrying out private acts.
ex: The court considered whether the private care home acted as a hybrid public authority when housing council-funded residents.

def: The latitude domestic courts afford to the executive or Parliament on matters of policy or expertise when assessing compatibility with Convention rights.
ex: On national security assessments, the court accorded the Home Secretary a wide discretionary area of judgment.

def: The heightened intensity of review a court applies where a decision engages fundamental rights such as life or liberty.
ex: Because removal could expose him to torture, the decision attracted anxious scrutiny.

def: The constitutional practice, now placed on a statutory footing, of laying a treaty before Parliament for twenty-one sitting days before ratification.
ex: MPs complained that the trade agreement had been ratified with scant debate despite compliance with the Ponsonby rule.

def: The parliamentary procedure requiring a statutory instrument to be expressly approved by both Houses before it can be made or remain in force.
ex: Because the regulations created new criminal offences, the parent Act required the affirmative procedure.

def: The parliamentary procedure under which a statutory instrument becomes or stays law unless either House annuls it within a set period.
ex: Most of the technical amendments passed under the negative procedure without any debate.

def: Acts of Parliament, as opposed to rules and regulations made under powers those Acts confer.
ex: Since the restriction was contained in primary legislation, the court could only issue a declaration of incompatibility.

def: The convention that Westminster will not normally legislate on devolved matters without the consent of the relevant devolved legislature.
ex: The Supreme Court held the Sewel convention to be a political constraint rather than a legally enforceable rule.

def: A motion by which a devolved legislature agrees to Westminster legislating on a matter within its competence.
ex: The Senedd refused to pass a legislative consent motion, but the bill proceeded regardless.

def: The convention that ministers must publicly support Cabinet decisions or resign.
ex: Collective responsibility was suspended to allow ministers to campaign on opposite sides of the referendum.

def: The legal immunities enjoyed by Parliament and its members, notably freedom of speech in debate, which cannot be questioned in any court.
ex: The MP named the businessman in the Commons, protected by parliamentary privilege from any defamation claim.

def: The authoritative treatise on the law, privileges, procedure and usage of the UK Parliament.
ex: The Clerk cited Erskine May in advising the Speaker that the amendment was out of order.

def: The rule permitting courts to consult ministerial statements in Hansard to interpret ambiguous legislation.
ex: Counsel sought to rely on Pepper v Hart, but the judge found the provision clear enough to need no aid from Hansard.

def: The interpretive presumption that Parliament does not intend to override fundamental rights unless it does so in clear and express terms.
ex: Applying the principle of legality, the court read the general power narrowly so as not to curtail access to justice.

def: An Act regarded as fundamental to the constitutional order and therefore not subject to implied repeal.
ex: The judge treated the Human Rights Act as a constitutional statute that only express words could displace.

def: The doctrine that where two statutes are inconsistent, the later Act impliedly repeals the earlier to the extent of the conflict.
ex: The council argued that the 2019 Act effected an implied repeal of the older licensing provision.

def: The theory that a legislature may bind its successors as to the procedure by which future legislation on a subject must be enacted.
ex: The seminar debated whether a referendum requirement could bind Parliament under a manner and form theory.

def: The statutory duty on public authorities to have due regard to eliminating discrimination and advancing equality of opportunity when exercising their functions.
ex: The library closures were quashed because the council had ignored its public sector equality duty.

def: The obligation on a decision-maker to take reasonable steps to acquaint itself with the information needed to decide properly.
ex: The claimants argued that the minister breached the Tameside duty by failing to consult any clinical evidence.

def: A mistake as to an established and uncontentious fact that played a material part in a decision, rendering it unlawful.
ex: The planning refusal was quashed for a material error of fact about the site's flood zone.

def: A ministerial order amending legislation to remove an incompatibility with Convention rights following a court declaration.
ex: The government laid a remedial order to cure the incompatibility identified by the Supreme Court.

def: The compensation the European Court of Human Rights may award to a victim of a Convention violation.
ex: Strasbourg found a violation but held that the judgment itself constituted just satisfaction.

def: The principle that the Crown is not bound by a statute unless it is named expressly or by necessary implication.
ex: The prison argued Crown immunity exempted it from the local authority's enforcement notice.

def: Damages payable by a state to individuals for a sufficiently serious breach of EU law that caused them loss.
ex: The fishermen recovered Francovich damages after the court found the breach of EU law sufficiently serious.

def: A bill certified by the Speaker as dealing only with taxation or public expenditure, which the Lords cannot delay beyond one month.
ex: Once the Speaker certified it as a money bill, the Lords' objections became largely symbolic.

def: The convention that ministers are accountable to Parliament for the conduct of their departments and their own actions.
ex: Opposition MPs invoked ministerial responsibility in demanding the Home Secretary's resignation over the data leak.

def: The convention that the House of Lords will not reject at second reading a government bill implementing a manifesto commitment.
ex: Peers voiced strong objections but, mindful of the Salisbury convention, allowed the manifesto bill a second reading.

def: A hearing in judicial review at which the questions of permission and the substantive merits are decided together.
ex: Given the urgency, the judge directed a rolled-up hearing for the following week.

def: The agreed window of dates within which a chartered vessel must arrive and tender notice of readiness, failing which the charterer may cancel.
ex: The vessel missed the laycan by two days, entitling the charterers to cancel the fixture.

def: Describing a period during which a time charterer is relieved from paying hire because the vessel cannot work as required, for example through breakdown.
ex: The charterers placed the ship off-hire for the three days spent repairing her main engine.

def: A charterparty clause requiring the owners to give the charterer notice and a grace period to pay late hire before withdrawing the vessel.
ex: The withdrawal was invalid because the owners had not served the notice required by the anti-technicality clause.

def: A berth which, absent abnormal occurrences, a vessel can reach, use and leave without being exposed to danger not avoidable by good seamanship.
ex: The owners claimed damages after the vessel grounded at a berth the charterers had warranted as a safe berth.

def: A non-negotiable bill of lading naming a specific consignee, to whom alone the goods are to be delivered.
ex: Under a straight bill of lading, the carrier must still require production of the original before releasing the cargo.

def: A 1978 UN convention on the carriage of goods by sea, more favourable to cargo interests than the Hague-Visby regime.
ex: Because the cargo was loaded in a contracting state, the shipper argued the Hamburg Rules applied.

def: A 2008 UN convention covering door-to-door carriage of goods wholly or partly by sea, not yet in force.
ex: The lecturer explained that the Rotterdam Rules would extend carrier liability to the inland legs of a multimodal journey.

def: The cap on a carrier's liability for cargo loss calculated per package or unit, or by weight, under the cargo conventions.
ex: The carrier invoked the package limitation, arguing the container rather than each carton counted as one package.

def: The period of carrier responsibility from the moment goods are hooked on for loading until they are unhooked on discharge.
ex: Since the damage occurred in the terminal before loading, it fell outside the tackle to tackle period.

def: A person who voluntarily renders successful assistance to a vessel or property in danger at sea and so becomes entitled to a salvage reward.
ex: The salvor claimed a reward assessed on the salved value of the tanker and her cargo.

def: The Special Compensation P&I Clause, a supplement to Lloyd's Open Form guaranteeing salvors a tariff-based payment for environmental efforts where the traditional award would be inadequate.
ex: With little cargo to save but a serious oil threat, the salvors invoked SCOPIC on day two.

def: The service of towing a vessel, or the charge for it, governed by contract and distinct from salvage.
ex: The tug owners claimed the job had escalated from towage into salvage once the vessel began drifting towards rocks.

def: The International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, which set the rules of navigation and lookout for vessels.
ex: The Admiralty judge apportioned fault after finding both masters had breached the COLREGs.

def: A fund constituted by a shipowner in court, equal to its limit of liability, from which all claims arising from an incident are paid.
ex: Following the collision, the owners constituted a limitation fund in the Admiralty Court.

def: A charter term under which the cost of loading and discharging cargo is borne by the charterer or cargo interests rather than the shipowner.
ex: Because the fixture was free in and out, the stevedores' invoices went to the charterers.

def: The specialist court of the King's Bench Division hearing claims relating to ships, including collision, salvage and actions in rem.
ex: The bank issued proceedings in the Admiralty Court and had the vessel arrested at Southampton.

def: Marine insurance covering physical loss of or damage to the ship itself, including its engines and equipment.
ex: The grounding damage was claimed under the hull and machinery policy, while cargo claims went to the P&I club.

def: A loss where the insured property is destroyed, so damaged as to cease to be a thing of the kind insured, or irretrievably taken from the assured.
ex: The vessel sank in deep water and was accepted by underwriters as an actual total loss.

def: Notice by an assured electing to treat a constructive total loss as a total loss and offering to cede the insured property to the insurer.
ex: Once repair costs exceeded the vessel's value, the owners tendered notice of abandonment to underwriters.

def: A shipowner's right under a time charter to intercept freight owed by sub-charterers or shippers to the charterer in order to recover unpaid hire.
ex: When the charterers stopped paying hire, the owners exercised their lien on sub-freights by notifying the shippers directly.

def: Additional freight payable for carrying goods onward or back when delivery cannot be made at the agreed destination for reasons on the cargo side.
ex: With no receiver collecting the cargo, the carrier returned it to Antwerp and claimed back freight.

def: A bill of lading clause extending the carrier's defences and limits to its servants, agents and subcontractors such as stevedores.
ex: The stevedores escaped full liability because the Himalaya clause gave them the benefit of the package limit.

def: An agreement between P&I clubs, incorporated into NYPE charters, that apportions liability for cargo claims between owners and charterers.
ex: Under the Inter-Club Agreement, the shortage claim was split equally between owners and charterers.

def: The state in which a ship is registered and whose law and jurisdiction govern it on the high seas.
ex: The flag state launched an inquiry into the officers' certification after the casualty.

def: The inspection of foreign ships in a nation's ports to verify compliance with international safety, pollution and labour standards.
ex: Port state control detained the bulk carrier after finding defective lifeboats.

def: Registration of a ship in a state other than that of its owners, typically to benefit from lower taxes, costs or regulatory burdens.
ex: Unions criticised the operator for trading under a flag of convenience to avoid collective agreements.

def: A non-governmental body that sets technical standards for ship construction and maintenance and surveys vessels for compliance.
ex: The buyers insisted the vessel be delivered with her classification society certificates free of recommendations.

def: A charterparty clause providing that the charterer's liability ceases once cargo is loaded, typically balanced by an owners' lien on the cargo.
ex: The charterers relied on the cesser clause to resist the demurrage claim at the discharge port.

def: A contractual provision entitling a master or owner to refuse or deviate from voyages to areas exposed to war, piracy or similar dangers, and allocating the resulting costs.
ex: Citing the war risks clause, the owners refused orders to transit the Red Sea and sailed via the Cape.

def: An intermediary who negotiates charters, sales or purchases of ships between owners and charterers or buyers, usually for a commission.
ex: The shipbroker's recap email became central to deciding whether a binding fixture had been concluded.

def: Personal data relating to criminal convictions, offences or related security measures, which may be processed only under official authority or a specific legal condition.
ex: The recruiter could not run background checks until it identified a condition for processing criminal offence data.

def: A lawful basis for processing where it is necessary to protect someone's life, typically in an emergency.
ex: The hospital relied on vital interests when sharing the unconscious patient's allergy records with paramedics.

def: A lawful basis for processing necessary to perform a task in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller.
ex: The council relied on public task, not consent, when processing residents' data for school admissions.

def: Consent obtained separately for distinct processing purposes rather than bundled into a single agreement.
ex: The regulator criticised the app for failing to obtain granular consent for advertising and analytics.

def: The data protection principle that personal data must be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date, with inaccuracies erased or rectified without delay.
ex: Relying on an old address to issue debt notices breached the accuracy principle.

def: The principle requiring personal data to be processed with appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised access, loss or damage.
ex: Storing unencrypted patient files on a shared drive breached the principle of integrity and confidentiality.

def: The written inventory a controller or processor must keep of its processing operations, purposes, data categories, recipients and retention periods.
ex: The auditors began by requesting the company's records of processing activities.

def: An assessment of whether the law and practice of a destination country would undermine the protection given by a transfer mechanism such as standard contractual clauses.
ex: Before routing HR data to the US vendor, counsel completed a transfer impact assessment on surveillance laws.

def: Mechanisms, such as standard clauses or binding corporate rules, that permit transfers of personal data to a country without an adequacy decision.
ex: Without an adequacy decision, the transfer to Brazil could proceed only with appropriate safeguards in place.

def: A further transfer of personal data from the original recipient in a third country to another recipient, which must maintain equivalent protection.
ex: The contract restricted any onward transfer by the processor to sub-processors outside the EEA.

def: Describing a data subject request plainly made without genuine intent to exercise rights, such as one used to harass, which a controller may refuse or charge for.
ex: The firm refused the former employee's twentieth access request as manifestly unfounded.

def: The GDPR procedure through which the European Data Protection Board ensures supervisory authorities apply the Regulation uniformly, including binding dispute resolution.
ex: Disagreement among regulators over the fine was referred under the consistency mechanism.

def: The EU body of national supervisory authorities that issues guidelines and binding decisions to ensure consistent application of the GDPR.
ex: The company revised its cookie banners after the European Data Protection Board published new guidelines.

def: The UK's independent regulator for data protection and freedom of information.
ex: The breach was reported to the Information Commissioner within seventy-two hours.

def: A formal notice from a regulator requiring an organisation to take, or stop, specified steps to comply with data protection law.
ex: The ICO served an enforcement notice ordering the retailer to stop processing biometric data.

def: A notice from the Information Commissioner requiring a controller or processor to permit an audit of its compliance.
ex: The insurer received an assessment notice and had to grant auditors access to its claims systems.

def: A notice by which the Information Commissioner imposes a monetary penalty for an infringement of data protection law.
ex: After representations, the proposed fine in the penalty notice was reduced substantially.

def: The Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations, the UK rules on electronic marketing, cookies and communications confidentiality.
ex: The text message campaign breached PECR because recipients had never consented.

def: The exemption allowing a business to email marketing to existing customers about similar products, provided they were given a simple chance to refuse.
ex: The charity could not rely on the soft opt-in because its supporters were donors, not customers.

def: The threshold question in a misuse of private information claim, asking whether the claimant objectively expected the information to remain private.
ex: The court held that a suspect has a reasonable expectation of privacy in the fact of a police investigation.

def: The English tort protecting against unjustified disclosure or use of information in which a person has a reasonable expectation of privacy.
ex: The footballer sued the tabloid for misuse of private information over photographs taken at his home.

def: The equitable wrong of using or disclosing information imparted in circumstances importing an obligation of confidence.
ex: The former engineer faced a claim for breach of confidence after taking client lists to a rival.

def: A contract between controllers setting out the purposes, safeguards and responsibilities for sharing personal data between them.
ex: The NHS trust and the university signed a data sharing agreement before exchanging research datasets.

def: A document specifying how long each category of records or personal data is kept and when it is to be deleted.
ex: Under the firm's retention schedule, unsuccessful candidates' CVs are deleted after six months.

def: The exercise of identifying what personal data an organisation holds, where it flows and who has access, as a foundation for compliance.
ex: A thorough data mapping exercise revealed customer data stored on servers no one had documented.

def: The ability to isolate records relating to one individual in a dataset, which indicates the data has not been effectively anonymised.
ex: Because unique postcodes allowed singling out, the regulator treated the dataset as personal data.

def: A test of anonymisation asking whether a reasonably competent person without specialist skills, determined to identify individuals, could do so.
ex: The release failed the motivated intruder test once public social media profiles were combined with the dataset.

def: A legal requirement that certain data be stored or processed within the territory of a particular country.
ex: New data localisation rules forced the bank to build a data centre within the country.

def: A contractual provision in which a party acknowledges that it has not relied on any pre-contractual statement in deciding to enter the agreement.
ex: The buyer's misrepresentation claim foundered because the share purchase agreement contained a robust non-reliance clause.

def: Illegitimate commercial pressure that leaves a party no practical choice but to agree, rendering the resulting contract voidable.
ex: The shipbuilder argued economic duress after the supplier threatened to halt deliveries unless the price was doubled.

def: A shared and fundamental error by both parties about a basic fact that may render a contract void.
ex: Both parties believed the painting was a genuine Constable, so the buyer pleaded common mistake when it proved to be a copy.

def: An error made by one party about the terms of a contract which the other party knows of or ought to know of.
ex: The court refused to hold the seller to a price of ten pounds per tonne, finding a unilateral mistake the buyer must have spotted.

def: A clause providing that a specified remedy, such as service credits, is the only one available for a particular breach.
ex: Because of the sole remedy clause, the customer could claim service credits for the outage but not general damages.

def: A clause stating that a contract may be varied only in writing signed by the parties.
ex: Following Rock Advertising, the landlord relied on the anti-oral variation clause to reject the tenant's claim that a rent reduction had been agreed by phone.

def: Damages designed to put the claimant in the position it would have been in had the contract been properly performed.
ex: Counsel quantified the expectation loss by reference to the profits the distributor would have earned over the remaining term.

def: Damages that restore the claimant to its pre-contract position by compensating expenditure incurred in reliance on the contract.
ex: Unable to prove lost profits, the promoter claimed its reliance loss, chiefly the venue deposits it had paid.

def: Costs a party incurred in performing or preparing to perform a contract that are rendered useless by the other party's breach.
ex: The film company recovered its wasted expenditure on sets and crew after the lead actor walked out.

def: A long-term contract requiring close cooperation and mutual trust, into which courts may imply a duty of good faith.
ex: The franchisee argued that the twenty-year arrangement was a relational contract carrying an implied obligation of fair dealing.

def: A real commercial advantage gained by a promisor which can amount to consideration for a promise to pay more for existing performance.
ex: Applying Williams v Roffey, the court held that avoiding a penalty for late completion was a practical benefit supporting the extra payment.

def: A statement that appears to be a promise but leaves performance entirely at the promisor's discretion and so cannot constitute consideration.
ex: A clause allowing the buyer to order nothing at all was attacked as an illusory promise that made the supply deal unenforceable.

def: A consistent pattern of previous transactions between the parties from which terms may be incorporated into a later contract.
ex: Although no terms were sent with the final order, the haulier's conditions applied through a long course of dealing.

def: The principle that parties who agree in their contract that a certain state of affairs exists are bound by that agreement even if it is untrue.
ex: The bank relied on contractual estoppel, pointing to the client's signed acknowledgement that no advice had been given.

def: The innocent party's clear election to treat a contract as terminated following the other party's repudiatory breach.
ex: The owner's letter withdrawing the vessel was treated as an unequivocal acceptance of repudiation, ending the charter.

def: A supervening event caused by a party's own choice or fault, which does not discharge the contract under the doctrine of frustration.
ex: Having allocated its licences to other vessels, the charterer could not escape the contract because the frustration was self-induced.

def: A change in the law after formation that makes performance of a contract unlawful and may frustrate it.
ex: New sanctions banning exports to the region gave rise to supervening illegality, discharging the remaining deliveries.

def: A provision giving a counterparty rights, such as termination, if ownership or control of the other party changes.
ex: Due diligence flagged a change of control clause in the key supply contract that the acquisition would trigger.

def: An implied term that a contractual discretion must be exercised rationally and in good faith, not arbitrarily or capriciously.
ex: The employee argued that the bonus decision breached the Braganza duty because the committee ignored relevant performance data.

def: An obligation to pursue all reasonable courses of action towards an objective, generally viewed as sitting between reasonable and best endeavours.
ex: The developer undertook to use all reasonable endeavours to obtain planning permission by the end of the year.

def: Performance that departs only trivially from the contract, entitling the performing party to payment subject to a deduction for defects.
ex: The builder recovered the contract price less the cost of minor snagging, as the work amounted to substantial performance.

def: A contractual ceiling on the total amount a party can be required to pay for breach or other liabilities.
ex: The supplier insisted on a liability cap equal to twelve months' fees, with carve-outs for fraud and death or personal injury.

def: The leading case establishing the two limbs of remoteness, under which recoverable loss must arise naturally or have been within the parties' contemplation.
ex: Lost profits on a lucrative side contract failed the second limb of Hadley v Baxendale because the supplier was never told of it.

def: A contractual obligation that must be performed completely before any payment becomes due.
ex: Because the seaman's wages were an entire obligation, his death mid-voyage meant his estate could claim nothing under the contract.

def: The rule that performing, or promising to perform, an obligation already owed is not good consideration for a fresh promise.
ex: Relying on the pre-existing duty rule, the shipowner argued that the crew's promise to finish the voyage could not support extra wages.

def: A contract whose performance is split into separate parts, each with its own payment, so that each part can be enforced independently.
ex: Since the deliveries were priced instalment by instalment, the tribunal treated the arrangement as a divisible contract.

def: One of two or more persons who are each liable in full for the same damage caused by a shared tortious act.
ex: As joint tortfeasors, the contractor and the architect were each liable for the whole loss, leaving them to seek contribution from one another.

def: An unlawful and unreasonable interference with another person's use or enjoyment of land, or rights over it.
ex: Residents sued the speedway operator in private nuisance over the noise from weekend races.

def: An act or omission that endangers or obstructs the public in exercising rights common to all, actionable by an individual only on proof of special damage.
ex: The haulier recovered for public nuisance after a collapsed scaffold blocked the highway and cost it a week of deliveries.

def: The rule imposing strict liability where something likely to cause mischief, brought onto land in a non-natural use, escapes and causes damage.
ex: The neighbour's claim under Rylands v Fletcher failed because storing water in domestic pipes was not a non-natural use of land.

def: Direct and unjustified entry onto, or interference with, land in another's possession, actionable without proof of damage.
ex: The landowner obtained an injunction for trespass to land after the crane's jib repeatedly swung over its airspace.

def: The tort of instituting proceedings against someone maliciously and without reasonable cause, where they end in that person's favour.
ex: After his acquittal, the director sued his former partner for malicious prosecution, alleging the fraud complaint was fabricated.

def: A tort committed by a public officer who exercises power in bad faith, knowing of or reckless as to the harm likely to result.
ex: Depositors brought a claim for misfeasance in public office, alleging the regulator knowingly ignored warnings about the bank.

def: A recognised mental illness, as distinct from ordinary grief or distress, for which damages may be recovered in negligence.
ex: The firefighter's claim for psychiatric injury depended on medical evidence of diagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder.

def: A person who suffers psychiatric harm from witnessing injury to another and who must satisfy strict control mechanisms to recover.
ex: Because she learned of the accident hours later, the mother failed the proximity requirements for a secondary victim.

def: The voluntary undertaking of a task or advisory role towards another which grounds a duty of care, particularly for pure economic loss.
ex: By answering the bank's reference request without a disclaimer, the referee was found to have made an assumption of responsibility.

def: A claim for the lost opportunity of a better outcome, recoverable in some contexts even where the outcome itself cannot be proved on balance.
ex: The client recovered for loss of chance because the solicitor's delay deprived it of a real prospect of settling the action.

def: A modified causation test under which a defendant is liable if its breach contributed more than negligibly to cumulative harm.
ex: Where several dust sources caused the lung disease, the claimant relied on material contribution rather than but-for causation.

def: The relaxed causation rule allowing mesothelioma claimants to sue an employer whose breach materially increased the risk of the disease.
ex: Under the Fairchild exception, the widow succeeded against two former employers even though neither exposure could be proved to be the cause.

def: Damages exceeding compensation, awarded exceptionally to punish oppressive conduct by officials or conduct calculated to make a profit.
ex: The jury awarded exemplary damages against the police after finding officers had fabricated evidence.

def: The qualification to the Bolam standard requiring that a responsible body of professional opinion must also withstand logical analysis.
ex: Applying the Bolitho test, the judge rejected the experts' view because it ignored an obvious and easily avoided risk.

def: A tort arising where a statute intended to protect a class of persons is breached and Parliament intended a civil remedy.
ex: The claim for breach of statutory duty failed because the regulations expressly excluded civil liability.

def: The rejected defence that a claimant cannot complain of a nuisance that existed before they moved to the area.
ex: The motocross club argued coming to the nuisance, but the Supreme Court confirmed it is no defence.

def: Careless advice or information given in a relationship of reliance, giving rise to liability for resulting economic loss.
ex: Investors sued the valuer for negligent misstatement after relying on an inflated report to fund the development.

def: The threefold approach to novel duty situations, asking whether harm was foreseeable, the relationship proximate, and a duty fair, just and reasonable.
ex: Since the claim fell outside any established category, counsel took the court through each limb of the Caparo test.

def: A fixed statutory sum payable to specified close relatives of a person killed by a wrongful act.
ex: In addition to the dependency claim, the widower received the statutory award of bereavement damages under the Fatal Accidents Act.

def: A defamation defence protecting statements made under a duty or interest to a recipient with a corresponding interest, unless made maliciously.
ex: The former employer's reference was protected by qualified privilege because there was no evidence of malice.

def: A complete defamation defence for statements made in specified contexts such as court proceedings or parliamentary debate, regardless of motive.
ex: The witness's allegations in the courtroom attracted absolute privilege, so the libel claim was struck out.

def: A statutory defamation defence for a statement of opinion, indicating its basis, that an honest person could have held on the facts.
ex: The restaurant critic pleaded honest opinion, arguing that her scathing review was plainly a judgement rather than an assertion of fact.

def: The economic tort of knowingly and intentionally persuading a person to break a contract with the claimant.
ex: The record label sued its rival for inducing breach of contract after it lured the singer away mid-term.

def: An economic tort where two or more persons combine to use unlawful acts intending to injure the claimant, causing loss.
ex: The bank pursued the fraudsters for unlawful means conspiracy, alleging they coordinated forged invoices to drain the facility.

def: A duty to ensure that care is taken, which remains with the defendant even if performance is entrusted to an independent contractor.
ex: The council was liable for the swimming instructor's negligence because it owed the pupils a non-delegable duty.

def: The test for vicarious liability asking whether the wrongful act was so closely connected with authorised activities that liability is fair and just.
ex: Applying the close connection test, the court held the supermarket liable for an assault committed by its kiosk attendant.

def: Actuarial tables used in personal injury and fatal accident claims to calculate multipliers for future losses.
ex: Both experts used the Ogden tables, but they disagreed over the claimant's life expectancy and the discount rate.

def: The financial support that dependants would have received from a deceased person, recoverable in a fatal accident claim.
ex: The children's loss of dependency was calculated from their father's net earnings and the services he provided at home.

def: The land that benefits from an easement or restrictive covenant over neighbouring land.
ex: The right of way could not be used to reach a field that formed no part of the dominant tenement.

def: A covenant requiring the covenantor to do something or spend money, the burden of which does not generally run with freehold land.
ex: The obligation to maintain the shared drive was a positive covenant, so it did not bind the later purchaser directly.

def: The largest estate in land, lasting indefinitely and freely transferable, equivalent in practice to freehold ownership.
ex: The trustees held the fee simple absolute in possession of the estate on trust for the beneficiaries.

def: A leasehold estate of fixed or ascertainable duration, recognised as one of the two legal estates in land.
ex: The tenant held a term of years absolute expiring in 2045, with a contractual right to renew.

def: A tenancy terminable by either party at any time, often arising when someone occupies pending negotiation of a lease.
ex: While the lease terms were still being agreed, the retailer traded from the unit under a tenancy at will.

def: A tenancy that continues from one period to the next, such as week to week or month to month, until terminated by notice.
ex: When the fixed term expired and rent continued to be accepted monthly, a periodic tenancy arose.

def: A landlord's forfeiture of a commercial lease by physically retaking empty premises without court proceedings.
ex: After three quarters of unpaid rent, the landlord effected peaceable re-entry by changing the locks overnight.

def: Conduct by a grantor that substantially undermines the purpose for which land or a right was granted, which the law forbids.
ex: Letting the adjoining unit to a rival pharmacy was argued to be a derogation from grant to the existing tenant.

def: Physical presence on registered land that allows a person's proprietary interest to override a later registered disposition.
ex: The wife's beneficial interest bound the lender because she was in actual occupation when the mortgage was granted.

def: Any trust whose property includes land, governed in England and Wales by the Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996.
ex: Because the cohabitants owned the house beneficially, it was held under a trust of land and either could apply for an order for sale.

def: A mortgage term that unfairly prevents or restricts the mortgagor's right to redeem, which equity will strike down.
ex: The option allowing the lender to buy the property outright was void as a clog on the equity of redemption.

def: A mortgagee's right to sell the mortgaged property to recover the debt once the power has arisen and become exercisable.
ex: The lender exercised its power of sale but was criticised for failing to obtain the best price reasonably obtainable.

def: A security interest over property recognised in equity, conferring rights to apply for sale or the appointment of a receiver but no legal estate.
ex: An informal agreement to secure the loan on the house took effect only as an equitable charge.

def: Permission to be on land given without consideration, revocable at any time on reasonable notice.
ex: The neighbour's dog walkers had only a bare licence, which ended as soon as the owner put up a sign.

def: Permission to occupy or use land granted under a contract, conferring personal rather than proprietary rights.
ex: The concession stand operated under a contractual licence, so it had no security of tenure when the agreement ended.

def: A contract to create or convey a legal estate, including an option or right of pre-emption, which takes effect as an equitable interest.
ex: The developer protected its option as an estate contract by entering a notice on the register.

def: A right to an equitable remedy, such as rectification or rescission, that is ancillary to property but weaker than a full equitable interest.
ex: Until the court ordered rectification of the transfer, the seller had only a mere equity in the strip of land.

def: A tenancy binding the parties to it even though the landlord had no legal estate out of which to grant it.
ex: Although the housing association held only a licence, its occupants enjoyed a tenancy by estoppel as against it.

def: A statutory right of a tenant to remain in occupation or to a renewal lease, removable only on specified grounds.
ex: The landlord could not simply evict the café owner because the business tenancy carried security of tenure.

def: A tenant's continued occupation of premises after the contractual term of the lease has expired.
ex: The tenant was holding over under the 1954 Act while terms for a new lease were negotiated.

def: An agreement under which an outgoing tenant guarantees the immediate assignee's performance of the lease covenants.
ex: The landlord consented to the assignment on condition that the outgoing tenant entered into an authorised guarantee agreement.

def: The relationship between the current landlord and current tenant of the same lease, allowing covenants to be enforced between them.
ex: Although they never signed the lease, the assignee and the new landlord were bound to each other through privity of estate.

def: The requirement that a covenant must affect the land itself, rather than merely benefit a person, for it to run with the land.
ex: A promise to pay the vendor's personal debts did not touch and concern the land, so it did not bind successors.

def: The leading case establishing that the burden of a restrictive covenant can bind a successor in title in equity.
ex: Under the rule in Tulk v Moxhay, the buyer of the garden square was bound by the covenant against building on it.

def: A development in which plots are sold subject to common restrictive covenants that are mutually enforceable by all plot owners.
ex: Because the estate was laid out under a building scheme, any homeowner could enforce the ban on business use.

def: An historic estate descending only to the lineal heirs of the original grantee, which can no longer be created in England and Wales.
ex: The family seat had once been held in fee tail, which explained why it passed down the male line for centuries.

def: An equitable right to enjoy property or its income for the duration of a person's life.
ex: Under the will, the widow took a life interest in the house, with the capital passing to the children on her death.

def: An easement implied where land would otherwise be unusable, typically a right of way to an otherwise landlocked plot.
ex: Because the paddock had no access to any road, the court implied an easement of necessity across the seller's retained land.

def: The rule by which quasi-easements that are continuous, apparent and necessary for reasonable enjoyment pass on a sale of part.
ex: The buyer claimed a right to use the drainage pipe under Wheeldon v Burrows, as it was obvious on inspection at the time of sale.

def: The procedure by which landlord and tenant agree to exclude statutory security of tenure from a business lease.
ex: Because the warning notice was served too late, the contracting out was defective and the tenant gained protection.

def: An arrangement in which a seller offers contracts to several buyers at once, agreeing to sell to whoever first exchanges.
ex: The seller's solicitor gave written notice of a contract race, so each buyer's firm rushed to deliver a signed contract and deposit.

def: The HM Land Registry form used to transfer the whole of a registered title.
ex: The seller signed the TR1 before completion so that it could be dated and released once the funds arrived.

def: A conveyance of only a portion of a registered title, requiring a plan and usually new easements and covenants.
ex: The transfer of part of the garden needed a precise plan and fresh rights of drainage for the new plot.

def: A lender's statement of the exact sum needed to pay off a mortgage on a given date.
ex: The seller's solicitor ordered a redemption statement so the existing mortgage could be cleared on completion.

def: A document at least fifteen years old dealing with the whole legal and equitable interest, from which unregistered title is traced.
ex: The 1998 conveyance on sale was accepted as a good root of title for the unregistered farmland.

def: A schedule listing the documents that prove an unregistered title, supplied with copies of those documents.
ex: The seller's solicitors sent an epitome of title tracing ownership from the 1985 conveyance.

def: A traditional summary of the deeds and events showing how unregistered land has passed to the current owner.
ex: Older files still contained a handwritten abstract of title summarising every conveyance since the Victorian era.
