ex: Midstream operators earn steady fees from pipelines regardless of the oil price.

def: A bridge-like overhead frame supporting cranes or equipment that moves loads within a yard or factory.
ex: Automated gantry cranes now unload the vessels around the clock.

def: The introduction of machines to perform work previously done by hand.
ex: Mechanisation of the sorting hall doubled parcel throughput without extra staff.

def: The actual quantity of goods produced or delivered, as opposed to the quantity forecast or stated.
ex: The cargo outturn at discharge was two per cent below the weight on the manifest.

def: The capacity of parts or products to be substituted for one another without modification.
ex: Interchangeability of fasteners across models let the plant cut its parts catalogue in half.

def: The preliminary screening of suppliers to confirm they meet minimum standards before they may bid.
ex: Firms that failed prequalification on financial stability were excluded from the tender.

def: A business supplying provisions and equipment for ships, or the goods it sells.
ex: The port's chandlery restocked the vessel with spares and provisions overnight.

def: A ship or aircraft designed primarily to carry cargo.
ex: The airline converted two ageing passenger jets into freighters to meet e-commerce demand.

def: A party that hires a ship or aircraft from its owner for a voyage or period of time.
ex: Under the contract, the charterer bears the cost of fuel and port fees.

def: A contract to hire all or part of a vessel's capacity for the carriage of goods.
ex: The miner signed a contract of affreightment covering twelve ore shipments a year.

def: An intermediary who negotiates the chartering, sale, or purchase of ships between owners and clients.
ex: Our shipbroker found a suitable vessel within hours of the original charter falling through.

def: The owner who grants a lease of property or equipment to another party.
ex: The container lessor raised daily rates as box shortages spread across Asia.

def: The party who holds and uses property or equipment under a lease.
ex: As lessee, the haulier is responsible for routine maintenance of the trailers.

def: An interruption of work or production, often caused by a fault or industrial action.
ex: An unplanned stoppage at the paint shop cost the plant two hundred vehicles.

def: Loaded with cargo or goods.
ex: Fully laden lorries are barred from the bridge until repairs are complete.

def: Not carrying a load; used especially of a vehicle's weight without cargo.
ex: The trailer's unladen weight left ample payload within the legal limit.

def: Relating to or measured by volume rather than weight.
ex: Bulky but light parcels are charged at their volumetric weight.

def: The cubic content or volume of a space or load.
ex: Planners maximised trailer cubage by redesigning the outer cartons.

def: The amount of goods a business keeps in inventory, or the practice of holding them.
ex: Reducing stockholding released millions in working capital tied up in slow-moving lines.

def: A retailer that regularly carries a particular brand or product for sale.
ex: The brand cut its network of stockists to focus on premium department stores.

def: The right or franchise to distribute a manufacturer's products within a defined territory.
ex: The family firm holds the exclusive distributorship for the pumps across the Gulf.

def: A company granted the right to operate a facility or sell goods within a defined site or territory.
ex: The terminal concessionaire must invest in new cranes under the thirty-year agreement.

def: An official order or requisition for goods, especially one placed with a foreign supplier.
ex: The site manager raised an indent for replacement filters through the central stores.

def: Stock or orders remaining from one period that are transferred into the next.
ex: Heavy carryover from last season left little room for new autumn ranges.

def: The grouping of individual items into a single standard unit, such as a pallet or container, for handling.
ex: Unitisation of loose cartons onto pallets halved loading times at the dock.

def: The inland region served by a port or distribution hub.
ex: Improved rail links extended the port's hinterland deep into central Europe.

def: An officer or manager responsible for supplies, stores, and provisioning.
ex: Acting as the expedition's quartermaster, she tracked every ration and spare part.

def: The supply of food and provisions, especially to ships or large organisations.
ex: Victualling contracts for the cruise fleet are awarded to a single wholesaler each season.

def: The smoothing of production volume and mix over time to avoid peaks and troughs in workload.
ex: Production levelling evened out demand on suppliers and cut overtime at the plant.

def: The degree to which a person, asset, or risk is acceptable for insurance cover.
ex: Repeated flooding has called the insurability of the riverside warehouses into question.

def: Too risky or unpredictable to be covered by an insurer on any commercial terms.
ex: Underwriters warned that coastal properties could become uninsurable within a decade.

def: Covered by a policy whose sum insured is lower than the true value at risk.
ex: After the fire, the bakery discovered it was badly underinsured and received only half its rebuild costs.

def: Describing cover that pays out automatically when a measured trigger, such as wind speed, is reached.
ex: The island government bought parametric hurricane cover so that funds would arrive within days of a storm.

def: The event of a loss or measurement surpassing a specified threshold, used in modelling probability.
ex: The model puts the annual probability of exceedance for a loss of that size at one in two hundred.

def: A cap within a policy that restricts payment for a particular type of loss below the overall limit.
ex: The cyber policy carried a sublimit of only fifty thousand pounds for ransom payments.

def: To transfer part of an insurer's own risk to another insurer in return for a share of the premium.
ex: The carrier chose to reinsure most of its earthquake exposure before the renewal season.

def: To pass on reinsured risk to a further reinsurer.
ex: The reinsurer retroceded a quarter of the catastrophe book to a Bermuda vehicle.

def: A reinsurer that accepts risk passed on by another reinsurer.
ex: Several retrocessionaires withdrew capacity after two years of heavy storm losses.

def: An insurer that transfers part of its risk to a reinsurer.
ex: The reinsurer audited the cedent's claims files before agreeing to renew the treaty.

def: A firm authorised by an insurer to accept risks and issue policies on its behalf.
ex: The Lloyd's syndicate appointed a Canadian coverholder to write small commercial property risks.

def: The condition of holding cover for less than the full value of what is at risk.
ex: Inflation in building costs has driven widespread underinsurance among homeowners.

def: The condition of holding cover worth more than the actual value of the insured item.
ex: Insurers watch for overinsurance because it can create an incentive to stage a loss.

def: The tendency of higher-risk people to buy insurance more readily than lower-risk ones.
ex: Allowing customers to buy cover after diagnosis would expose the fund to severe antiselection.

def: The failure to reveal information that one is obliged to share, especially to an insurer.
ex: The claim was declined for nondisclosure of a previous burglary at the premises.

def: To refuse to accept or honour a contract, claim, or obligation.
ex: The insurer repudiated the policy after finding the applicant had lied about his driving record.

def: The principle of an organisation being owned by and run for the benefit of its members.
ex: The society's board insisted that mutuality kept premiums lower than at listed rivals.

def: Failure to act in accordance with a rule, regulation, or requirement.
ex: Persistent noncompliance with reporting deadlines led to a formal warning from the regulator.

def: A breach of a rule or law, typically a minor one.
ex: The auditors logged each infraction of the gifts policy, however trivial.

def: The checking of a risk model's accuracy by applying it to historical data.
ex: Backtesting revealed that the model had underestimated losses in three of the last five crises.

def: The process of setting insurance prices based on expected losses, expenses, and profit.
ex: Telematics data has transformed ratemaking for young drivers.

def: The act of officially clearing someone of blame or liability.
ex: The inquiry's findings amounted to a full exoneration of the claims manager.

def: A person or organisation that commits a civil wrong causing harm to another.
ex: The insurer pursued the tortfeasor's liability carrier to recover what it had paid out.

def: The extent to which a consequence could reasonably have been anticipated.
ex: The court held that the lack of foreseeability of the flood defeated the negligence claim.

def: In law, the degree to which a loss is too distantly connected to a breach to be recoverable.
ex: The supplier argued that the lost profits failed on grounds of remoteness.

def: Occurring later and interrupting or altering an existing chain of events.
ex: A supervening act by a third party broke the chain of causation between the leak and the damage.

def: The rate or process by which policies end because premiums go unpaid.
ex: Rising living costs pushed lapsation on protection policies to a ten-year high.

def: Serious enough to justify an official penalty or disciplinary action.
ex: Backdating the policy documents was a sanctionable breach of conduct rules.

def: The responsibility or duty to do or prove something.
ex: The onus is on the policyholder to show that the loss falls within the insured perils.

def: Having the quality of proving or helping to prove a fact.
ex: The adjuster's photographs had little probative value because they were taken weeks later.

def: Giving sufficient grounds for legal action.
ex: Counsel advised that the broker's failure to place cover was actionable negligence.

def: Within the jurisdiction of a court or capable of being judicially examined.
ex: The tribunal ruled that the dispute over policy wording was cognisable under the arbitration clause.

def: In a way based on statistical calculation of risk and life expectancy.
ex: The pension scheme's deficit was actuarially assessed at four hundred million pounds.

def: Of damages, fixed in advance by a contract as the sum payable for a specific breach.
ex: The builder faced liquidated damages of five thousand pounds for every week of delay.

def: A factor whose effect cannot be estimated or assessed with any precision.
ex: Political instability remains the great imponderable in the project's risk register.

def: Impossible to predict or anticipate in advance.
ex: The force majeure clause covered only events that were genuinely unforeseeable at signing.

def: Deserving censure or responsibility for a fault or wrong.
ex: The review found no blameworthy conduct by staff, only a flawed process.

def: Conscious disregard of an obvious risk of harm.
ex: The policy excluded losses arising from the director's recklessness.

def: Done deliberately and knowingly rather than by accident.
ex: Cover is void where the damage results from the insured's wilful act.

def: Lack of proper attention that leads to an unintended mistake.
ex: The firm argued that the missed disclosure was a matter of inadvertence, not dishonesty.

def: Involved with others in an unlawful or wrongful activity.
ex: Regulators asked whether senior managers had been complicit in hiding the losses.

def: The quality of being hard to understand or see into, especially regarding information.
ex: The opacity of the fund's derivative positions alarmed its auditors.

def: A body of officials responsible for inspecting and enforcing standards.
ex: The health and safety inspectorate visited the plant after the second accident.

def: The granting of a licence to practise a regulated profession or activity.
ex: Brokers must maintain licensure in each jurisdiction where they place business.

def: The right of a firm authorised in one country to operate across a wider regulated area.
ex: Losing passporting forced the London insurer to open a subsidiary in Luxembourg.

def: The principle that rules or penalties should match the scale and risk of what they govern.
ex: Under the principle of proportionality, smaller insurers face lighter reporting duties.

def: A possible event or outcome, especially an unwelcome one.
ex: The continuity plan was designed to cover every eventuality from cyber attacks to floods.

def: Of a debt, unlikely ever to be paid by the debtor.
ex: The finance team reclassified the broker's balance as uncollectible after six months of silence.

def: The simulation of a crisis or adversarial scenario to test how an organisation would respond.
ex: The board's wargaming of a ransomware attack exposed gaps in the communications plan.

def: The replacement of identifying details in data with artificial identifiers to protect privacy.
ex: Pseudonymisation allowed the insurer to share claims data with researchers lawfully.

def: Not allowed under the rules or law.
ex: Using genetic test results to set premiums is impermissible in several markets.

def: The act of officially forbidding something.
ex: The proscription of the group made any payment to it a criminal offence for the bank.

def: To officially exclude a person or firm from doing something.
ex: The contractor was debarred from public tenders for three years after the bribery finding.

def: The quality of being allowed as a deduction from taxable income.
ex: Advisers questioned the deductibility of regulatory fines in the group's tax return.

def: Not occurring at the same time, so that one process can continue without waiting for another to finish.
ex: Switching to asynchronous processing let the checkout page respond instantly while payments cleared in the background.

def: The process of importing data from various sources into a storage or processing system.
ex: The analytics team rebuilt its ingestion layer after nightly loads began overrunning the morning reports.

def: To remove identifying details from data so that individuals cannot be recognised.
ex: Patient records were anonymised before being shared with the start-up's research partners.

def: The creation of software-based versions of computing resources such as servers, storage or networks.
ex: Virtualisation allowed the bank to retire half its physical servers without losing capacity.

def: The conversion of aspects of life or business activity into quantifiable data that can be tracked and analysed.
ex: The datafication of warehouse work means every pick and pause is now logged and scored.

def: The adoption of digital technologies to transform business processes and models.
ex: The insurer's digitalisation programme moved claims handling from paper forms to a mobile app.

def: Relating to or carried out by a set of rules that a computer follows to solve a problem or make a decision.
ex: Regulators questioned whether the lender's algorithmic credit scoring disadvantaged younger applicants.

def: Each of four equal groups into which a ranked set of data can be divided.
ex: Stores in the bottom quartile for conversion were singled out for a merchandising review.

def: The extent to which findings from one sample or context hold true in others.
ex: Because the pilot ran only in London, the board doubted the generalisability of its results.

def: The degree to which a person can understand how a model arrives at its outputs.
ex: The compliance team chose a simpler model, trading a little accuracy for far greater interpretability.

def: The capacity of an automated system to give understandable reasons for its decisions.
ex: Customers denied a loan are entitled to a degree of explainability under the new rules.

def: The accuracy with which a copy, model or simulation reproduces the original.
ex: The digital twin's fidelity was good enough for engineers to test changes before touching the real plant.

def: The automatic switch to a backup system when the primary one fails.
ex: Automatic failover to the Dublin data centre kept the trading platform online during the outage.

def: To restructure existing code to improve its design without changing what it does.
ex: Before adding new features, the developers spent a sprint refactoring the billing module.

def: To mark a software feature as outdated and discouraged, usually ahead of its removal.
ex: The platform deprecated its old reporting endpoint and gave partners six months to migrate.

def: Software that connects separate applications or systems and lets them exchange data.
ex: A layer of middleware let the retailer's ageing stock system talk to its new e-commerce site.

def: Designed so that new capabilities can be added easily in future.
ex: An extensible architecture meant partners could build their own plug-ins on top of the core product.

def: Organised so that separate units keep control of their own resources while operating as a coordinated whole.
ex: With a federated data model, each region owns its figures but publishes them to a shared catalogue.

def: Relating to techniques for securing information by encoding it so only authorised parties can read it.
ex: Every transaction is signed with a cryptographic key to prove it has not been altered.

def: To assign subjects or items by chance so that results are not skewed by selection.
ex: Shoppers were randomised into two groups to test whether free delivery lifted basket size.

def: The ability to obtain the same results when an analysis is repeated with the same data and methods.
ex: Version-controlled notebooks improved reproducibility, so auditors could rerun every figure in the report.

def: Lasting only a very short time before disappearing or being deleted.
ex: The app's ephemeral messages vanish after a day, which reassured privacy-conscious users.

def: Unable to be changed once created.
ex: Audit logs are written to immutable storage so no one can quietly edit past entries.

def: The ability of a system to handle several tasks or users at the same time.
ex: Ticket sales exposed the site's poor concurrency when thousands of fans logged on at once.

def: The practice of splitting a computing task into parts that run simultaneously.
ex: By exploiting parallelism across forty machines, the bank cut its risk calculation from hours to minutes.

def: The splitting of a large database into smaller pieces spread across several servers.
ex: Sharding the customer table by region solved the slow queries that had plagued peak trading.

def: The division of data or a system into distinct segments for easier management or faster access.
ex: Date-based partitioning meant analysts scanned only last month's sales instead of the whole archive.

def: A departure from what is normal or expected, often regarded as a one-off.
ex: Management dismissed the dip in weekly users as an aberration caused by a bank holiday.

def: The identification of the real-world location of a device or user.
ex: Geolocation lets the delivery app show riders the nearest open restaurants.

def: Relating to the measurement of unique physical features, such as fingerprints or faces, for identification.
ex: The bank replaced passwords with biometric log-in using customers' phone cameras.

def: Drawing conclusions about a wider population from evidence gathered in a sample.
ex: Inferential statistics allowed the pollster to project national preferences from two thousand interviews.

def: Information that describes other data, such as its source, format or date of creation.
ex: Without proper metadata, nobody could tell which version of the sales file was the final one.

def: Accepted as the single authoritative or standard version.
ex: The finance team insisted its ledger be treated as the canonical source of revenue figures.

def: To reproduce the behaviour of one system using another, typically through software.
ex: Testers emulate older handsets to check the app still works for customers who rarely upgrade.

def: Irregular variation in the timing of data packets travelling across a network.
ex: Video calls with the Singapore office kept freezing because of severe network jitter.

def: The unauthorised transfer of data out of an organisation's systems.
ex: Forensic analysts found evidence of exfiltration dating back three months before the breach was announced.

def: To clean data by removing sensitive, harmful or invalid content before it is used or shared.
ex: All form inputs are sanitised to stop attackers slipping malicious code into the database.

def: The removal or blacking out of sensitive information from a document before release.
ex: Heavy redaction of the supplier contract left investors guessing at the real terms.

def: The recorded sequence of clicks a user makes while navigating a website or app.
ex: Clickstream analysis revealed that most shoppers abandoned their baskets on the delivery options page.

def: The identification of a device or user by combining technical attributes rather than using cookies.
ex: Privacy campaigners objected to the ad network's use of fingerprinting to track people across sites.

def: To arrange data systematically in rows and columns.
ex: The survey responses were tabulated by age band before being presented to the board.

def: To gather information from different sources and combine it in an organised way.
ex: An analyst spent the week collating regional sales figures into a single quarterly pack.

def: Able to work with many different systems or platforms without favouring any particular one.
ex: Being cloud-agnostic let the firm switch providers when prices rose.

def: Describing a cloud model in which the provider manages servers automatically and charges only for actual usage.
ex: Moving to a serverless setup slashed the start-up's hosting bill during quiet months.

def: Present but hidden or not yet visible or developed.
ex: The model uncovered latent demand for weekend delivery that no survey had picked up.

def: To convert text, images or other data into numerical arrays that a machine can process.
ex: The search team vectorised every product description so customers could find items by meaning rather than keywords.

def: Capable of being proved wrong by evidence or testing.
ex: The growth team was told to frame each hypothesis so it was falsifiable within a single test cycle.

def: A confident but false or fabricated output produced by an artificial intelligence system.
ex: A hallucination in the chatbot's answer quoted a refund policy the airline had never offered.

def: Describing data that has a meaningful order but no consistent interval between values.
ex: Satisfaction ratings from one to five are ordinal, so averaging them can mislead.

def: Describing data that falls into distinct groups or labels rather than numerical values.
ex: Region and payment method were treated as categorical variables in the churn model.

def: To add labels, notes or explanations to data or a document.
ex: Contractors annotated thousands of call recordings so the model could learn to spot complaints.

def: Relating to data that is linked to specific locations on the earth's surface.
ex: Geospatial analysis showed the chain was opening stores too close to its own branches.

def: To verify the identity of a user or the validity of a request before granting access.
ex: Staff must authenticate with a hardware key before opening the payroll system.

def: Redundant, outdated or badly written material that accumulates in software or systems over time.
ex: The new CTO's first project was clearing years of cruft from the checkout codebase.

def: Impossible to understand or interpret.
ex: Merchants complained that the marketplace's ranking algorithm was entirely inscrutable.

def: Able to be expressed or measured as a number.
ex: Investors wanted quantifiable evidence that the new feature had improved retention.

def: To convert continuous values into a limited number of separate categories or intervals.
ex: Analysts discretised customer age into bands to make the segmentation easier to explain.

def: A simplified representation that hides underlying complexity so a system is easier to use or build on.
ex: A clean abstraction over the payment providers let engineers add a new gateway in a day.

def: A start-up that has reached at least one hundred million dollars in annual recurring revenue.
ex: Investors now care less about unicorn valuations and more about which companies can become centaurs.

def: The stream of investment opportunities that reaches an investor or fund.
ex: The new partner was hired largely for the dealflow she brought from her university network.

def: A single effort by a company or fund to raise a defined amount of capital from investors.
ex: The CEO spent four months on the fundraise and barely touched the product.

def: A direct stake taken by a limited partner alongside a fund in a specific deal, usually on reduced or no fees.
ex: The pension scheme asked for co-investment rights as a condition of its commitment.

def: Start-ups built on substantial scientific or engineering breakthroughs, typically with long development cycles.
ex: Fusion and quantum computing sit at the far end of deeptech, where exits can take fifteen years.

def: A privately held start-up valued at one hundred billion dollars or more.
ex: Only a handful of hectocorns have ever existed, and most are household names.

def: A person or institution holding warrants that entitle it to buy shares at a fixed price.
ex: The venture lender became a warrantholder as part of the debt facility.

def: The disproportionate share of profits awarded to a sponsor or general partner once investors pass a return threshold.
ex: The sponsor's promote kicked in only after investors had cleared an eight per cent return.

def: Describing fund distributions that the general partner may call back from investors for reinvestment.
ex: The early proceeds were recallable, so the LPs could not treat them as true returns yet.

def: The practice of committing more to private funds than the target allocation, anticipating that not all capital will be called at once.
ex: Aggressive overcommitment left the foundation scrambling for cash when calls bunched together.

def: The practice of a large company investing in or partnering with outside start-ups, usually through a dedicated unit.
ex: The carmaker's corporate venturing arm has backed thirty battery start-ups.

def: A prolific individual investor who writes larger and more frequent early cheques than a typical angel.
ex: Landing a well-known superangel gave the round instant credibility with institutional funds.

def: The use of an outsized investment to anoint one company as the presumed winner of its category.
ex: Critics called the two-hundred-million cheque pure kingmaking in a market that barely existed.

def: Describing a right that lets investors sell their shares on the same terms when a founder sells.
ex: Thanks to the co-sale clause, the Series A fund could join the founder's sale to the strategic buyer.

def: A fast-growing start-up widely expected to reach a billion-dollar valuation soon.
ex: The report listed fifty European soonicorns, most of them in fintech.

def: Describing a round raised through notes or similar instruments that defer setting a share price.
ex: An unpriced round let them close quickly without arguing over valuation.

def: Describing a convertible instrument with no ceiling on the valuation at which it converts.
ex: Seasoned angels rarely accept uncapped notes because a big next round leaves them with very little.

def: Describing a company's valuation including the new capital raised in a round.
ex: A ten-million raise at a fifty-million post-money valuation gives the investors a fifth of the company.

def: Describing a company's valuation immediately before new capital is added in a round.
ex: They argued the pre-money figure upward by pointing to three signed enterprise contracts.

def: Describing preferred shares whose holders must choose between their liquidation preference and converting to share pro rata.
ex: Most founder-friendly term sheets specify non-participating preferred.

def: Describing dividends on preferred shares that lapse if not declared, rather than building up as an obligation.
ex: The dividend was non-cumulative, so skipped years cost the company nothing.

def: An obligation on a fund's investors to return distributions so the fund can meet liabilities such as indemnity claims.
ex: The LPs capped the giveback at a quarter of the distributions they had received.

def: A clause that measures a price, return or entitlement by reference to an earlier period or event.
ex: The investors insisted on a lookback so the conversion price would reflect any lower round within a year.

def: Describing a fund clause that suspends new investments if named senior partners leave or stop devoting enough time.
ex: When two founding partners retired, the key-person clause froze the fund's investment period.

def: The imposition of a new vesting schedule on shares a founder already owns outright, usually as a condition of investment.
ex: The lead investor required revesting of half the founders' stakes over four years.

def: A founder or employee who departs, classified as good or bad to determine what happens to their shares.
ex: As a bad leaver he had to sell his shares back at their nominal value.

def: Describing acceleration that vests unvested equity on one event alone, usually the sale of the company.
ex: Acquirers dislike single-trigger acceleration because key staff can walk away fully vested.

def: Describing acceleration that requires both a sale of the company and the holder's subsequent dismissal.
ex: The compromise was double-trigger acceleration for the whole leadership team.

def: Unable to attract investment because of its terms, structure, market or history.
ex: A messy cap table with a departed co-founder holding forty per cent made the company unfundable.

def: To share the lead role in a financing round with another investor, jointly setting terms.
ex: Two London funds agreed to co-lead the Series A, each taking four million.

def: Describing an investment released in instalments, each conditional on agreed milestones.
ex: The biotech accepted a tranched round, with the second half due after phase one results.

def: An employee or other person holding options to acquire shares in a company.
ex: Every optionholder received a letter explaining how the acquisition affected their grants.

def: A single venture financing of one hundred million dollars or more.
ex: Mega-rounds dried up as soon as crossover funds retreated.

def: Earning just enough to cover the founders' frugal living costs, removing the need to raise money to survive.
ex: Being ramen-profitable gave them leverage, because they could walk away from a bad term sheet.

def: Generating substantial growth or revenue relative to the amount of investment consumed.
ex: The most capital-efficient company in the portfolio reached profitability on a single seed round.

def: Describing a company that has not yet generated any sales income.
ex: Valuing a pre-revenue start-up is mostly a judgement about the team and the market.

def: Describing mature private companies, or the rounds that fund them, typically close to a possible exit.
ex: Late-stage valuations fell first when public tech multiples collapsed.

def: Describing an investment view that most peers reject but which may prove correct and highly profitable.
ex: The best returns tend to come from non-consensus bets that look foolish at the time.

def: Describing a further investment by an existing backer in a later round of the same company.
ex: The fund set aside half its capital for follow-on cheques in its winners.

def: Describing committed capital that a fund has not yet called from its investors.
ex: Undrawn commitments gave the firm ample firepower when valuations fell.

def: Describing a clause entitling an investor to any better terms later granted to another investor in the same instrument or fund.
ex: The early angels had most-favoured-nation protection, so they inherited the lower cap given to the later investor.

def: Describing a fund clause that lets a supermajority of investors remove the general partner or end the fund without proving misconduct.
ex: Unhappy with performance, the LPs threatened to invoke the no-fault removal provision.

def: Describing a carry structure in which the manager earns profit share on each exit individually rather than on the fund as a whole.
ex: Under the deal-by-deal waterfall the partners were paid on the first big exit, before losses elsewhere were known.

def: Describing a carry structure that pays the manager only after investors have recovered all contributed capital across the fund.
ex: European LPs generally insist on a whole-fund waterfall to protect their capital.

def: Financed by venture capital investors in exchange for equity.
ex: Venture-backed companies are under pressure to grow far faster than bootstrapped rivals.

def: Describing a round funded mainly by a company's existing investors rather than a new outside lead.
ex: The market read the insider-led round as a sign that no new fund would set a price.

def: The provision of initial capital to launch a new company or a new investment fund.
ex: The family office specialises in the seeding of first-time managers in exchange for a share of fees.

def: Describing an investor's right to buy enough of a new round to maintain its percentage ownership.
ex: The seed fund exercised its pro-rata allocation in the Series A to avoid dilution.

def: Describing an investor or set of terms that leaves founders substantial control and avoids onerous protections.
ex: The firm built its brand on founder-friendly terms and rarely asked for board seats.

def: Contractual protection that adjusts an investor's conversion price so a later cheaper issue does not erode their stake.
ex: The seed investors insisted on broad-based antidilution before they would sign the term sheet.

def: The immediate vesting of some or all unvested shares when a specified event such as an acquisition occurs.
ex: Her contract gave her full acceleration if she was let go within a year of the sale.

def: Describing preferred dividends that, if unpaid in a given period, are lost rather than carried forward.
ex: Most venture deals now use noncumulative dividends, so nothing piles up while the startup reinvests.

def: Describing preferred shares that receive their preference or their converted share of proceeds, but not both.
ex: The founders pushed for nonparticipating preferred so that a modest exit would still reward them.

def: The act of issuing again shares that a company previously bought back or cancelled.
ex: The board approved the reissuance of repurchased shares into the refreshed option pool.

def: The condition of an option being currently capable of being exercised under its grant terms.
ex: Early exercisability let her buy her unvested shares and start the capital gains clock sooner.

def: A party that transfers a right or asset, such as intellectual property, to another party.
ex: As the assignor of the original code, the founder signed over every patent claim to the company.

def: A party to whom a right, contract or asset is legally transferred.
ex: Investors wanted the company named as assignee on every invention the founders had filed.

def: To replace one party to a contract with another so that the new party assumes all rights and obligations.
ex: Before the round closed, the founder's personal supplier contracts were novated to the new company.

def: A person or entity to whom shares or other property are transferred.
ex: The articles required any transferee to sign a deed of adherence to the shareholders' agreement.

def: A person or entity that transfers shares or other property to another.
ex: The transferor must first offer the shares to existing holders under the pre-emption clause.

def: Not permitted to be sold, given or assigned to another person.
ex: Staff options are nontransferable, so she could not gift them to her sister.

def: Describing shares held electronically on a register rather than evidenced by paper certificates.
ex: Moving to uncertificated shares made the secondary sale settle in days instead of weeks.

def: An investor who puts money into a deal alongside a lead investor, usually on the same terms.
ex: The lead brought in two coinvestors to fill the remainder of the allocation.

def: A direct investment made by limited partners or others alongside a fund in a particular company.
ex: The fund offered its largest backers a coinvestment right in the breakout portfolio company.

def: An investor who receives newly issued shares in a private placing.
ex: Each placee had to confirm in writing that they qualified as a sophisticated investor.

def: A person to whom a company has allotted new shares.
ex: The return of allotments listed every allottee and the price they paid per share.

def: Describing securities that holders are entitled to have registered for public sale under registration rights.
ex: The investors' rights agreement defined which shares counted as registrable on a listing.

def: Describing a right letting shareholders include their shares in a registration the company files for itself.
ex: Their piggyback rights meant the early backers could sell alongside the company in its offering.

def: Describing a class of shares that carries economic rights but no right to vote on company matters.
ex: Employees received nonvoting shares so that control stayed with the founding team.

def: Calculated on issued shares only, ignoring options, warrants and convertibles that could add new shares.
ex: On an undiluted basis she owned thirty per cent, but the pool and notes cut that sharply.

def: Able or due to be issued, especially shares that will arise on conversion or exercise.
ex: The fully diluted count included every share issuable under outstanding warrants.

def: To make already vested founder shares subject to a fresh vesting schedule, typically at an investor's request.
ex: The lead asked both founders to revest half their holdings over four years.

def: Describing a cash bonus scheme that tracks share value without issuing any actual equity.
ex: The family firm offered phantom shares so managers could share the upside without diluting the owners.

def: In proportion to each holder's share or entitlement.
ex: Remaining proceeds were distributed ratably among the common and preferred on an as-converted basis.

def: Describing shares that a company may issue but has not yet assigned to any holder.
ex: The directors had authority over enough unallotted shares to complete the option grants.

def: Describing option pool shares reserved for future grants but not yet granted to anyone.
ex: Investors counted the unallocated pool in the pre-money, which quietly shifted dilution onto the founders.

def: Lacking a ready market in which the security can be sold, which justifies a valuation discount.
ex: The valuer applied a hefty discount because the common stock was effectively unmarketable.

def: Describing short-term finance that carries a company until its next priced equity round.
ex: Existing investors put in a bridging note to extend runway by six months.

def: The acquisition of a startup chiefly to recruit its team rather than to obtain its product.
ex: The deal was an acquihire, so the preferred got their money back and the common got jobs.

def: Describing funding, such as grants or debt, that does not require issuing new shares.
ex: They stretched the seed round with nondilutive research grants before raising again.

def: A lender to whom shares are pledged as security for a loan.
ex: The bank, as pledgee, could take the founder's shares if he defaulted on the liquidity loan.

def: Describing a board whose directors serve overlapping terms so only some seats are elected each year.
ex: A staggered board made it far harder for activist shareholders to seize control quickly.

def: Describing directorships or shareholdings that link companies through common board members or cross-ownership.
ex: Regulators questioned the interlocking directorships between the fund and its portfolio companies.

def: Describing authorised shares that the company has not yet issued to anyone.
ex: The charter left ample unissued shares for the conversion of the outstanding notes.

def: The improper practice of dating an option grant earlier than its approval to lock in a lower strike price.
ex: The audit uncovered backdating that had handed executives options already in the money.

def: A holder of shares in a corporation, the usual American term for a shareholder.
ex: The Delaware charter required majority stockholder consent for any new senior series.

def: Describing shares a company has bought back and holds itself rather than cancelling.
ex: The company used treasury shares to satisfy option exercises without a fresh allotment.

def: To infer the value of each share class by working backwards from the price of a recent financing.
ex: The valuer backsolved the common price from the Series A to set the option strike.

def: Describing options or warrants that have been granted but not yet converted into shares.
ex: Unexercised options lapsed ninety days after he left, so he had to find the cash quickly.

def: To increase the size of a funding round beyond the amount originally planned.
ex: Demand was so strong that the founders upsized the round to admit two more funds.

def: Describing shares that the company has a right to buy back, usually unvested founder stock.
ex: Until his cliff passed, all of his restricted stock remained repurchasable at cost.

def: The extent to which a contractual right or security may be legally transferred to another party.
ex: The acquirer checked the assignability of every key licence before agreeing the price.

def: Not capable of being legally transferred to another party.
ex: The pro rata right was unassignable, so the angel could not sell it to a larger fund.

def: The quality of a share that entitles its holder or issuer to have it bought back on agreed terms.
ex: Redeemability gave the fund a route to its money if no exit materialised within seven years.

def: Describing a convertible note or preferred share that has not yet turned into common equity.
ex: Several unconverted notes sat on the books, ready to swamp the cap table at the next round.

def: Describing an option that cannot yet be exercised because conditions such as vesting are unmet.
ex: Most of her grant was still unexercisable when the acquisition offer arrived.

def: A founder who grows a company on revenue and savings without taking outside investment.
ex: As a lifelong bootstrapper, she still owned every share when the buyer called.

def: Ending or lasting for the same period, such as an option term matching a service agreement.
ex: The adviser's vesting was coterminous with her consulting contract, so both ended together.

def: Growing more slowly than the input that drives it, so each additional unit yields less.
ex: Support costs stayed sublinear relative to revenue thanks to the self-service help centre.

def: A structured review held after a launch or failure to establish what went wrong and why.
ex: The postmortem traced the outage to a single untested configuration change.

def: A startup that generates just enough revenue to survive but has no realistic prospect of growth or further funding.
ex: After two flat years the investors quietly wrote the company off as a zombie.

def: The practice of adding staff faster than revenue or workload justifies, often after a large funding round.
ex: Overhiring in 2021 left the firm with a payroll its pipeline could not support.

def: The degree to which content or a product feature is designed to be passed on by users to others.
ex: Adding a one-tap export to stories transformed the shareability of the year-end summary.

def: Spreading from person to person through imitation and cultural transmission in the manner of a meme.
ex: The product's memetic launch video did more for sign-ups than the entire paid budget.

def: An exceptionally devoted user who engages heavily, pays more and actively promotes a product.
ex: We built the beta programme around two hundred superfans who answered every survey.

def: A secondary metric monitored during an experiment to ensure an improvement does not cause unacceptable harm elsewhere.
ex: The new checkout lifted conversion, but the refund guardrail turned red within a week.

def: Describing the portion of a market that a company's product could realistically serve and sell to.
ex: Expanding into Spanish trebled our addressable market overnight.

def: An early customer who has an urgent problem, will buy an unfinished product and champions it to others.
ex: Our first earlyvangelist cobbled together a spreadsheet workaround before we had even shipped.

def: The point at which a growth curve changes direction or rate, often marking the start of rapid scaling.
ex: The integration with the accounting platform was the inflexion that took us from linear to exponential.

def: Relating to customers larger than small businesses but smaller than large enterprises.
ex: Our midmarket accounts churn less than small firms yet close far faster than enterprises.

def: Involving intensive personal attention from sales or support staff for each customer.
ex: High-touch onboarding works for six-figure contracts but bankrupts a cheap plan.

def: Describing a premium, highly personalised level of service given to important customers.
ex: Enterprise clients receive white-glove migration with a dedicated engineer.

def: Testing demand for an idea with a cheap simulation before building even a basic prototype.
ex: Pretotyping with a fake order button told us within days that nobody wanted the add-on.

def: A manipulative design tactic that words the decline option so as to make users feel guilty for refusing.
ex: The regulator singled out the confirmshaming on the cancellation screen.

def: A campaign or process aimed at persuading lapsed customers to return.
ex: Our winback offer recovered nearly a tenth of last quarter's cancellations.

def: The return of a previously inactive user to regular use, tracked as a distinct growth input.
ex: Resurrection now accounts for more weekly actives than brand-new sign-ups.

def: How easily users can find a feature or how easily a product can be found by potential customers.
ex: Moving the feature into the main menu fixed a discoverability problem, not a demand problem.

def: The ease with which information or content within a product can be located by users.
ex: Better tagging improved findability so much that search queries dropped by half.

def: Tailoring a general product to the specific workflows and needs of a single industry.
ex: Verticalisation for dental clinics gave us pricing power the generic version never had.

def: Testing several variables at once to measure how their combinations affect an outcome.
ex: A multivariate test of headline, image and button colour needed far more traffic than we had.

def: To promote a product or idea with missionary zeal, especially to developers or early users.
ex: Our first hire spent her days evangelising the API at meet-ups.

def: The tendency to keep adding features until a product becomes complicated and loses focus.
ex: Featuritis crept in once every enterprise client could demand a custom toggle.

def: Software overloaded with unnecessary features that consume resources and confuse users.
ex: Reviewers dismissed the new release as bloatware that took twice as long to load.

def: To invest more engineering effort or capacity in a product than current demand warrants.
ex: We overbuilt the reporting suite before learning that customers only exported to spreadsheets.

def: The degree to which a decision can be undone cheaply, which determines how cautiously it should be made.
ex: Given its reversibility, the pricing test could ship without a board discussion.

def: Collaboration between competing businesses in areas where cooperation benefits both.
ex: The rival booking apps entered a coopetition deal to share a payments rail.

def: Operating at a scale able to serve hundreds of millions of users with rapidly expandable infrastructure.
ex: Only hyperscale platforms can absorb that kind of traffic spike without warning.

def: To remove the constraint that limits the throughput of a process or system.
ex: Automating contract review debottlenecked the sales cycle almost immediately.

def: The level that a curve, such as cohort retention, approaches but flattens towards over time.
ex: A retention curve with a healthy asymptote is the clearest sign of product-market fit.

def: Any of ten equal groups into which a population is divided according to a measured value.
ex: The top decile of users generates over half of all shared content.

def: A user or customer who spends vastly more than average and accounts for a large share of revenue.
ex: Losing a single whale wiped out the month's revenue growth.

def: A user who consumes content on a platform regularly but rarely posts or contributes.
ex: Most community members are lurkers, so we redesigned the feed to nudge a first reply.

def: An easy entry point that eases new users into a product before they adopt its fuller capabilities.
ex: The free template gallery serves as an onramp to the paid design suite.

def: Revenue from prepaid services or credits that customers pay for but never use.
ex: Annual gym-style plans rely heavily on breakage to stay profitable.

def: Freely available without requiring users to register, pay or supply contact details.
ex: Making the research report ungated tripled its reach but halved our lead capture.

def: Accessible only to users who have paid, with the content or feature locked behind a payment barrier.
ex: Keeping offline mode paywalled became the main driver of upgrades.

def: The extent to which a product is woven into a customer's daily workflows and systems, making removal costly.
ex: Deep embeddedness in payroll explains why their churn is almost zero.

def: The act of a user closing or suspending an account, tracked as a signal of dissatisfaction.
ex: Deactivations spiked the week the redesign removed the classic layout.

def: Efforts to bring disengaged users back to active use of a product.
ex: The re-engagement push reminded dormant users of unfinished projects.

def: Intensive guidance given to customers to help them adopt or succeed with a product.
ex: Without weeks of handholding, most clients never finished setting up integrations.

def: Resourcefulness in achieving results quickly with minimal money and improvised methods.
ex: Investors loved the scrappiness of a team that landed its first customers through cold DMs.

def: The breaking of a product or market into very small, independent units that can be sold or consumed separately.
ex: The atomisation of the album into single tracks reshaped music economics.

def: A release sent to a small fraction of users first so that problems surface before a full rollout.
ex: The canary caught a crash on older phones before it reached the wider user base.

def: Exposing a new feature to controlled groups of users in stages to measure its impact.
ex: Flighting the new search ranking to five per cent of traffic revealed a drop in clicks.

def: A mechanism that lets a team instantly disable a feature in production if it misbehaves.
ex: Within minutes of the billing error, the engineer flipped the killswitch.

def: Letting existing customers keep their old price or terms after new ones are introduced.
ex: Grandfathering early users on the old price softened the backlash to the rise.

def: Describing an advertising audience built from people whose traits resemble a company's best existing customers.
ex: Lookalike audiences seeded from our top payers halved the cost per trial.

def: An algorithmic system that suggests items to users based on their behaviour and that of similar users.
ex: Retuning the recommender lifted session length more than any feature launch that year.

def: Bringing relevant content or features prominently to a user's attention at the right moment.
ex: Smarter surfacing of shared folders drove a jump in collaboration.

def: The gradual degradation of a platform as it shifts value from users to business customers and then to itself.
ex: Critics called the extra ads and pricier tiers a textbook case of enshittification.

def: A platform owner building a feature that replicates a popular third-party app, undermining it.
ex: The note-taking startup never recovered from its sherlocking by the operating system update.

def: A narrow initial product or use case that gains entry to a market before a company expands into adjacent offerings.
ex: Invoicing was the wedge; full accounting came two years later.

def: Describing customers given more performance than they need or will pay for, leaving them open to simpler rivals.
ex: Overserved small firms were happy to swap the enterprise suite for a cheaper app.

def: The situation in which potential customers go without any solution because existing ones are too costly or complex.
ex: Competing against nonconsumption meant our real rival was a paper notebook.

def: Spending disproportionate time debating trivial details while important decisions receive little scrutiny.
ex: Forty minutes on the button colour was pure bikeshedding while pricing went undiscussed.

def: The formal phasing out of a feature or interface, with users warned to migrate before it is removed.
ex: The deprecation notice gave developers six months to move to the new endpoint.

def: Capable of being turned into a reliable source of revenue.
ex: Investors doubted that casual teenage users were a monetisable audience.

def: The quality in an argument or story that moves an audience by appealing to their emotions.
ex: Her opening story about her grandmother's clinic gave the pitch real pathos.

def: The appeal to reason, evidence and logical structure within a persuasive argument.
ex: The cohort data supplied the logos that the founder's passion alone could not.

def: The opportune moment at which a message or argument will be most persuasive.
ex: Pitching a grid-storage start-up the week after the blackout was a masterclass in kairos.

def: An argument in which one premise is left unstated because the audience is expected to supply it.
ex: "Every bank will need this, and we are the only compliant option" is an enthymeme that leaves the conclusion to the investor.

def: The concluding part of a speech, designed to sum up and inspire the audience.
ex: He saved the vision of a fossil-free fleet for his peroration.

def: The opening section of a speech or argument, intended to win the audience's attention and goodwill.
ex: Her exordium was a single startling statistic followed by silence.

def: The deliberate repetition of a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses for rhetorical effect.
ex: The founder used anaphora, beginning each line with "Imagine a world where".

def: The repetition of a word or phrase at the end of successive clauses or sentences.
ex: Ending three sentences with "in under a minute" was an epistrophe the room remembered.

def: A rhetorical series of three parallel words, phrases or clauses.
ex: "Faster, cheaper, safer" was the tricolon that anchored the whole deck.

def: A figure of speech in which the order of terms in the first clause is reversed in the second.
ex: She closed with a chiasmus: "We don't chase the market; we make the market chase us."

def: A short moral story or fable used to illustrate a point.
ex: He opened with an apologue about two farmers and a broken well.

def: The final part of a narrative in which the strands are drawn together and resolved.
ex: The traction slide served as the denouement of the customer's story.

def: The central theme or thread that connects every part of a story or presentation.
ex: Trust in the supply chain was the throughline from the problem slide to the ask.

def: A one-sentence summary capturing the core premise and hook of a story or venture.
ex: Before refining the deck, the accelerator made every founder perfect their logline.

def: The use of explicit verbal cues to tell an audience where a presentation is going next.
ex: Clear signposting kept the partners oriented through a dense financial section.

def: A figure of speech in which a part stands for the whole or the whole for a part.
ex: Calling the sales team "boots on the ground" is a synecdoche investors hear constantly.

def: A short illustrative story or example used to support an argument or moral point.
ex: The case of the Leeds pharmacy became the exemplum she used in every meeting.

def: A later reference in a talk to an image or line introduced earlier, creating cohesion and recognition.
ex: His closing callback to the leaking bucket drew knowing nods from the panel.

def: The rhetorical device of anticipating an objection and addressing it before it is raised.
ex: Through prolepsis, she dealt with competition concerns before anyone could ask.

def: Drawing attention to something by claiming not to mention it.
ex: "I won't dwell on our 300 per cent growth" was a cheeky piece of apophasis.

def: Understatement that affirms something by negating its opposite.
ex: Describing a tenfold return as "not a bad outcome" is classic investor litotes.

def: A figure in which one word governs two others in different senses.
ex: "We closed the round and the gap on our rivals" was a zeugma that landed well.

def: The deliberate use of many conjunctions in close succession for rhythmic or cumulative effect.
ex: Her polysyndeton, "and faster and cheaper and greener", built a sense of momentum.

def: The omission of conjunctions between clauses to create a brisk, forceful rhythm.
ex: "We built it, shipped it, sold it" uses asyndeton to suggest relentless execution.

def: The patterns of rhythm, stress and intonation in spoken delivery.
ex: A voice coach worked on the CEO's prosody so the key numbers rang out.

def: The skill of clear, expressive speech, especially in articulation and pronunciation.
ex: His elocution was polished, but the substance of his pitch was thin.

def: A sudden reversal of fortune or circumstances that turns a narrative.
ex: The pivot after the failed pilot was the peripeteia of the founding story.

def: The moment in a story when a character makes a critical discovery or recognition.
ex: Her anagnorisis came when she realised customers were using the tool for something else entirely.

def: A conventional theme or line of argument that speakers draw on repeatedly.
ex: The garage origin story has become a tired topos of start-up pitches.

def: In rhetoric, the central point of disagreement on which an argument turns.
ex: Finding the stasis early showed the debate was about timing, not the technology.

def: The construction of a compelling, often embellished story around a founder or company.
ex: Seasoned investors tend to discount the mythmaking in founding stories.

def: A person skilled at telling stories in an engaging way.
ex: A natural raconteur, he had the partners laughing within minutes.

def: A characteristic routine or gimmick a presenter relies on.
ex: His schtick of tearing up a paper invoice on stage had worn thin by the third pitch.

def: Presenting a fact or problem from a different perspective to change how it is perceived.
ex: Her reframing of the churn figure as a pricing signal won the room over.

def: The deliberate effort to win favour by flattery or by aligning oneself with another's views.
ex: Name-dropping the partner's past deals came across as clumsy ingratiation.

def: Capable of being won over by argument or appeal.
ex: The associate seemed persuadable, but the senior partner had already made up her mind.

def: To present data or events in the form of a story.
ex: The analyst learned to narrativise the quarterly numbers for the board.

def: The archetypal hero's journey narrative structure shared across many stories.
ex: Most founder stories follow the monomyth, from ordinary job to call to adventure.

def: The device of posing a question and immediately answering it oneself.
ex: "Why now? Because regulation changed in March" is hypophora at its most efficient.

def: The repetition of words in successive clauses in reverse order.
ex: "We don't sell software to clinics; we bring clinics to software" is a neat antimetabole.

def: Breaking off a sentence deliberately, leaving the audience to complete the thought.
ex: "And if we don't fix this by 2030, well," he said, letting the aposiopesis hang.

def: The repetition of a word or phrase with a few words in between for emphasis.
ex: "Speed, real speed, is our advantage" uses diacope to drive the point home.

def: A series of clauses of equal length and parallel structure.
ex: The tagline's isocolon gave it a rhythm investors could repeat.

def: Skill in managing the theatrical aspects of a presentation, such as movement, timing and props.
ex: Her stagecraft turned a dry hardware demo into the highlight of demo day.

def: Glossing over a difficult point with vague assertion rather than evidence.
ex: The partner flagged a lot of handwaving around customer acquisition costs.

def: Asserting more traction, capability or certainty than the evidence supports.
ex: Overclaiming on the pipeline slide cost the founders their credibility in diligence.

def: The craft of dramatic structure and staging applied to a performance or presentation.
ex: The launch event's dramaturgy built steadily to the price reveal.

def: An abrupt, often ludicrous drop in style or mood from the lofty to the trivial.
ex: After promising to end loneliness, revealing a calendar app felt like bathos.

def: Describing speech that is pompously full, rich and imposing in tone.
ex: His orotund delivery suited a keynote but grated in a small partner meeting.

def: To deliver a speech at length or conclude it with a rhetorical flourish.
ex: She perorated on the future of food for ten minutes before showing a single number.

def: A formal expression of high praise.
ex: The reference call turned into an encomium for the founder's work ethic.

def: Planning a presentation or narrative as a sequence of sketched frames before building it.
ex: An afternoon of storyboarding on sticky notes fixed the deck's muddled order.

def: Describing risk specific to a single company or sector that can be reduced through diversification.
ex: Holding forty stocks rather than four strips out most of the unsystematic risk.

def: Able to be eliminated by spreading investments across many unrelated holdings.
ex: Markets do not reward you for bearing diversifiable risk, so a concentrated portfolio needs a strong thesis.

def: The property whereby the average outcome across many investors equals the average outcome a single investor experiences over time.
ex: Advocates of ergodicity economics warn that a bet with positive expected value can still ruin an individual who keeps repeating it.

def: Buying and selling investments so frequently that costs and poor timing erode returns.
ex: The study found that overtrading cost retail accounts nearly two percentage points a year.

def: The automatic shifting of a pension fund from growth assets into lower-risk assets as the saver nears retirement.
ex: Lifestyling moved his pot into gilts just before bond yields spiked, which hit him hard.

def: The gradual reduction of a portfolio's exposure to volatile or uncertain assets.
ex: The scheme began derisking once its funding level crossed 105 per cent.

def: A reduction in the degree to which the returns of two assets move together.
ex: The sudden decorrelation of gold and real yields puzzled the macro desk.

def: Holding less of an asset class than a target or benchmark prescribes.
ex: The investment committee flagged a persistent underallocation to private credit relative to policy.

def: In performance analysis, the effect whereby only funds or firms that survived remain in the data, making past results look better than they were.
ex: Once you correct for survivorship, the average active fund's track record looks far less impressive.

def: A company able to reinvest its earnings at high returns for many years, steadily growing its intrinsic value.
ex: He refuses to sell a genuine compounder just because the valuation looks stretched.

def: An investment that rises to ten times its original purchase price.
ex: The obscure small-cap she bought in 2015 turned into a tenbagger.

def: An investor who selects individual shares on their merits rather than buying the whole market.
ex: Even celebrated stockpickers struggle to beat the index once fees are deducted.

def: Capable of being offset with a derivative or an opposing position.
ex: Currency exposure is cheaply hedgeable, whereas political risk largely is not.

def: A measure of dispersion that counts only returns falling below a chosen threshold.
ex: Using semivariance instead of standard deviation stops upside surprises being penalised as risk.

def: An asset added to a portfolio chiefly because its returns behave differently from existing holdings.
ex: Trend-following funds proved a valuable diversifier during the 2022 sell-off.

def: Combining exposure to several return drivers, such as value, momentum and quality, within one strategy.
ex: The pension switched to a multifactor equity mandate to smooth out the swings of any single style.

def: Holding so many positions that additional ones add cost and complexity without meaningfully reducing risk.
ex: Owning nine overlapping global funds is a classic case of overdiversification.

def: Too concentrated in a few holdings to have shed company-specific risk.
ex: Employees with half their savings in their employer's shares are dangerously underdiversified.

def: A long-dated bond issued by the German federal government, widely used as the eurozone benchmark.
ex: Italian spreads over the bund widened sharply after the budget announcement.

def: Backed by assets worth more than the debt they secure, giving lenders a buffer against losses.
ex: The senior tranche was heavily overcollateralised, which earned it a top rating.

def: Describing a data series whose statistical properties, such as its mean or variance, shift over time.
ex: Because asset correlations are nonstationary, last decade's optimal mix may fail in the next.

def: Non-standard derivatives with complex payoff features, such as barrier or digital options.
ex: The bank's exotics desk lost heavily when the underlying index broke through the barrier levels.

def: Describing a fund free to invest without reference to a benchmark or fixed asset limits.
ex: Unconstrained bond funds can go short duration when they expect rates to rise.

def: Trading at a price that does not reflect the asset's fundamental value.
ex: The activist argued the conglomerate's shares were mispriced because the market ignored its property portfolio.

def: One of five equal groups into which a ranked universe of securities is divided.
ex: Stocks in the cheapest quintile outperformed the most expensive by four points a year.

def: To cap extreme values in a data set at a chosen percentile so that outliers have less influence.
ex: The analysts winsorise valuation ratios at the first and ninety-ninth percentiles before ranking stocks.

def: A distinct portfolio within an umbrella fund, with its own objective and segregated assets.
ex: Each subfund is ring-fenced, so losses in one cannot spill over into another.

def: Having returns that show no consistent relationship with those of another asset.
ex: Truly uncorrelated return streams are rare, and they grow rarer still in a crisis.

def: Tending to move in the opposite direction to another asset.
ex: Stocks and government bonds were anticorrelated for two decades, which is why the sixty-forty portfolio worked so well.

def: The statistical independence of one factor's or strategy's returns from another's.
ex: The quant team tested each new signal for orthogonality to existing factors before adding it.

def: One of three equal groups into which a ranked set of securities is divided.
ex: Only firms in the top quality tercile made it into the portfolio.

def: Treated as carrying no default risk, typically referring to short-dated government debt used as a pricing baseline.
ex: The strategy's returns are quoted as an excess over the riskless rate.

def: To increase a holding's proportion within a portfolio.
ex: The strategist advised clients to upweight Japanese equities ahead of the governance reforms.

def: To reduce a holding's proportion within a portfolio.
ex: We downweighted high-yield credit as spreads tightened to historic lows.

def: To adjust the proportions of the holdings in a portfolio or index.
ex: The index provider reweights its constituents every quarter.

def: The degree to which a market or asset can practically be bought in size, given its liquidity, access and restrictions.
ex: Capital controls cast doubt on the investability of the country's onshore bond market.

def: Impossible or impractical to offset with a derivative or an opposing position.
ex: Regulatory risk in the sector is essentially unhedgeable, so the fund caps its exposure.

def: Describing a pension scheme whose assets exceed the present value of its liabilities.
ex: Now overfunded, the scheme is exploring a buyout with an insurer.

def: A bond whose coupon and principal are adjusted in line with inflation.
ex: Pension funds bought linkers to hedge their inflation-sensitive liabilities.

def: Fixed-coupon government bonds that are not linked to inflation, as distinct from index-linked issues.
ex: The gap between linker and conventional yields implies the market expects inflation of around three per cent.

def: Describing a bond portfolio whose maturities are spread evenly across successive years.
ex: A laddered portfolio of gilts gives him a predictable lump of cash every spring.

def: A fall in a security's price relative to comparable assets or to its estimated fair value.
ex: The cheapening of thirty-year bonds versus swaps attracted relative-value funds.

def: A rise in a security's price relative to comparable assets or to its estimated fair value.
ex: Heavy pension demand caused a sharp richening at the long end of the curve.

def: Combining quantitative screening models with traditional fundamental company analysis.
ex: The firm rebranded its process as quantamental after layering machine-learning screens onto analyst research.

def: Describing a distribution with thinner tails and fewer extreme outcomes than a normal distribution.
ex: Unlike most equity returns, the strategy's monthly payoffs were platykurtic.

def: A preliminary prospectus issued before pricing, containing most offer details except the final price and size.

def: The phase before a deal launches in which banks gauge investor appetite and likely valuation.

def: The practice of subscribing for new shares purely to sell them quickly for a profit once trading opens.

def: The return of a company's shares to trading on an exchange after a period off the market.

def: To issue a further amount of an existing bond line on the same terms.

def: A dollar-denominated bond issued in the United States by a foreign borrower.

def: An issuer, such as a development bank, owned by several governments and operating across borders.

def: A German covered bond backed by a ring-fenced pool of mortgages or public-sector loans.

def: To allocate more securities than the base deal size, creating a short position covered later.

def: The shares left untaken by existing holders in a rights issue, later placed with other investors.

def: Describing shares trading without the entitlement to take part in a current rights issue.

def: Describing a loan or issue arranged and distributed by a group of banks rather than one lender.

def: A situation in which investor orders fall short of the number of securities offered.

def: The company whose shares are the subject of a takeover offer.

def: The party making a takeover bid or an offer of securities.

def: The transfer by a shareholder of rights to new shares to another person before they are taken up.

def: Describing an issue whose proceeds are guaranteed by banks that will buy any unsold securities.

def: Long-term financing raised to repay a short-term bridge facility.

def: Describing a company or security that has little or no trading history in public markets.

def: The bank that structures a loan or bond and organises the group that funds or sells it.

def: Describing depositary receipts created by a bank without the participation of the underlying company.

def: To transfer or give up an entitlement to new shares in a rights issue.

def: The small residual equity stake left with shareholders after a leveraged recapitalisation or buyout.

def: A single issue of securities drawn from an existing shelf registration.

def: Describing an exceptionally large bond or equity deal relative to normal market size.
ex: The jumbo financing for the merger was split across five currencies.

def: Describing an issuer's first ever bond or offering in a particular market.

def: Trading ahead of a known pending order or deal to profit from its expected price impact.

def: A firm that stands ready to quote buy and sell prices in a security to provide liquidity.

def: To close out all positions so that one holds no net exposure.

def: Confirmation from a lender that shares can be borrowed before a short sale is placed.
ex: Compliance blocked the order because nobody had obtained a locate.

def: The curved pattern formed when implied volatility is plotted against strike price.

def: To trade against a prevailing move in the expectation that it will reverse.
ex: Seasoned traders faded the opening spike and were rewarded by lunchtime.

def: To set an order so that its price automatically tracks a reference such as the midpoint or best bid.

def: An order that simultaneously takes liquidity across several price levels or venues.

def: Describing a trading venue that displays its orders publicly before execution.

def: A reported trade appearing on the consolidated tape.
ex: A huge print at the offer suggested someone was building a position.

def: Describing a market where sellers dominate and prices are being pushed lower.

def: Describing a market in which the best bid is higher than the best offer, usually across separate venues.

def: Describing a market in which the best bid and best offer are at the same price.

def: To cancel an executed trade after the fact, typically because it was clearly erroneous.

def: The whole-number part of a price, which traders omit when quoting the decimals.

def: The smallest standard price increment in a currency pair, usually the fourth decimal place.

def: The execution of all or part of an order at a given price.

def: A single tranche or standard size of a trade, often a large round amount.

def: A period of sideways trading after a decline, seen as a sign that selling pressure is exhausted.

def: The simultaneous expiry of several classes of futures and options, typically causing volume spikes.

def: The rate at which an option's delta changes with the passage of time.

def: The minimum permitted price movement of an instrument.

def: Describing a limit order sitting in the book and waiting to be executed.

def: Describing securities that are available to be lent out to short sellers.

def: A clearing member that guarantees and settles trades on behalf of its clients.

def: The post-trade step in which counterparties confirm the details of an executed trade before settlement.

def: An auction or internal match in which buy and sell orders are executed against each other at a single price.

def: Holding a position that is losing money because the market has moved against it.

def: To sell immediately at a counterparty's quoted bid price.

def: The best bid and best offer currently available in a market.

def: Describing the portion of a purchased loan's expected cash flows above its carrying value that is recognised as income over time.

def: To adjust figures from companies with different financial year-ends so that they cover the same calendar period.

def: The conversion of a figure for a shorter period into its equivalent over a full year.

def: Describing a cost or price spread evenly in present-value terms over the whole life of an asset.

def: Describing a valuation input that cannot be drawn from market data and must be estimated by the valuer.

def: Describing a property let at a rent above its current open-market rental value.

def: To type a fixed number into a spreadsheet cell instead of linking it to a formula or input.

def: To test how a model's output changes when one or more key assumptions are varied.

def: The proportion of additional revenue that converts into additional operating profit.

def: A cost or revenue loss that arises from combining or separating businesses, offsetting expected synergies.

def: A loop in a financial model where a calculation depends, directly or indirectly, on its own result.

def: To strip the effect of borrowing out of a risk measure, or to reduce a company's debt relative to its earnings.

def: Describing an analysis that values a holding by its proportionate share of the underlying companies' figures.

def: Calculated as if all options, warrants and convertible securities had been turned into ordinary shares.
