def: The practice of planning and communicating which product capabilities a team intends to build and in what order over time.
ex: Quarterly roadmapping sessions forced the team to admit they had promised three launches in one month.

def: The regular review of a product backlog to clarify, estimate and reorder items before they are scheduled for work.
ex: After an hour of grooming, half the stale tickets had been closed outright.

def: The point at which a new user first experiences a product's core value, used as a key early-stage metric.
ex: Activation jumped once new users were prompted to invite a colleague on day one.

def: A short, time-limited piece of investigative work done to reduce technical uncertainty before committing to an estimate.
ex: We scheduled a two-day spike to see whether the legacy API could handle real-time updates.

def: An urgent patch released outside the normal schedule to correct a serious defect in live software.
ex: A hotfix went out within the hour after customers reported being charged twice.

def: A chronological record of the notable changes made in each version of a product.
ex: Power users scour the changelog every Friday to see what has shipped.

def: To apply a fix or feature developed for a newer version of software to an older, still-supported version.
ex: Enterprise clients insisted that the security fix be backported to last year's release.

def: A design approach in which digital interfaces imitate the appearance and textures of physical objects.
ex: The calendar app abandoned skeuomorphism, dropping its fake leather stitching for flat colour.

def: A feature that users do not expect but which, when present, disproportionately increases their satisfaction.
ex: The playful confetti on completing a goal turned out to be a genuine delighter.

def: A static, visually detailed representation of a screen or interface used to review design before it is built.
ex: The stakeholders approved the mockup, then asked why the live version looked different.

def: A visualisation that uses colour intensity to show where users click, scroll or look on a page.
ex: The heatmap revealed that nobody scrolled far enough to see the pricing table.

def: To move a task or initiative lower in order of importance so that other work can proceed first.
ex: We deprioritised the dark mode request to free the team for the compliance deadline.

def: A visual or sensory cue in an interface that indicates where and how an action can be performed.
ex: Without a shadow or underline, the button lacked any signifier that it was clickable.

def: To redefine the boundaries and requirements of a project, usually to fit a new deadline or budget.
ex: Rather than slip the date, the team rescoped the release to the three most-requested features.

def: A defined set of criteria and weightings used to score and compare options consistently.
ex: Every proposal was scored against the same rubric of reach, impact and effort.

def: A research method in which a researcher observes users performing their real work in its natural setting.
ex: A day of shadowing nurses revealed workarounds that no survey would have surfaced.

def: A basic attribute whose absence causes strong dissatisfaction but whose presence earns little credit.
ex: Reliable login is a classic dissatisfier: nobody praises it, but everyone complains when it fails.

def: A direct, unedited quotation from a customer collected in research or feedback.
ex: She opened the review with three customer verbatims that made the problem impossible to ignore.

def: The practice of a whole team focusing together on a single high-priority item until it is finished.
ex: Swarming on the outage ticket cleared it in an afternoon instead of a week.

def: Software that a customer has paid for but does not actually use.
ex: Seats that never log in become shelfware, and shelfware rarely renews.

def: The short pieces of interface text, such as labels, hints and error messages, that guide users through a product.
ex: Rewriting the microcopy on the sign-up form reduced abandonment by a fifth.

def: A navigational trail showing users where they are within a site's hierarchy and how to return to higher levels.
ex: Adding a breadcrumb to the settings pages stopped users getting lost three levels deep.

def: To move a product or service onto a different underlying technology platform.
ex: Replatforming the storefront froze new feature work for two quarters.

def: To redesign the fundamental technical structure of a system to meet new requirements.
ex: Supporting offline mode meant rearchitecting how the app stored and synced data.

def: A large application built as a single, tightly coupled unit that is hard to change or deploy in parts.
ex: Every small change to the monolith required a full regression run.

def: Visible stuttering or lag in an interface caused by dropped frames during scrolling or animation.
ex: The redesign looked gorgeous on desktop but introduced terrible jank on older phones.

def: Describing a survey technique that asks people to choose between bundles of attributes to reveal how they value each one.
ex: The conjoint study showed customers would trade storage space for faster support.

def: The process of drawing out requirements and needs from stakeholders and users.
ex: Requirements elicitation with the finance team took longer than building the report itself.

def: Describing a usability test that participants complete on their own without a researcher guiding them live.
ex: We ran an unmoderated study overnight and had fifty recordings by morning.

def: A short questionnaire used to select research participants who match the target profile.
ex: A sloppy screener let in students instead of the procurement managers we needed.

def: A structured list of themes and tags used to categorise qualitative research data consistently.
ex: Two researchers coded the interviews against a shared codebook to keep the analysis consistent.

def: The activity of devising specific solutions, often criticised when it begins before the problem is understood.
ex: The workshop slid into solutioning before anyone had agreed what the customer's problem was.

def: To generate a wide range of ideas or possible solutions, typically in a structured session.
ex: Each squad spent the morning ideating on ways to shorten the onboarding flow.

def: A formal planning session in which teams agree their mutual commitments and dependencies for a coming period.
ex: The quarterly interlock exposed that three teams were waiting on the same platform change.

def: The degree to which a product can be adapted to different needs through settings rather than custom code.
ex: Enterprise buyers demanded configurability, but every new toggle added support costs.

def: Describing a product that deliberately enforces one preferred way of working rather than offering many options.
ex: The tool is opinionated about workflow, which delights small teams and frustrates large ones.

def: Software that impresses in a demonstration but lacks the robustness needed for real use.
ex: The analytics module was demoware: beautiful on stage, unusable with real data volumes.

def: A holding area for backlog ideas that are not rejected but have no current plan to be worked on.
ex: The social sharing idea went into the icebox until the core product was stable.

def: A period devoted to fixing defects and improving stability before a release rather than adding features.
ex: We reserved the final sprint for hardening after the beta surfaced dozens of edge cases.

def: To add tracking to a product so that user behaviour and system performance can be measured.
ex: We forgot to instrument the new export button, so nobody knew whether it was used.

def: A hybrid working method combining the planning cadence of scrum with the continuous flow of kanban.
ex: The support squad switched to scrumban because urgent tickets kept wrecking sprint plans.

def: A pre-production environment that mirrors the live system and is used to test changes before release.
ex: The bug never appeared on staging because it only occurred with real customer data.

def: An architecture in which a single instance of software serves many separate customers whose data is kept isolated.
ex: Moving to multitenancy cut their hosting bill in half but made every upgrade a fleet-wide event.

def: Describing software in which one shared deployment serves many customers with logically separated data.
ex: The bank refused the multitenant edition and insisted on a dedicated environment.

def: A prospective customer currently using a product during a free or discounted trial period.
ex: Only one trialist in five ever enters a card before day fourteen.

def: The amount actually invoiced to customers in a period, as distinct from revenue recognised.
ex: Analysts watched billings closely because they hinted at future revenue before it hit the income statement.

def: The planned, gradual withdrawal of a product, feature or plan from availability.
ex: The sunsetting of the legacy tier was announced a full year in advance.

def: The deliberate limiting of how much a customer can use a service within a given time.
ex: Free-plan throttling pushed heavy users towards the paid tier.

def: The alignment of add-on subscriptions so that they all expire on the same date as the master agreement.
ex: Cotermination meant finance received a single, tidy renewal invoice each January.

def: The party that grants another the right to use its software or intellectual property.
ex: The licensor retained the right to audit usage once a year.

def: A licence granted by a licensee to a third party under rights it holds from the original owner.
ex: The reseller could only issue a sublicence on terms no broader than its own.

def: Offering or buying several distinct products from the same vendor rather than a single one.
ex: Multiproduct customers churned at a fraction of the rate of single-product accounts.

def: Structured so that most payments or revenue fall towards the end of a contract or period.
ex: The deal was backloaded, with the steepest price increases in year three.

def: Structured so that most payments, costs or effort fall at the beginning of a contract or period.
ex: Implementation fees made the first year heavily frontloaded for the customer.

def: Covering a commitment of more than one year, typically in exchange for a lower price.
ex: They traded a deeper discount for a multiyear commitment with prepayment.

def: Offered without measurement or charge for the volume used.
ex: Unmetered storage looked generous until a few customers uploaded petabytes.

def: Allowing usage to exceed a committed baseline temporarily, usually at an extra charge.
ex: The burstable plan let them absorb Black Friday traffic without upgrading permanently.

def: Turned from a bespoke service into a standardised, repeatable offering with fixed scope and price.
ex: Their productised onboarding package replaced months of custom consulting.

def: Describing a model in which the basic software is free and open source while advanced features are sold commercially.
ex: The open-core strategy built a huge community before a single enterprise contract was signed.

def: A licensing approach requiring that modified versions of software be distributed under the same open terms.
ex: Legal flagged the copyleft dependency before it could contaminate the proprietary product.

def: The act of changing the licence under which software is offered, often to restrict commercial reuse.
ex: The relicensing provoked a community fork within a fortnight.

def: The ease with which a customer can extract their data from a platform in usable form.
ex: Procurement scored exportability highly to avoid being trapped with one vendor.

def: A customer who has cancelled or failed to renew a subscription.
ex: Exit surveys showed most churners had never used the core feature.

def: A customer's decision or formal notice not to extend a subscription at the end of its term.
ex: The nonrenewal notice arrived exactly sixty days before the contract expired.

def: Capable of being ended under the terms of a contract, often at a stated notice period.
ex: The agreement was terminable for convenience on ninety days' notice.

def: The practice of grouping customers by a shared start date or trait to track their behaviour over time.
ex: Cohorting by signup month revealed that retention had quietly worsened since spring.

def: A clause that reduces a salesperson's commission rate on deals below quota or with deep discounts.
ex: The decelerator meant heavily discounted deals paid the rep almost nothing.

def: The rearrangement of which features sit in which plans, often without changing the headline prices.
ex: A clever repackaging moved single sign-on into the premium tier and lifted average deal size.

def: Describing a free trial that does not require payment details at sign-up.
ex: Cardless trials tripled signups but halved the conversion rate.

def: To use your own company's product internally in order to test it and expose its flaws.
ex: The team dogfooded the billing tool for months before any customer saw it.

def: A period of intensified support immediately after a customer goes live on new software.
ex: The vendor staffed a two-week hypercare window after the migration.

def: One of the very largest cloud infrastructure providers operating vast global data centres.
ex: Selling through a hyperscaler's marketplace let customers draw down their existing cloud commitments.

def: Predictable enough to be projected with confidence, particularly of recurring revenue.
ex: Investors paid a premium for such forecastable revenue.

def: An increase in the size of an existing customer's contract through more seats, usage or tiers.
ex: Upsizing at renewal accounted for most of the year's net new revenue.

def: A third-party firm that implements and connects software for customers, often as a sales partner.
ex: The integrator brought in a quarter of all enterprise deals.

def: Occurring once rather than repeating each billing period, such as setup or consulting fees.
ex: Nonrecurring services revenue was stripped out before valuing the business.

def: The removal of a user's access and licences from a system, typically on departure or cancellation.
ex: Automated deprovisioning freed up seats the moment an employee left.

def: A small, independently deployable software component that handles one narrow business capability and communicates with others over a network.
ex: Splitting billing into its own microservice let that team release twice a day without waiting on anyone.

def: The tendency of an automated test to pass or fail unpredictably without any change to the code under test.
ex: Test flakiness had grown so bad that engineers simply reran the pipeline until it went green.

def: Manual, repetitive operational work that scales with service size and adds no lasting value, so it ought to be automated away.
ex: The team capped toil at half its week and spent the rest automating certificate renewals.

def: The degree to which separate software modules depend on one another's internals, making them hard to change independently.
ex: Tight coupling between checkout and inventory meant a minor schema tweak broke both.

def: The design practice of hiding a component's internal state and exposing only a deliberate, stable interface.
ex: Good encapsulation let them swap the payment provider without touching a single caller.

def: The deliberate removal of features or requirements from a planned piece of work to protect a date or budget.
ex: Some aggressive descoping kept the launch on schedule, with offline mode pushed to the next quarter.

def: The redefinition of a project's boundaries and deliverables after new information changes what is feasible.
ex: The vendor's API limits forced a full rescoping of the integration project.

def: Competition between processes or teams for the same limited resource, causing waits and slowdowns.
ex: Lock contention on the orders table explained the latency every Monday morning.

def: A single version-control repository holding the code for many projects or services across an organisation.
ex: Moving into the monorepo let one change update the shared library and every consumer at once.

def: The entire body of source code that makes up a particular software system or product.
ex: New hires spent their first week reading the codebase before touching a ticket.

def: The automated static checking of source code for stylistic errors, suspicious constructs and rule violations.
ex: Stricter linting caught dozens of unused variables before they ever reached review.

def: A script that rewrites source code automatically to perform a large, mechanical change across a codebase.
ex: A single codemod migrated four thousand call sites to the new logging interface overnight.

def: A thin layer of code that adapts one interface to another so older callers keep working during a transition.
ex: We left a shim in place so legacy clients could still call the old endpoint.

def: Code that supplies a modern feature in older environments that do not support it natively.
ex: Dropping the polyfill for old browsers cut the bundle size by a fifth.

def: The isolation of knowledge, tools or decisions within individual teams so that others cannot see or use them.
ex: Years of siloing meant only one person understood how the billing jobs were scheduled.

def: The migration of an application onto a new underlying infrastructure or technology stack with limited functional change.
ex: The replatforming onto managed databases took a year but halved the operations headcount needed.

def: A fundamental redesign of a system's structure and component boundaries, usually to meet new scale or change demands.
ex: Leadership balked at funding a full rearchitecture and approved incremental extraction instead.

def: The ease with which software can be understood, corrected and extended by engineers over its lifetime.
ex: The clever optimisation was rejected because it would wreck maintainability for a tiny speed gain.

def: Reactive work spent handling urgent problems and incidents at the expense of planned, preventive engineering.
ex: Constant firefighting left the platform team no time to fix the root causes.

def: Describing an incident review culture that examines systemic causes rather than punishing the individuals involved.
ex: Because the review was blameless, the junior engineer openly explained the command she had mistyped.

def: A common response to a recurring problem that seems sensible but reliably produces poor outcomes.
ex: Sharing one database between every service is an antipattern that the architects keep flagging.

def: Designing a solution with more complexity, flexibility or generality than the actual problem requires.
ex: A plugin framework for a script used by three people was textbook overengineering.

def: Concerning the interplay between an organisation's people and structures and the technical systems they build.
ex: Slow releases turned out to be a sociotechnical problem, rooted in team boundaries more than tooling.

def: An informal community of practice that connects engineers with a shared specialism across different teams.
ex: The front-end guild meets fortnightly to agree conventions across every product squad.

def: To reduce the uncertainty or potential for failure in a plan by tackling its riskiest elements early.
ex: We built the payment flow first to derisk the integration before anything cosmetic.

def: Unsustainable individual over-effort, such as late nights, that a team relies on to meet commitments.
ex: The release only shipped through weekend heroics, which the director said must not become routine.

def: A pre-agreed threshold that, once crossed, automatically triggers a decision such as halting or reviewing a project.
ex: We set a tripwire: if the migration slips by a month, we revisit the whole approach.

def: A minor, non-blocking comment in a code review about style or naming rather than correctness.
ex: He prefixed the comment as a nitpick so the author knew it would not hold up the merge.

def: The degree to which software is designed so its behaviour can be verified easily and in isolation.
ex: Injecting the clock as a dependency greatly improved the scheduler's testability.

def: The property of a build, test or process always producing the same output given the same inputs.
ex: Pinning every dependency restored determinism to the build after weeks of mysterious failures.

def: The tendency of a system or test suite to break under small, unrelated changes.
ex: The brittleness of the UI tests meant any copy change failed half the suite.

def: The main shared branch of a repository into which all engineers integrate their changes frequently.
ex: Everyone merges to trunk at least daily, with unfinished features hidden behind flags.

def: To replay a branch's commits on top of a newer base so its history reads as a straight line.
ex: Please rebase onto main before review, as the branch is forty commits behind.

def: The practice of copying a third-party dependency's source directly into one's own repository rather than fetching it at build time.
ex: Vendoring the library protected us when its maintainer deleted the package overnight.

def: Creating an independent copy of a codebase that then develops separately from the original.
ex: Forking the open-source tool gave us control but saddled us with merging every upstream fix.

def: Measuring where a program spends its time and memory in order to locate performance problems.
ex: Profiling showed ninety per cent of the request time went on a single unindexed query.

def: A state in which a system has finished in-flight work and accepts no new tasks, making it safe to change or shut down.
ex: The deploy script waits for quiescence before draining each node.

def: A mechanism by which an overloaded component signals upstream producers to slow down instead of being overwhelmed.
ex: Without backpressure, the queue swelled until the consumers ran out of memory.

def: A design pattern that isolates resources into separate pools so that a failure in one part cannot exhaust the rest.
ex: A bulkhead around the recommendations service kept checkout alive when recommendations collapsed.

def: Allocating more computing capacity than workloads need, usually as insurance against spikes, at extra cost.
ex: An audit found chronic overprovisioning, with most servers idling below ten per cent.

def: The automatic addition or removal of computing resources in response to changing load.
ex: Autoscaling absorbed the traffic surge after the advert aired without anyone being paged.

def: The set of programs used together to build, test and ship software, from compiler to deployment tools.
ex: Standardising the toolchain across teams cut onboarding from a week to a day.

def: A retry strategy that waits progressively longer between attempts after each failure.
ex: Adding exponential backoff stopped the clients from hammering the recovering server.

def: A state in which a system or team spends most of its effort switching between tasks and makes little real progress.
ex: With five competing priorities, the team was thrashing and nothing reached done.

def: A periodic signal sent by a service to show it is alive, so its absence can trigger an alert or failover.
ex: When the worker's heartbeat stopped, the scheduler reassigned its jobs within seconds.

def: The guarantee that a system keeps making progress, or a check that confirms a process is still running properly.
ex: The liveness probe restarts any container that stops responding for thirty seconds.

def: A cryptocurrency designed to hold a steady value by being pegged to a reserve asset such as a fiat currency.
ex: The exchange settled most cross-border trades in a dollar stablecoin to avoid overnight volatility.

def: A local institution appointed by a global custodian to hold client assets in a particular market.
ex: Assets in Brazil are held through a subcustodian that the global bank audits every year.

def: The underlying networks and protocols along which payments are routed and settled.
ex: The start-up moved its payouts onto instant rails so that couriers were paid within seconds.

def: Technology that helps financial firms meet regulatory requirements more efficiently.
ex: The bank bought a regtech platform to automate its suspicious-activity reporting.

def: The use of technology to redesign how insurance is priced, sold and administered.
ex: An insurtech that prices cover by the mile has unsettled the incumbent motor insurers.

def: Digital tools and platforms that automate investment management and financial advice.
ex: Wealthtech apps have made portfolio rebalancing available to savers with only a few hundred pounds.

def: Splitting cash transactions into smaller amounts to evade reporting thresholds.
ex: The analyst flagged a pattern of structuring after spotting dozens of deposits just under the limit.

def: A person who lets their account be used to receive and move illicit funds on behalf of criminals.
ex: Fraud teams traced the stolen money through three student accounts acting as mules.

def: A business that accepts card payments under the account of a payment facilitator rather than its own merchant account.
ex: Each yoga studio on the platform is onboarded as a submerchant within minutes.

def: The magnetic strip on a payment card that stores account data in a readable but easily copied form.
ex: Fallback to magstripe is now blocked at most terminals because it invites cloning.

def: The quality of a payment that cannot be recalled or cancelled once it has been sent.
ex: The irrevocability of instant transfers makes them a favourite of scammers.

def: The point at which a settled transaction becomes unconditional and legally irreversible.
ex: Central-bank money offers settlement finality that private ledgers struggle to match.

def: A cryptographic credential stored on a device that replaces a password for signing in.
ex: Since the bank switched to passkeys, phishing losses on its app have fallen sharply.

def: A device or app that generates or confirms a second factor to verify a user's identity.
ex: High-value transfers require approval in the authenticator as well as the usual login.

def: A register of approved entities, such as payees or addresses, that are permitted to transact.
ex: Withdrawals can only go to wallets already on the corporate allowlist.

def: A register of entities, such as cards or devices, that are blocked from transacting.
ex: The compromised card numbers were pushed to the denylist within an hour.

def: Grouping many transactions together to be processed or submitted at once.
ex: Nightly batching meant suppliers waited a full day to see their funds.

def: Built from interchangeable modules that can be combined and recombined to create new products.
ex: A composable banking stack let the retailer launch a branded card in weeks.

def: Describing a system that provides back-end functionality through interfaces without its own customer-facing front end.
ex: They run a headless checkout so each brand can design its own payment screen.

def: Not yet matched against a corresponding record, leaving a discrepancy to be investigated.
ex: Auditors queried the growing pile of unreconciled items in the suspense account.

def: Adding context such as merchant names, logos and categories to raw transaction data.
ex: Without enrichment, customers saw cryptic codes instead of the shop they had paid.

def: Depositing money in advance in an account abroad so that outgoing payments can be paid out immediately.
ex: Prefunding in a dozen currencies ties up capital that could otherwise earn interest.

def: Secured by collateral worth less than the amount owed, leaving the lender exposed.
ex: The protocol failed when a market drop left thousands of positions undercollateralised.

def: To lose the fixed exchange value a currency or token is meant to maintain.
ex: Panic spread when the token began to depeg and traded at ninety cents.

def: Requiring approval from several independent keys before a transaction can be executed.
ex: Treasury funds sit in a multisignature wallet that needs three of five directors to sign.

def: Restricted so that only approved participants can read, write or validate entries on a network.
ex: The banks chose a permissioned ledger so regulators could see exactly who was transacting.

def: A participant on a network who checks and confirms transactions before they are added to the ledger.
ex: A bug in one client briefly knocked a third of the validators offline.

def: The queue of unconfirmed transactions waiting to be included in a block.
ex: Fees spiked as the mempool swelled with thousands of pending transfers.

def: A condition that prevents funds or code changes from taking effect until a set time has passed.
ex: A forty-eight-hour timelock gives users a chance to exit before any upgrade goes live.

def: A condition that releases funds only when a secret matching a published hash is revealed.
ex: The swap used a hashlock so neither party could take the coins without the other's secret.

def: Describing money or payments that carry coded rules governing when and how they can be spent.
ex: Programmable grants can only be spent at approved suppliers and expire if unused.

def: Held by a neutral party until agreed conditions are met.
ex: The escrowed funds are released to the seller once the buyer confirms delivery.

def: Relating to the side of card processing that signs up merchants and receives card payments on their behalf.
ex: The fintech applied for an acquiring licence so it could stop relying on a partner bank.

def: To replace sensitive data such as a card number with a substitute value that is useless if stolen.
ex: Phone wallets tokenise the card so the merchant never sees the real number.

def: A one-time code generated by a chip or device to prove a card transaction is genuine.
ex: The issuer declined the payment because the cryptogram failed verification.

def: Securely storing customers' payment credentials so they can be charged again without re-entering details.
ex: Card vaulting lets subscribers renew with a single tap.

def: Replacing a physical cheque with a digital image so it can be cleared electronically.
ex: Cheque truncation cut clearing times from six days to one.

def: A merchant's resubmission of a disputed card transaction with evidence to reverse a chargeback.
ex: With delivery photos attached, the representment won back most of the disputed sales.

def: An automated message one system sends to another when a specified event occurs.
ex: Our ledger updates as soon as the processor's webhook confirms the payment.

def: Producing the same result however many times an operation is repeated.
ex: Because the endpoint is idempotent, a retried request will never charge the customer twice.

def: The design of a crypto token's supply, distribution and incentives.
ex: Investors balked at tokenomics that handed half the supply to insiders.

def: Locking up crypto assets to help secure a network in return for rewards.
ex: Regulators questioned whether staking rewards amounted to an unregistered security.

def: The forfeiture of a validator's staked assets as a penalty for misbehaviour or downtime.
ex: The operator lost a chunk of its deposit to slashing after signing two conflicting blocks.

def: A free distribution of tokens to wallet holders, usually to reward early users or drive adoption.
ex: The airdrop attracted thousands of fake accounts trying to farm the reward.

def: A bank's closure of a customer's accounts or refusal to serve them, often on risk grounds.
ex: The crypto firm blamed debanking for its sudden inability to pay staff.

def: The practice of a foreign bank accessing a correspondent account through another bank's relationship.
ex: Compliance found that nesting had let an unvetted lender route payments through its account.

def: Allowing third parties to use a correspondent account indirectly through a respondent bank.
ex: The contract explicitly prohibits downstreaming without prior approval.

def: A very small payment, often fractions of a penny, made for digital content or usage.
ex: Card fees make micropayments uneconomic, so the publisher bundles articles instead.

def: Able to hold, receive or pay out balances in several currencies within one account.
ex: A multicurrency account let the agency pay freelancers in euros without converting twice.

def: Automatically moving surplus balances between accounts according to set rules.
ex: Overnight sweeping moves idle cash into a higher-yielding account.

def: Combining the balances of a group's accounts so that surpluses offset deficits.
ex: Cash pooling cut the group's overdraft costs across its European subsidiaries.

def: The legal duty of a payment or e-money firm to protect customer funds separately from its own money.
ex: The regulator fined the wallet provider for safeguarding failures uncovered in its audit.

def: Keeping client funds in accounts separate from a firm's own operating money.
ex: Proper segregation meant customers were repaid in full when the broker collapsed.

def: Improperly mixing customer funds with a firm's own money.
ex: Investigators found commingling of deposits with the exchange's trading capital.

def: A single mobile platform bundling payments, messaging, shopping and other services.
ex: In Asia, the superapp has made standalone banking apps almost redundant.

def: Occurring or measured within a single business day.
ex: Real-time payments have made intraday liquidity management a board-level concern.

def: A state in which demand grows faster than an economy's productive capacity, pushing up inflation and wages.
ex: Rate-setters warned that a tight labour market and booming credit pointed to overheating by the summer.

def: Relating to the idea that households save to offset government borrowing because they anticipate future tax rises.
ex: If consumers behave in a Ricardian way, the tax cut will barely lift spending.

def: A prolonged condition of near-zero interest rates, weak growth and persistent low inflation of the kind Japan experienced after 1990.
ex: Bond strategists fretted that the eurozone was sliding towards Japanification.

def: The spread of unviable firms that survive only because cheap credit lets them service their debts.
ex: Years of ultra-low rates were blamed for the zombification of the retail sector.

def: The pooling of debts or risks so that a group of states becomes jointly liable for them.
ex: Northern governments have long resisted any mutualisation of member states' borrowing.

def: The trio of the European Commission, European Central Bank and IMF that supervised eurozone bailout programmes.
ex: Athens bristled each time the troika's inspectors arrived to review the budget.

def: The band between a central bank's lending and deposit rates within which overnight market rates are kept.
ex: The bank narrowed its corridor to keep money-market rates closer to the policy target.

def: The process by which a change in the policy rate passes through to lending rates, spending and inflation.
ex: With most mortgages on fixed deals, transmission of the latest hike will take months.

def: The restoration of a metal, note or asset to the status of legal money, or the replenishing of cash after its withdrawal.
ex: Banks queued for new notes as remonetisation lagged far behind the government's promises.

def: To offset the effect of currency intervention on the domestic money supply through opposing open-market operations.
ex: The central bank issued short-term bills to sterilise its massive dollar purchases.

def: The sale of more government debt to the non-bank public than is needed to cover the deficit, in order to drain money from the economy.
ex: Overfunding was a favoured monetarist tool for curbing broad money in the early 1980s.

def: A policymaker's inclination to favour low interest rates and support for growth over fighting inflation.
ex: Sterling slid as markets digested the governor's unexpected dovishness.

def: A policymaker's inclination to favour higher interest rates to keep inflation in check.
ex: The minutes revealed a hawkishness that few analysts had anticipated.

def: The first interest-rate rise after a long period of rates held at or near zero.

ex: The retailer rejected dozens of executory leases on its first day in court.

def: Describing a creditor whose collateral is worth less than the debt it secures.
ex: Being undersecured, the bank was left with a large unsecured deficiency claim.

def: Describing a creditor whose collateral is worth more than the debt it secures, entitling it to post-filing interest and fees.
ex: As an oversecured lender, it could keep accruing default interest throughout the case.

def: Describing a claim whose amount has not yet been fixed or agreed.
ex: Personal-injury claims remained unliquidated until the estimation hearing.

def: A court's or office-holder's rejection of a creditor's claim against an insolvent estate.
ex: The liquidator sought disallowance of the inflated claim from the former chief executive.

def: The practice of letting a company collapse and restarting the same business through a new entity, leaving creditors behind.
ex: Regulators cracked down on phoenixism in the construction sector.

def: An investor who owns a company's bonds, loans or other debt instruments.
ex: The debtholders formed an ad hoc group to negotiate with management.

def: A plan provision shielding estate fiduciaries from liability for conduct during the restructuring case.
ex: The trustee objected that the exculpation clause reached far too many parties.

def: The imposition of a restructuring plan on a dissenting senior class using the votes of more junior classes.
ex: The sponsor attempted a rare cram-up against the secured lenders.

def: An agreement by a parent company to maintain a subsidiary's solvency or financial ratios, falling short of a formal guarantee.
ex: Bondholders discovered that the keepwell gave them no enforceable claim against the parent.

def: Describing a restructuring or plan imposed without the agreement of every affected class.
ex: A nonconsensual plan invites months of valuation litigation.

def: A condition that prevents a borrower from drawing further funds under a facility, typically after a default.
ex: The drawstop on the revolver turned a squeeze into a liquidity crisis.

def: Describing a bankrupt who has not yet been released from the bankruptcy and its restrictions.
ex: An undischarged bankrupt cannot act as a company director without permission.

def: A regime in which a regulator or appointee takes control of a failing institution to preserve its assets and operations.
ex: The mortgage giants were placed into conservatorship at the height of the crisis.

def: A person or body appointed to manage and protect a distressed institution's assets.
ex: The conservator replaced the board within a week.

def: The courtesy by which courts in one country recognise and assist insolvency proceedings in another.
ex: Relying on comity, the judge enforced the foreign scheme against local creditors.

def: Describing transactions entered into before insolvency that an office-holder may investigate and challenge.
ex: The administrators began a review of antecedent transactions.

def: The wasteful or deliberate removal of assets that would otherwise be available to creditors.
ex: Fears of dissipation persuaded the court to grant a freezing order.

def: Describing a debt that survives bankruptcy and is not wiped out by the debtor's discharge.
ex: Fraud-related judgments are typically nondischargeable.

def: Whether a particular debt can be released through a bankruptcy discharge.
ex: The creditor filed a complaint contesting the dischargeability of the loan.

def: A debtor's agreement to remain liable for a debt that would otherwise be discharged in bankruptcy.
ex: She signed a reaffirmation to keep the car loan and the car.

def: Whether a proposed plan of reorganisation meets the legal requirements for court approval.
ex: Objectors attacked the plan's confirmability on feasibility grounds.

def: Describing a guarantee or security given by one subsidiary for the debts of a sister company.
ex: The cross-stream guarantees exposed every subsidiary to the group's bank debt.

def: A loosely drafted covenant provision allowing assets to be moved out of the lenders' collateral net.
ex: Lenders now hunt for trapdoors before signing any new credit agreement.

def: An investor holding positions in more than one layer of a distressed company's capital structure.
ex: As a crossholder, the fund was torn between its secured and unsecured positions.

def: A debtor that keeps control of its business and assets while reorganising under court protection.
ex: As debtor-in-possession, management continued running the factories day to day.

def: The automated routing of parcels or items to the correct outbound lane within a distribution centre.
ex: Peak volumes exposed a bottleneck in the sortation system, so parcels sat on the belt for hours.

def: The framework of shelving and beams used to store pallets and goods in a warehouse.

def: A freestanding double-sided shelving unit that forms the aisles of a shop floor.
ex: Snacks were moved to the gondola nearest the tills to capture last-minute spend.

def: A single product unit placed at the front of a shelf so that it faces the shopper, used as a measure of shelf space.

def: The practice of store staff building long-term personal relationships with individual customers using their purchase history and preferences.
ex: The luxury chain equipped its sales associates with tablets to support clienteling between visits.

def: Theft in which a cashier deliberately fails to scan or undercharges items for friends or family.
ex: Exception reports on voided scans helped the loss-prevention team uncover sweethearting at two stores.

def: The practice of buying an item, using it briefly, and then returning it for a full refund.
ex: Prom season brought a spike in wardrobing, so the retailer began attaching non-removable tags to evening dresses.

def: The pricing convention of setting the retail price at double the wholesale cost.

def: The software-driven selection of the optimal box size and packing configuration for each outbound order.

def: The process of deciding which products a retailer will stock and in which stores.

def: The resale of previously owned goods through dedicated online or retail channels.

def: A middleman who buys surplus or distressed stock in bulk and resells it to other traders.

def: Describing content such as a video, image or post that lets viewers buy the featured products directly from it.

def: Combining physical retail spaces with digital technology to create a blended shopping experience.
ex: The flagship's phygital fitting rooms let shoppers request other sizes from a mirror screen.

def: A scheduled programme that automatically reorders and dispatches consumable products to a customer at set intervals.

def: An unauthorised marketplace seller who attaches offers, often counterfeit, to another brand's product listing.

def: Fraud in which criminals test stolen card details by making small online purchases.

def: The design, manufacture and installation of fixtures, fittings and interiors for retail premises.

def: The signage and spatial cues that help shoppers navigate a store or shopping centre.

def: The area just inside a store entrance where shoppers adjust to the space and tend to ignore merchandise.

def: The selection and arrangement of display units, racks and shelving within a retail space.
ex: Lower fixturing in the centre of the floor opened up sightlines to the back wall.

def: A small promotional sign attached to a shelf edge by a flexible strip so that it moves as shoppers pass.

def: A shelf-mounted card or sign that calls out a product feature or offer at the point of sale.
ex: The barker highlighting the price cut was hidden behind a stack of boxes all weekend.

def: An outer film or wrapping placed around a product or multipack to protect, bundle or brand it.

def: Describing core products that are continuously restocked rather than bought once for a season.

def: Describing a refund given without requiring the customer to send the item back, typically when return shipping costs exceed its value.

def: Discontinued or surplus merchandise sold off at a steep reduction to clear it entirely.

def: Goods with minor manufacturing flaws that are sold at a reduced price.

def: Describing a retail model that sells branded goods below normal prices using surplus or opportunistically bought stock.
ex: Off-price chains thrive when full-price retailers are stuck with excess inventory.

def: The retail category of durable non-textile goods such as appliances, hardware, furniture and sporting equipment.
ex: She moved from buying knitwear to managing hardlines, starting with garden tools.

def: The retail category of textile-based goods such as clothing, footwear, bedding and towels.
ex: Softlines margins suffered when unseasonal weather left winter coats on the rails.

def: A small, limited collection of products released together, often as a collaboration or seasonal drop.

def: The use of entertainment, events and experiences within stores to attract shoppers and extend their visits.

def: The percentage of stock received that is actually sold to consumers over a given period.

def: Focused on a very small geographic area, such as a single neighbourhood or postcode.

def: Order picking from small automated warehouses located close to customers to enable rapid delivery.

def: Placing a winning bid in the final seconds of an online auction to deny rivals time to respond.

def: A trader who buys goods intended for one market or channel and resells them in another without the brand's authorisation.

def: Describing a store in which sensors and cameras charge shoppers automatically, removing the need to stop at a till.
ex: The checkoutless format worked well at the station, where commuters had only seconds to spare.

def: A company that stores, picks, packs and ships orders on behalf of a seller.
ex: They switched fulfillers after one too many missed delivery cut-offs.

def: The use of automated scripts to buy up limited-release products faster than human shoppers can.
ex: Rampant botting meant the trainers sold out in seconds and reappeared on resale sites at triple the price.

def: A curated set of styled photographs presenting a brand's collection to buyers, press or customers.

def: The use of filterable attributes such as size, colour and price on a website so shoppers can narrow search results.

def: The practice of tuning on-site search results to promote particular products, ranges or margins.

def: The restriction of access to an online shop, prices or products based on the visitor's geographic location.

def: A magnetic or mechanical device used at the till to remove security tags from merchandise.

def: Displaying complementary products from different categories together to prompt additional purchases.

def: The division of a sales floor into distinct areas by category, customer type or purpose to guide shopping behaviour.

def: The measure of whether a served display or video advert actually appeared on a user's screen long enough to be seen.

def: The act of a user clicking an advert or link to reach its destination, or the rate at which this happens.

def: The paid or organic effort to extend the reach of a piece of content beyond its initial audience.

def: A hyperlink from an external website pointing to one's own, valued as a signal of authority by search engines.

def: The ease with which search engine bots can discover and navigate the pages of a website.
ex: Moving the catalogue behind client-side rendering wrecked our crawlability for months.

def: The practice of signalling to search engines which of several near-duplicate URLs is the authoritative version.

def: The exclusion of specified contacts or audiences from a campaign, typically existing customers or unsubscribed users.

def: A server-to-server notification sent to an ad network or attribution partner confirming that an install or conversion occurred.

def: Describing tracking or targeting that works without third-party browser cookies.

def: The matching of anonymous website visitors to identifiable companies or individuals.

def: The grouping of a user's raw tracking events into discrete visits for analysis.
ex: Changing the sessionisation timeout from thirty minutes to ten inflated our session count overnight.

def: An experimentation method that mixes results from two ranking algorithms in one list to see which users prefer.
ex: Interleaving let the search team detect a winning ranker with a fraction of the traffic an ordinary split would need.

def: A video advert that plays before the content a viewer has chosen to watch.
ex: Our six-second pre-roll had to land the brand before viewers could hit skip.

def: The delivery of different adverts or content to users based on their geographic location.
ex: Tight geotargeting kept the launch spend inside the three cities where delivery was available.

def: Describing marketing that breaks into what someone is doing, such as pop-ups or unskippable ads.

def: The assignment of users to test and control groups by chance so that results are not biased.
ex: A bug in the randomisation sent all mobile users to the variant, invalidating the test.

def: The web page or source from which a visitor arrived, as recorded by analytics.
ex: Traffic with no referrer spiked after the app update, hiding where those visitors had really come from.

def: The process of winning back a customer who had previously been lost, often counted separately from new acquisition.
ex: Our cheapest growth last quarter came from reacquisition of users who had cancelled during the summer.

def: Describing access that allows a fixed number of free uses or articles before payment is required.
ex: The paper's metered model gave readers five free stories a month before the paywall appeared.

def: Descriptive data about organisations, such as size, sector and revenue, used to segment business buyers.
ex: We scored inbound leads on firmographics first and only then looked at their engagement.

def: Relating to data about which software and technologies a company already uses.
ex: Technographic filters let us target only firms already running the rival's checkout plugin.

def: A very narrowly defined group of customers sharing specific traits or behaviours, targeted with tailored messaging.

def: The tactic of bidding on a competitor's brand terms or audiences to intercept their prospective customers.
ex: Conquesting on the market leader's name was expensive but brought in buyers who were already comparing options.

def: The flow of user and placement data broadcast to bidders during real-time advertising auctions.
ex: Regulators questioned how much personal information leaked into the bidstream with every page load.

def: The arrangement by which a brand runs paid adverts through a creator's social account with their permission.

def: Describing a video advert that viewers may dismiss after a few seconds.

def: A single loading of a web page by a visitor, recorded as a basic unit of traffic.
ex: Splitting the article into a slideshow inflated pageviews but annoyed readers.

def: The point in a funnel or flow where a share of users abandons before completing the next step.
ex: The biggest drop-off in onboarding came at the screen asking for contact permissions.

def: A modal overlay that dims the page behind it to focus attention on a sign-up form or offer.

def: An exceptionally engaged customer whose heavy usage and advocacy drive disproportionate value and referrals.

def: The growth tactic of acquiring users by tapping into an established platform's existing audience.

def: A small intermediate action, such as adding to a wishlist, that signals progress towards the main conversion.

def: The degree to which a plan or project can realistically be carried out successfully.

def: The set of reasons underlying a particular decision or course of action.

def: A brief summary giving the main points of a longer document.

def: A section of supplementary material placed at the end of a report or book.

def: Carried out gradually in planned stages rather than all at once.

def: An estimate of a future figure or trend based on current data.

def: The process of reorganising a company's structure or operations to improve efficiency.

def: To declare public or formal approval of a plan, person or product.

def: The total amount of money that an organisation spends over a period.

def: The extent to which a business or activity generates profit.

def: An improvement or increase in economic activity or business performance.

def: To rise and fall irregularly in number or amount.

def: The act of deciding the order of importance of tasks or goals.

def: To support or form the basis of an argument, strategy or system.

def: Possible to achieve with the time, money and resources available.

def: Clear and definite enough to be measured or observed.

def: Coming before a fuller or more important action or event.

def: Arranged or existing for the present but possibly changed later.

def: Referred to previously in the same text.

def: In a warm and sincere but formal way.

def: From this time onwards.

def: To give a short statement of the main points.

def: To pay back money that someone has spent or lost.

def: The greeting at the beginning of a letter or email.

def: Typical of informal conversation rather than formal writing.

def: Sensible and recommended in a particular situation.

def: To relate to or be connected with a particular subject.

def: Arranged in the order in which events happened.

def: Logical and clearly organised so that the parts fit together.

def: To give more details or explain something more fully.

def: To list things individually, often with their costs.

def: The feeling of not being pleased with something.

def: A frequent, smaller-scale natural hazard such as hail, wildfire or flash flooding, as opposed to major hurricanes or earthquakes.
ex: Reinsurers raised prices after secondary perils drove most of the year's insured catastrophe losses.

def: A reinsurance provision that treats all losses from a peril within a set number of hours as a single event.
ex: Under the seventy-two-hour clause, the storm's losses were split into two separate events.

def: A reinsurance contract that pays out only if total insured industry losses from an event exceed a stated trigger.
ex: The insurer bought an industry loss warranty that triggers once market-wide hurricane losses pass thirty billion dollars.

def: A rating system that lowers premiums for claim-free years and raises them after claims.
ex: Under the bonus-malus scale, a single at-fault crash wiped out four years of discount.

def: Describing a career policy in which staff who are not promoted within a set time are expected to leave the firm.
ex: The firm's up-or-out culture means most analysts leave within three years.

def: A specialised division of a consulting or professional services firm focused on a particular industry or capability.
ex: She was hired to build the firm's supply-chain practice area from scratch.

def: Informal shorthand for a steering committee, the senior group that oversees a project's direction and key decisions.
ex: We need the cost model finished before Thursday's steerco.

def: A post-acquisition roadmap of initiatives a private equity owner will pursue to raise a company's worth before exit.
ex: The consultants drafted the value creation plan during due diligence so work could start on day one.

def: The process of actually realising the cost savings and revenue gains promised as the rationale for a merger.
ex: Eighteen months after closing, synergy capture stood at barely half the target announced to investors.

def: An analysis of how many direct reports each manager has and how many management levels separate the top from the front line.

def: A budgeting method that requires every cost to be justified from scratch each period rather than adjusted from last year.

def: A structured programme to remove a defined amount of cost from an organisation's base.

def: A dataset that classifies an organisation's purchasing by supplier, category and business unit to reveal savings opportunities.

def: A simulation in which teams role-play competitors and other players to test how a strategy might fare in response.

def: Visible support from a senior leader that protects a team or initiative from internal resistance.

def: A formal amendment to a signed engagement that alters its scope, timeline or fees.

def: A payment due to an adviser only if a specified outcome, such as a completed deal or achieved savings, is delivered.

def: A firm's standard schedule of daily or hourly fees for each grade of staff.

def: A single average fee rate for a team that mixes staff of different seniority levels.

def: A paid service that connects consultants and investors with industry specialists for short research interviews.

def: Estimating the total potential revenue or volume of a market, often by structured assumptions when data is scarce.
ex: The candidate opened the case with a quick market sizing of electric scooters in Madrid.

def: Describing a rough, quick calculation made to test whether an idea is plausible.

def: A framework that rates an organisation's capability in an area on a staged scale from basic to advanced.

def: A central team that tracks, coordinates and enforces delivery of a company-wide transformation programme.

def: A fact-based argument explaining why an organisation cannot continue as it is and must transform.

def: A small circle filled in quarters, used in comparison tables to show the degree to which an option meets a criterion.

def: The quality of a presentation in which reading only the slide titles in sequence tells the complete story.

def: A communication principle of stating the conclusion or recommendation before presenting the supporting analysis.

def: The estimated total value an initiative could unlock if fully delivered.

def: Describing analysis built from external sources and the customer's or market's viewpoint before access to internal data.
ex: The team presented an outside-in view of the company's cost position before the client opened its books.

def: The agreed body of data and analysis on which a team's recommendations are built.
