ex: The retrospective surfaced the same handover pain twice running, so we finally reworked the process.

def: The formal transfer of responsibility, knowledge or a deliverable from one party to another.
ex: A rushed handover left the support team without runbooks, and the first outage exposed it immediately.

def: The process of assigning and balancing people, skills and assets across the work a project requires.
ex: Our resourcing is too thin in the test phase, so I've flagged a two-person gap to the sponsor.

def: To reorder the relative importance of tasks or deliverables in response to changed circumstances.
ex: When the regulator moved the deadline, we had to reprioritise the whole backlog overnight.

def: To formally remove features or work from a project's agreed scope, usually to protect time or budget.
ex: Rather than blow the deadline, we agreed to descope the reporting module and deliver it in a fast follow.

def: The amount of time a task can be delayed without affecting the project's finish date.
ex: That task has five days of float, so I'm comfortable letting it slip while we firefight the critical path.

def: Spare time or capacity in a schedule that allows delay without knock-on impact.
ex: There's almost no slack left in the plan, so any surprise this week will hit the delivery date.

def: An issue that completely prevents a task from progressing until it is removed.
ex: The missing test credentials were a blocker, so the whole story sat untouched for two days.

def: A defect or problem so severe that it prevents release or continuation until resolved.
ex: We found a showstopper in the payment flow the night before launch and had to pull the release.

def: A temporary means of bypassing a problem to keep work moving while a permanent fix is pending.
ex: We shipped a manual workaround for the export bug so the client wasn't blocked over the weekend.

def: The framework of roles, decision rights and controls through which a project is directed and held to account.
ex: Weak governance meant no one owned the go/no-go call, so the decision drifted for a fortnight.

def: To revise a projection of cost, time or effort in light of actual performance to date.
ex: After two overrunning sprints we had to reforecast the completion date and brief the sponsor.

def: The amount by which actual cost or time exceeds what was budgeted or scheduled.
ex: A thirty-per-cent cost overrun on the integration work wiped out the entire contingency.

def: To take deliberate action that reduces the likelihood or impact of a threat to a project.
ex: We de-risked the migration by running a full dress rehearsal against a copy of production first.

def: A planned action taken to reduce the probability or severity of an identified risk.
ex: Our mitigation for the single-supplier risk is to qualify a second vendor before the build phase.

def: The ordering of tasks so that dependencies are respected and resources are used efficiently.
ex: Poor sequencing meant the painters arrived before the plastering was dry, and everyone lost a day.

def: To compress a schedule by running normally sequential phases in parallel, accepting the added risk.
ex: We fast-tracked design and procurement together to claw back time, though it meant more rework.

def: The founding document that authorises a project and defines its objectives, scope and sponsor.
ex: Nothing was properly mandated until the sponsor signed the charter and released the budget.

def: A large body of work that is broken down into smaller stories or tasks for delivery.
ex: The checkout redesign is a single epic spanning three teams and most of the quarter.

def: To rapidly assess and rank issues by severity so the most urgent are addressed first.
ex: We triaged the sixty defects into fix-now, fix-later and won't-fix within an hour.

def: The division of a project into distinct sequential stages, each with its own gate or objective.
ex: Smart phasing let us release value early instead of holding everything back for one big launch.

def: A formal decision point between phases where a project must be approved to continue.
ex: The project failed its second tollgate because the business case no longer stacked up.

def: A concrete work product, such as a plan, diagram or report, generated during a project.
ex: Every phase produces a defined set of artefacts that the assurance team reviews before sign-off.

def: A documented set of step-by-step procedures for executing a routine or recovery operation.
ex: The cutover runbook listed every command and its rollback, so the on-call engineer wasn't improvising.

def: A structured analysis conducted after an event or project to identify what happened and why.
ex: The outage post-mortem was blameless, so people were honest about the missed warning signs.

def: A brief daily meeting where a team synchronises on progress, plans and blockers.
ex: The standup should be five minutes, but it kept sprawling into a status theatre for the manager.

def: A horizontal or vertical band in a process diagram that groups activities by the role responsible.
ex: Putting each team in its own swimlane made the handover points impossible to ignore.

def: The initial ramp-up in which a project's team, tools and governance are stood up and made ready.
ex: Mobilisation ran long because access approvals stalled, eating into the delivery window before we'd started.

def: The controlled retirement of a system, service or asset once it is no longer needed.
ex: Decommissioning the legacy platform freed up a licence bill that had quietly become the biggest line item.

def: The reversal of a change to restore the previous known-good state when a release fails.
ex: When the deploy corrupted orders, we triggered the rollback and were live again within twenty minutes.

def: The breaking down of a large deliverable into progressively smaller, manageable work packages.
ex: Careful decomposition of the scope into work packages made estimating far less of a guessing game.

def: The full set of work, features and deliverables that a project is agreed to produce.
ex: Before we commit to a timeline, we need to agree the scope with the client in writing.

def: Not included in the agreed boundaries of the project and therefore not covered by the current plan or budget.
ex: Translating the app into German is out of scope for this phase and would need a change request.

def: To reach a planned project checkpoint on or ahead of schedule.
ex: We hit the beta milestone two days early, so testing can start on Monday.

def: The active support and commitment of stakeholders to a project's goals and approach.
ex: Without stakeholder buy-in from finance, the budget will stall at the first review.

def: A living document that logs each identified project risk together with its likelihood, impact and owner.
ex: Add the supplier delay to the risk register and flag it as high impact.

def: To take deliberate action that reduces the likelihood or impact of a potential problem.
ex: We can mitigate the delivery risk by ordering the parts a month in advance.

def: A prepared course of action to follow if a specific risk actually materialises.
ex: Our contingency plan is to switch to the backup vendor if the shipment slips again.

def: A bar chart that maps project tasks against a timeline, showing durations, overlaps and dependencies.
ex: Pull up the Gantt chart so we can see where the two workstreams collide.

def: The planned schedule of a project's tasks and milestones over time.
ex: The client wants the launch in June, but that timeline is unrealistic for the current scope.

def: The first meeting that formally starts a project and aligns the team on goals, roles and scope.
ex: Let's use the kick-off to agree ways of working before any real work begins.

def: To give formal approval to a piece of work so it can proceed to the next stage.
ex: Once the sponsor signs off on the budget, procurement can place the order.

def: A formal proposal to alter the agreed scope, timeline or budget of a project.
ex: Adding single sign-on now means raising a change request and re-baselining the plan.

def: A grid that clarifies who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each project task.
ex: The RACI matrix should have stopped this, because two people thought they owned the same task.

def: Progressing according to plan and expected to meet the agreed schedule or target.
ex: Two of the three workstreams are on track; the third needs an extra developer.

def: Progressing more slowly than the plan requires, so that milestones are at risk of being missed.
ex: We are two sprints behind schedule and will need to move the launch date.

def: The point at which a product or system is released into live use by real users.
ex: We have a code freeze forty-eight hours before go-live to keep things stable.

def: The phased release of a product, service or change across users or locations.
ex: We'll pilot in one region first, then plan the wider rollout for Q3.

def: A delivery strategy that breaks a project into sequential stages rather than releasing everything at once.
ex: A phased approach lets us learn from the first market before scaling up.

def: The assigning of people, budget and equipment to the tasks that need them.
ex: Our resource allocation is off, because the senior engineers are all on one project.

def: The single person accountable for a task, risk or deliverable seeing it through.
ex: Every risk on the register needs a named owner, or it will drift.

def: A short report on where a task or project currently stands against its plan.
ex: I'll send a status update every Friday so the steering group stays informed.

def: A red, amber or green rating that signals at a glance whether a project or workstream is healthy, at risk or in trouble.
ex: The delivery workstream has gone from green to amber on this week's RAG status.

def: The justification for a project, setting out its costs, benefits and expected return.
ex: The business case only stacks up if we hit twenty thousand users in year one.

def: A document that defines exactly what work will be performed, to what standard and by when.
ex: Anything the client asks for beyond the scope of work is billable.

def: The specific conditions a deliverable must meet before the client will accept it as complete.
ex: The feature isn't done until it passes every one of the acceptance criteria.

def: The insights captured after a phase or project about what worked and what to improve next time.
ex: Let's run a lessons-learned session so we don't repeat the same handover mess.

def: A fixed date that cannot be moved, often tied to a regulatory or contractual obligation.
ex: The audit is a hard deadline, so everything else has to flex around it.

def: Caught up in excessive operational detail at the expense of the bigger picture.
ex: We're too in the weeds on wording; let's step back to the overall goal.

def: The founding document that formally authorises a project and sets out its objectives, scope and authority.
ex: The project charter names me as project manager and gives me sign-off up to fifty thousand.

def: The shared, explicit checklist that a piece of work must satisfy before it counts as complete.
ex: It isn't in our definition of done until it's tested, documented and deployed.

def: Tenure of property under a lease for a fixed term of years, as opposed to outright freehold ownership.
ex: The flat is sold as a leasehold with 92 years remaining, after which the interest reverts to the freeholder.

def: Absolute ownership of land and any buildings on it for an indefinite period.
ex: Investors preferred the freehold because it carried no ground rent or diminishing term.

def: A form of freehold ownership of an individual unit within a multi-occupancy building, with the common parts jointly managed.
ex: Converting the block to commonhold gave each owner a stake in the shared corridors and roof.

def: A right to use another's land for a specified purpose, such as access, light, or drainage.
ex: The rear plot was landlocked, so its owner relied on an easement over the neighbouring driveway.

def: The residual right of an owner to retake possession of property once a lease or lesser interest ends.
ex: With only a short lease outstanding, the freeholder's reversion was the more valuable asset.

def: Disrepair for which a tenant is liable, or the claim a landlord makes for such disrepair at the end of a lease.
ex: On surrender, the landlord served a schedule of dilapidations totalling £40,000 for unrepaired damage.

def: The legal transfer of title to real property from one party to another, or the document that effects it.
ex: Completion of the conveyance was delayed until the outstanding local searches were returned.

def: The lender who holds a mortgage as security over a borrower's property.
ex: On default, the mortgagee exercised its power of sale to recover the outstanding loan.

def: The borrower who grants a mortgage over their property to a lender.
ex: As mortgagor, she remained liable for the shortfall even after the house was repossessed.

def: The proportion of a property or market that is unoccupied and available to let.
ex: A rising vacancy rate signalled that the retail park was struggling to retain tenants.

def: A period during which a rental property produces no income because it stands empty between tenancies.
ex: A three-month void between lettings eroded the landlord's projected annual return.

def: The downward movement of the ground beneath a building, causing structural cracking and damage.
ex: Cracks above the bay window suggested subsidence, deterring buyers and inflating insurance premiums.

def: The strengthening or deepening of a building's foundations, often to remedy subsidence.
ex: Extensive underpinning was required before the lender would advance funds on the cracked terrace.

def: The state of a property being abandoned and left in a ruinous condition.
ex: Years of dereliction had left the mill roofless, though its riverside plot remained highly developable.

def: The transformation of a poorer urban area through the influx of wealthier residents and rising values.
ex: Rapid gentrification of the docklands doubled rents and displaced long-standing tenants.

def: Denoting previously developed land, often contaminated, that is available for redevelopment.
ex: Planning policy steered new housing onto brownfield sites to protect the surrounding countryside.

def: Denoting undeveloped land, typically in a rural setting, being considered for construction.
ex: The developer's greenfield proposal met fierce opposition from residents defending the green belt.

def: The process of increasing the number of dwellings or occupants within a given area of land.
ex: Urban densification allowed the city to add homes without extending its footprint.

def: The reclassification of land to permit a different category of use under planning rules.
ex: Rezoning the depot from industrial to residential unlocked a substantial development premium.

def: A minor right or asset that attaches to and passes with a principal property.
ex: The garage and its right of access passed to the buyer as an appurtenance of the house.

def: An item of movable personal property, as distinguished from real estate.
ex: The curtains and freestanding wardrobes were treated as chattels and excluded from the sale price.

def: An article once movable that has become legally part of the land by being attached to it.
ex: The fitted kitchen was a fixture and therefore automatically included in the conveyance.

def: A right granted to run cables, pipes, or access across another's land, typically for utilities.
ex: The electricity company paid an annual wayleave for the pylons crossing the farmer's fields.

def: A periodic sum charged on freehold land, payable to a party who holds no other interest in it.
ex: The Victorian rentcharge of a few pounds a year still bound the property to a distant estate.

def: A nominal rent or consideration used to make a lease or contract legally binding.
ex: The charity held the hall on a 99-year lease at a peppercorn rent of one pound a year.

def: A landlord's right to terminate a lease and re-enter the premises for the tenant's breach of covenant.
ex: Persistent non-payment of rent exposed the tenant to forfeiture of the shop lease.

def: A reduction or suspension of rent, or the removal of a legal nuisance affecting property.
ex: Because the flooded floor was unusable, the tenant claimed an abatement of rent for the period.

def: The transfer of ownership or an interest in property from one person to another.
ex: The lease contained an alienation clause requiring the landlord's consent to any assignment.

def: Relating to or situated on the bank of a river, and to the rights of landowners bordering it.
ex: As a riparian owner, the mill held rights to abstract water from the passing stream.

def: Relating to or situated on the shore of a sea or lake.
ex: The resort's littoral parcels commanded premium prices for their direct beach frontage.

def: The enclosed land immediately surrounding a dwelling and treated in law as part of it.
ex: The planners argued that the new decking lay within the curtilage and needed no separate consent.

def: A dwelling house together with its outbuildings and the adjacent land assigned to it.
ex: The deed conveyed the messuage and all barns, yards, and gardens belonging to it.

def: Any species of property capable of being inherited, whether corporeal or incorporeal.
ex: For rating purposes, each shop was assessed as a separate hereditament.

def: Denoting a property's assessed value used as the basis for local business rates.
ex: The refurbishment pushed the shop's rateable value up, sharply increasing its annual rates bill.

def: Describing a property occupied by several tenants under separate tenancies.
ex: The multi-let office spread risk across a dozen occupiers rather than a single covenant.

def: The transfer of property back to the borrower once a mortgage debt has been fully repaid.
ex: On final settlement, the lender executed a reconveyance releasing its charge over the title.

def: A release or transfer of whatever interest one holds in property, without any warranty of title.
ex: The departing partner signed a quitclaim, surrendering any residual stake in the development site.

def: A burden imposed on one property for the benefit of another, equivalent to an easement in civil and Scots law.
ex: A servitude of access ran with the title, obliging the owner to permit the neighbour's passage.

def: The right to use and enjoy another's property and its fruits without impairing its substance.
ex: Under her late husband's will, she held a usufruct over the estate for the rest of her life.

def: A vaulted space or storey beneath a building, often at or below ground level.
ex: The scheme tucked resident parking into an undercroft, freeing the courtyard for landscaping.

def: The set of prospective deals a salesperson is working, tracked by stage from first contact to close.
ex: Her pipeline looks healthy this quarter, with three enterprise deals in late stages.

def: A potential customer who fits the target profile but has not yet committed to buy.
ex: We qualified twelve new prospects at the trade show last week.

def: The activity of actively searching for and reaching out to potential new customers.
ex: He blocks out every morning for cold prospecting before meetings start.

def: To assess whether a potential customer has the need, budget, and authority to justify pursuing the deal.
ex: Always qualify a lead before you invest hours preparing a proposal.

def: A person or company that has shown some interest and may become a customer.
ex: Marketing passed us forty inbound leads from the webinar.

def: An unsolicited sales call to a prospect who has had no prior contact with the company.
ex: He booked the meeting off a single well-timed cold call.

def: Contacting prospects who have not engaged before, typically by email, phone, or social message.
ex: Our cold outreach reply rate doubled once we personalised the opening line.

def: A prospect who has already shown interest or been referred, making them more receptive to a sales approach.
ex: A warm lead from an existing client is far easier to convert.

def: To finalise an agreement with a customer so that the sale is confirmed.
ex: We closed the deal an hour before the end of the quarter.

def: The stage of the sale where the buyer is asked to commit and the agreement is completed.
ex: She is brilliant at discovery but needs coaching on closing.

def: The proportion of qualified opportunities that a salesperson successfully converts into sales.
ex: His close rate on inbound demos sits around thirty per cent.

def: The sales target a representative is expected to hit within a given period.
ex: She hit quota by the middle of the month for the first time.

def: To reach or exceed the sales target set for a period.
ex: Only three of the eight reps hit quota last quarter.

def: A concern or reason a prospect gives for hesitating to buy.
ex: Price is rarely the real objection; usually it is timing.

def: To respond to a prospect's concerns in a way that keeps the deal moving forward.
ex: A good rep learns to handle objections without becoming defensive.

def: An early conversation used to understand a prospect's needs, situation, and priorities before proposing a solution.
ex: On the discovery call we learned their contract was up for renewal in March.

def: A concise, persuasive presentation of a product's value aimed at winning the buyer's interest.
ex: Keep the pitch to five minutes and let the customer talk.

def: The work of maintaining and growing relationships with existing customers to retain and expand their business.
ex: She moved from new business into account management last year.

def: The person responsible for the ongoing relationship with a set of existing customers.
ex: Your account manager will handle renewals and any upsell opportunities.

def: A high-value customer whose business is strategically important and warrants dedicated attention.
ex: We assigned our most experienced rep to the key accounts.

def: To persuade an existing customer to buy a higher-tier or more expensive version of what they already use.
ex: We upsold them from the standard plan to enterprise at renewal.

def: To sell an existing customer an additional, complementary product or service.
ex: There is a clear chance to cross-sell the analytics module here.

def: The event of a customer extending their contract for a further term.
ex: The renewal is due in sixty days, so start the conversation now.

def: The typical length and sequence of steps from first contact to a closed sale.
ex: Enterprise deals have a sales cycle of nine months or more.

def: The act of turning a prospect at one stage into the next, ultimately into a paying customer.
ex: A faster follow-up dramatically improved trial-to-paid conversion.

def: To make further contact with a prospect after an initial meeting or message to keep the deal moving.
ex: I will follow up on Thursday once she is back from leave.

def: The person in an organisation who has the authority to approve a purchase.
ex: We wasted weeks pitching to someone who was not the decision-maker.

def: An internal advocate at the prospect's company who supports your solution and pushes it forward.
ex: Without an internal champion, the deal stalled at procurement.

def: A formal document setting out the recommended solution, scope, and price for a prospect.
ex: I will have the proposal on your desk by Monday morning.

def: A formal statement of the price at which a product or service is offered to a customer.
ex: Can you send over a quote for the fifty-seat licence?

def: To follow an outstanding matter through to a clear resolution and confirm it back to those involved.
ex: Let me close the loop with legal and get back to you by Friday.

def: Describing a deal that is being actively worked but not yet closed.
ex: We have two six-figure deals in the pipeline for next quarter.

def: The full set of accounts and customers a salesperson is responsible for.
ex: She grew her book of business by forty per cent in two years.

def: To increase sales activity or output steadily towards full productivity.
ex: New reps take about three months to ramp up to full quota.

def: A specific problem or frustration a prospect experiences that your product can solve.
ex: Their biggest pain point was reconciling data across three systems.

def: A soft, testing question that gauges how ready a prospect is to commit without asking outright for the sale.
ex: A well-placed trial close tells you whether to push for the signature.

def: Describing a deal that is being decided right up until the very last moment.
ex: It went down to the wire, but they signed before quarter-end.

def: To persuade a former customer who left to return and buy again.
ex: We ran a targeted campaign to win back the accounts we lost last year.

def: Describing business or revenue coming from customers who were not previously buying from you.
ex: Leadership wants more net-new logos, not just expansion of existing accounts.

def: A prediction of the revenue a salesperson or team expects to close within a period.
ex: Keep your forecast honest; sandbagging helps no one at review time.

def: The portion of the forecast a rep is confident enough to promise will close.
ex: Those two deals are in commit; the rest I would call best-case.

def: To make contact with a prospect or customer, typically to start or continue a conversation.
ex: I will reach out to the new contact she introduced us to.

def: The capacity of a business model to grow revenue much faster than its costs.
ex: Investors probed the platform's scalability, asking whether it could serve ten million users without a proportional rise in headcount.

def: An organisation that nurtures very early-stage startups with workspace, mentoring and seed resources.
ex: Fresh out of university, they joined a campus incubator that gave them desk space and a modest stipend.

def: A privately held startup valued at more than one billion dollars.
ex: Once a garage project, the fintech had become a unicorn valued at three billion pounds.

def: A company whose innovation upends the established order of an industry.
ex: The ride-hailing disruptor forced incumbent taxi firms to overhaul their pricing overnight.

def: The structured process of generating and developing new business ideas.
ex: The weekend hackathon was pure ideation, producing forty concepts before any were tested.

def: To refine a product through repeated cycles of building, measuring and learning.
ex: Rather than perfecting the design, the team chose to iterate weekly on feedback from early users.

def: To render a product so undifferentiated that it competes mainly on price.
ex: As open-source alternatives proliferated, the once-premium software was rapidly commoditised.

def: An acquisition made primarily to obtain a company's talent rather than its product.
ex: The struggling startup ended in an acqui-hire, with its engineers absorbed into the buyer's team.

def: Describing a growth curve that stays flat before bending sharply upward.
ex: The pitch deck promised hockey-stick growth once the product reached critical mass.

def: An anti-dilution mechanism that adjusts an investor's shareholding if later shares are issued more cheaply.
ex: A full ratchet clause badly diluted the founders when the next round priced lower.

def: To turn a bespoke service or capability into a standardised, sellable product.
ex: They productised their consulting methodology into a self-serve software tool.

def: A feature or quality that distinguishes a product from its competitors.
ex: Round-the-clock human support became their key differentiator in a market of chatbots.

def: The quality of a product that keeps users coming back over time.
ex: Daily habit loops gave the app a stickiness that kept churn remarkably low.

def: The strategy of splitting a bloated incumbent offering into focused standalone products.
ex: Fintech startups thrived on the unbundling of traditional banks, each attacking a single service.

def: Raising small sums from many people, typically online, to finance a venture.
ex: Their gadget hit its crowdfunding target within hours of the campaign going live.

def: Lacking sufficient funds to sustain or grow operations.
ex: Brilliant but undercapitalised, the startup folded just as demand began to surge.

def: The right of existing shareholders to buy new shares before outsiders, so as to avoid dilution.
ex: Exercising their pre-emption rights, the early backers maintained their percentage in the next round.

def: An entrepreneur who builds and runs a business entirely alone.
ex: As a solopreneur, she wrote the code, closed the sales and answered every support ticket herself.

def: An employee who develops new ventures within an established company.
ex: The intrapreneur secured internal funding to spin up a new product line inside the corporation.

def: Funded through revenue and personal means rather than outside investment.
ex: Proudly bootstrapped, the agency reached profitability without raising a single round.

def: A short-term loan that converts into equity at a later financing round.
ex: Early angels came in on a convertible rather than negotiating a price so soon.

def: A basic schematic layout of a product's interface used in early design.
ex: Before writing code, they sketched wireframes to test the checkout flow with users.

def: To grow a business rapidly while keeping unit costs under control.
ex: The model worked in one city, but nobody knew whether it would scale nationally.

def: An early working model built to test a concept before full development.
ex: A rough prototype was enough to convince the first investor to write a cheque.

def: The strategy or process by which a business generates revenue.
ex: The app had explosive growth but no monetisation, burning cash with every new user.

def: A wealthy individual who invests personal money in early-stage startups.
ex: A local angel wrote the first cheque long before any venture fund would engage.

def: To restructure a company's mix of debt and equity, often to rescue or reset it.
ex: Facing insolvency, they recapitalised the business by converting investor loans into shares.

def: To bring a product or invention to market for profit.
ex: The lab spun out a startup to commercialise the patented battery technology.

def: A strategy of advancing through small, cautious steps rather than bold, sweeping change.
ex: Their timid incrementalism let a nimbler rival redefine the category while they tweaked at the edges.

def: The degree to which a market is open to new entrants because barriers and exit costs are low.
ex: High contestability keeps incumbents disciplined, since a rival could plausibly enter overnight.

def: The discouragement of a rival's action by signalling a credible and costly response.
ex: Holding excess capacity serves as deterrence, warning entrants that any price war would be ruinous.

def: Building a company from its own revenue rather than relying on outside investment.
ex: Years of disciplined bootstrapping meant they owned the whole business when the buyout offer arrived.

def: The systematic comparison of one's performance against best-in-class competitors or standards.
ex: Benchmarking against the sector leader exposed just how bloated our overheads had become.

def: A short-sighted focus on immediate results that neglects longer-term strategic threats.
ex: Marketing myopia led them to defend the product they made rather than the need customers actually had.

def: An organisation's tendency to persist in its existing course and resist strategic change.
ex: Organisational inertia kept the firm chained to a distribution model the market had already abandoned.

def: Dominant influence or control exercised by one player over an entire market or sector.
ex: The search engine's hegemony let it set the terms on which every advertiser reached the web.

def: Deliberately going against prevailing opinion in the expectation that the crowd is wrong.
ex: Their contrarian bet on physical stores paid off just as everyone else fled to the internet.

def: A corporation made up of several diverse businesses operating in unrelated industries.
ex: The sprawling conglomerate was eventually broken up because investors valued its parts above the whole.

def: A massive and unstoppable organisation that crushes obstacles in its path.
ex: Competing head-on with the retail juggernaut would have been strategic suicide for the small chain.

def: The leading position at the forefront of a new development or trend.
ex: The firm placed itself in the vanguard of electrification while rivals hedged their bets.

def: To overtake a rival by skipping an intermediate stage and adopting a superior technology directly.
ex: Emerging markets leapfrogged fixed lines entirely and went straight to mobile networks.

def: Prioritising breakneck growth over efficiency to seize a market before rivals can respond.
ex: Blitzscaling won them dominance, but the reckless spending nearly bankrupted the company first.

def: The point at which a market has so few remaining buyers that further growth becomes very hard.
ex: With saturation approaching at home, the retailer had no option but to expand abroad.

def: A company that trails its peers in performance or in adopting new methods.
ex: Once the sector's laggard, the firm surprised everyone by out-innovating its former leaders.

def: Just coming into existence and beginning to show potential for growth.
ex: They staked out the nascent market years before it was obvious there would be a market at all.

def: A company newly entering a market in which established rivals already operate.
ex: Every new entrant faced the same brutal choice: match the incumbents' scale or stay a niche player.

def: Aimed at destroying competitors, typically by pricing below cost until they are forced out.
ex: The regulator ruled the loss-making tariff was predatory, designed purely to bankrupt the challenger.

def: Excessive self-confidence that leads a firm to overreach and ignore warning signs.
ex: Corporate hubris after a decade of success blinded the board to the threat until it was fatal.

def: An indirect effect in which activity in one area produces benefits or costs in another.
ex: The knowledge spillover from its research lab quietly lifted the whole regional cluster.

def: A feature or capability that lets a company outperform its rivals and win more customers.
ex: Our competitive advantage lies in a supply chain that no rival can match on speed or cost.

def: The benefit a company gains by being the first to enter a market or launch a type of product.
ex: They enjoyed a first-mover advantage for two years before the incumbents woke up and copied them.

def: An obstacle such as high cost or regulation that makes it difficult for new competitors to enter a market.
ex: The licensing regime is a huge barrier to entry, which is exactly why margins in this sector stay high.

def: To radically change an established market with a new model that displaces the incumbent players.
ex: Their pay-per-use pricing disrupted an industry that had run on annual licences for decades.

def: The distinct place a brand or product occupies in the minds of target customers relative to rivals.
ex: Our market positioning as the premium, trusted option lets us charge twenty percent above the field.

def: An uncontested market space created by generating new demand rather than fighting rivals in a crowded field.
ex: Instead of competing on price, we went after a blue ocean of customers no one else was serving.

def: Growth generated from a company's existing operations rather than through acquisitions.
ex: The chief executive prefers steady organic growth to the integration headaches of buying rivals.

def: A durable competitive advantage that protects a company's long-term profits from competitors.
ex: Their network effects create an economic moat that a well-funded challenger still couldn't cross.

def: The strategy of owning multiple stages of a supply chain, from production through to distribution.
ex: Vertical integration let them control quality end to end, but it tied up a lot of capital.

def: The company with the largest share and greatest influence in a particular market.
ex: Within four years the challenger had overtaken the market leader on both price and quality.

def: The specific price at which a product is offered, chosen to position it in the market.
ex: At that price point we sit awkwardly between the budget brands and the premium tier.

def: An advantage gained by beginning an activity before competitors do.
ex: Filing the patents early gave us a two-year head start on anyone trying to enter the space.

def: A group of potential customers that no company is yet serving effectively.
ex: Small rural clinics are an untapped market that the big vendors have always ignored.

def: The degree to which an acquisition, partnership, or initiative aligns with a company's overall strategy.
ex: The numbers looked attractive, but the strategic fit with our core business was weak.

def: A destructive pattern where rivals repeatedly cut prices until margins collapse for everyone.
ex: Matching every discount only starts a race to the bottom that the low-cost player always wins.

def: To win the dominant share of customers in a particular market.
ex: By bundling the product for free, they captured the market before anyone could charge for it.

def: Expansion that a company can maintain over the long term without straining its resources or finances.
ex: The board favoured sustainable growth over a land grab that would have burned through our reserves.

def: The overall picture of the rivals, dynamics, and forces at play in a given market.
ex: The competitive landscape shifted overnight when two of our rivals announced a merger.

def: Essential to the survival or core success of an organisation.
ex: Retaining that one client is mission-critical this quarter; losing them would wipe out our margin.

def: The strategic overhaul of a business's operations and models through digital technology.
ex: Digital transformation is less about the software and more about changing how people actually work.

def: To design a strategy or system so it remains effective despite future change.
ex: We future-proofed the platform by building it to run on any cloud provider from day one.

def: An objective a company must achieve to succeed or survive in its market.
ex: Reducing our reliance on a single supplier has become a strategic imperative after last year's shortage.

def: To commit even more strongly to a chosen strategy rather than change course.
ex: Instead of retreating, the chief executive chose to double down on the premium segment.

def: A single guiding metric or objective that aligns and directs a company's strategy.
ex: Weekly active users became our north star, and every team now measures itself against it.

def: Describing a market position or advantage that can be protected against competitors over time.
ex: Anyone can copy the feature, so it isn't a defensible advantage; the data we've gathered is.

def: The minimum capabilities a company must have simply to compete in a market.
ex: Mobile access used to be a differentiator, but now it's just table stakes in our category.

def: To keep someone regularly informed about the progress of a matter.
ex: Please keep me in the loop on any changes to the launch date.

def: A planned list of the topics to be discussed in a meeting.
ex: I've circulated the agenda in advance so everyone can prepare their points.

def: In British usage, to formally raise a topic for discussion; in American usage, to postpone it, so context matters.
ex: I'd like to table the budget question so the whole committee can weigh in.

def: To move a detailed or tangential discussion out of the current meeting into a smaller conversation later.
ex: That's a good point but it only affects two of us, so let's take it offline.

def: A list where off-topic points are noted to be addressed after the current agenda is finished.
ex: Let's put that idea in the parking lot and come back to it once we've decided the budget.

def: In full agreement and sharing the same understanding of a situation.
ex: Before we brief the client, I want to make sure the whole team is on the same page.

def: To secure the agreement and support of the people needed to move a decision forward.
ex: We won't get anywhere until we get buy-in from the regional managers.

def: To reach a shared position on a decision, priority, or approach.
ex: Can we align on the messaging before the press release goes out?

def: To remind someone about an outstanding task or request in order to speed it up.
ex: Can you chase up Finance about the invoice that was due last week?

def: To send someone a copy of an email so they are aware of it without being the main recipient.
ex: I've cc'd my manager so she's aware of the timeline we agreed.

def: A phrase signalling that information is shared for the reader to note, with no action required.
ex: For your awareness, the client has pushed the review meeting to next Tuesday.

def: A formal email closing that asks the recipient to give guidance or a decision.
ex: The two dates both work on our end, so please advise which you prefer.

def: An abbreviation for end of day, used to set a same-day deadline.
ex: Can you get me the draft by EOD so I can review it tonight?

def: An abbreviation for estimated time of arrival, used to ask when something will be ready or delivered.
ex: What's your ETA on the finance report? The board meets at three.

def: Something one is aware of and paying attention to, even if not acting on it yet.
ex: The renewal is on my radar, and I'll start the paperwork next week.

def: To share an idea or proposal with someone to get their opinion or approval.
ex: Let me run the wording by our lawyers before we publish it.

def: An obvious problem or awkward issue that everyone is avoiding talking about.
ex: Let's address the elephant in the room: we're three months behind schedule.

def: To start a process or activity so that progress can begin.
ex: To get the ball rolling, I'll draft the brief and share it by tomorrow.

def: To bring a meeting or piece of work to a close, often with a summary.
ex: Let's wrap up here so everyone can get to their next call on time.

def: To briefly summarise the main points that have been covered.
ex: Before we finish, let me recap the three decisions we've made today.

def: The specific actions to be taken following a meeting or decision.
ex: The next steps are clear: I'll draft the contract and you'll brief the client.

def: A key point or lesson that people should remember from a discussion or presentation.
ex: The main takeaway from the review is that we need to test earlier.

def: A thorough and detailed examination of a specific topic or dataset.
ex: Next week we'll do a deep dive into why churn spiked in the third quarter.

def: Describing an overview that covers the main points without going into detail.
ex: Give me a high-level summary first, and we can dig into the numbers afterwards.

def: A short prompt inviting someone to give their opinion or reaction.
ex: Here's the revised layout for the deck, your thoughts?

def: To explain something to someone step by step so they understand it clearly.
ex: Let me walk you through the numbers before we open it up for questions.

def: A phrase used to hand over to someone so they can speak or present.
ex: Thanks for the introduction, Sarah, the floor is yours.

def: A phrase that passes responsibility or the turn to speak to another person.
ex: I've covered the timeline, so over to you for the budget section, Tom.

def: A phrase used to add a related point by building on what someone has just said.
ex: To piggyback on that, we're seeing the same trend in the European market.

def: To send someone a quick message to get their attention or a fast reply.
ex: Ping me on Teams when you're free and we'll sort it out in two minutes.

def: An advance warning or notice that gives someone time to prepare.
ex: Just a heads-up that the client may join the call ten minutes early.

def: To pause a topic temporarily with the intention of returning to it later.
ex: Let's put a pin in the pricing debate and finish the rollout plan first.

def: To make sure people have a realistic understanding of what can be achieved and by when.
ex: I want to manage expectations early: this feature won't be ready before the summer.

def: To send someone a short, informal message.
ex: Drop me a line once you've had a chance to look over the proposal.

def: To draw attention to an issue or concern so it can be addressed.
ex: I want to flag a risk with the timeline before we commit to the client.

def: To meet briefly with someone to share updates and coordinate work.
ex: Let's sync up for fifteen minutes before the client call to align on our answers.

def: Relating to government revenue, spending and taxation.
ex: The budget tightened fiscal policy to cool demand.

def: Money paid by a government to support an industry or lower a price.
ex: A subsidy kept the rural bus routes running.

def: The amount by which spending exceeds income.
ex: The company ran a deficit for two straight quarters.

def: An amount left over when income exceeds spending.
ex: A trade surplus strengthened the currency.

def: To accept full responsibility for a task or outcome.
ex: She took ownership of the mistake and fixed it.

def: To formally put a proposal forward for discussion.
ex: The team tabled a proposal to move the deadline.

def: To arrive at general agreement within a group.
ex: After an hour they reached a consensus on the price.

def: To lead and manage a meeting.
ex: The deputy chaired the meeting in her absence.

def: To compromise so that each side gives up something.
ex: They met halfway on the delivery date.

def: Kept informed and included in what is happening.
ex: Keep me in the loop on any changes.

def: An official inspection of a company's accounts.
ex: The annual audit found no irregularities.

def: Money owed to a company by its customers.
ex: Chasing overdue receivables freed up much-needed cash.

def: The purchase of one company by another.
ex: The acquisition gave them a foothold in Asia.

def: The sale of a part of a business or a holding.
ex: Divestment of the loss-making unit lifted the share price.

def: A written note recording terms or setting out a proposal.
ex: Both sides signed a memorandum of understanding.

def: To obtain money to fund a business.
ex: The startup raised capital from three venture funds.

def: To reduce the amount a business spends.
ex: They cut costs without laying anyone off.

def: To finish something by the required time.
ex: The team worked the weekend to meet the deadline.

def: To sell shares in a company on a stock exchange for the first time.
ex: The firm went public at a valuation of two billion.

def: To confirm or give support to a statement, theory or finding with additional evidence.
ex: The survey data corroborate the hypothesis advanced in the opening chapter.

def: To provide evidence that proves the truth or validity of a claim.
ex: The author fails to substantiate her sweeping generalisation about medieval literacy.

def: To prove that a statement or theory is wrong by argument or evidence.
ex: Subsequent experiments decisively refuted the original conjecture.

def: To argue that a claim or accusation is false, typically by presenting counter-evidence.
ex: The discussion section rebuts three common objections to the model.

def: To put forward an idea or premise as a basis for argument or discussion.
ex: The paper posits a causal link between urbanisation and declining fertility.

def: To assume or assert the existence of something as a foundation for reasoning.
ex: Euclidean geometry postulates that parallel lines never meet.

def: To describe or define something precisely, marking out its boundaries.
ex: The introduction carefully delineates the scope of the investigation.

def: To make something clear by explaining it in greater detail.
ex: A worked example elucidates the otherwise opaque derivation.

def: To explain or set out an idea or theory systematically and in detail.
ex: In chapter three she expounds her theory of collective memory.

def: To analyse and develop an idea or text in order to reveal its meaning.
ex: The commentary explicates each stanza line by line.

def: To cite something, especially evidence or an example, as proof in support of an argument.
ex: The historian adduces parish records to date the settlement.

def: To infer or estimate unknown values by projecting from known data or trends.
ex: One should be cautious in extrapolating these results to other populations.

def: To estimate an intermediate value between two known points, or to insert material into a text.
ex: The missing readings were interpolated from adjacent measurements.

def: To found or base a claim, argument or condition on a particular assumption.
ex: The whole argument is predicated on the reliability of self-reported data.

def: To place an event, idea or text within its wider setting to clarify its meaning.
ex: The review contextualises the findings within the broader debate on inequality.

def: To treat something usually taken for granted as an issue requiring critical examination.
ex: The essay problematises the very notion of a neutral observer.

def: To make a particular idea or theme especially prominent in a discussion.
ex: Feminist readings foreground the silenced voices in the archive.

def: To emphasise or draw attention to the importance of something.
ex: These anomalies underscore the need for a revised methodology.

def: To define an abstract concept in terms of the measurable procedures used to study it.
ex: The authors operationalise 'wellbeing' as a composite of six survey indices.

def: To separate combined data into its component parts for closer analysis.
ex: When the results are disaggregated by gender, the effect disappears.

def: Relevant and closely connected to the matter under discussion.
ex: Only two of the cited studies are germane to the present question.

def: Most noticeable or important; standing out prominently.
ex: The table summarises the salient features of each competing theory.

def: Weak, slight or insubstantial, especially of a connection or argument.
ex: The link between the two datasets is, at best, tenuous.

def: Strongly critical or controversial in attacking an opinion or position.
ex: The pamphlet is polemical rather than dispassionately analytical.

def: Strongly influential and originating later developments in a field.
ex: Her seminal 1975 paper reshaped the discipline.

def: Regarded as authoritative and belonging to an accepted body of works or standards.
ex: The essay departs sharply from the canonical account of the revolution.

def: Relating to how things ought to be rather than how they actually are.
ex: The distinction between descriptive and normative claims is often blurred.

def: Saying the same thing twice so that a statement is true by definition and uninformative.
ex: The definition is tautological, explaining the term by restating it.

def: Oversimplifying something complex by treating it in terms of a single factor.
ex: Such a reductive account overlooks the cultural determinants of behaviour.

def: Characterised by subtle distinctions and shades of meaning.
ex: A more nuanced reading acknowledges the ambivalence of the narrator.

def: Strong and reliable, holding up under scrutiny or varied conditions.
ex: The finding proved robust across several alternative specifications.

def: Stated or appearing to be true, but not necessarily so.
ex: The ostensible aim of the reform was efficiency, though critics suspected otherwise.

def: Generally supposed or assumed to exist or to be the case.
ex: The putative benefits of the intervention have yet to be demonstrated.

def: Regularly found within and characteristic of a particular place or group.
ex: Corruption was endemic to the late imperial bureaucracy.

def: Naturally accompanying or occurring together with something else.
ex: Rapid growth brought a concomitant rise in inequality.

def: A thing or event that comes before and often gives rise to another.
ex: The report traces the intellectual antecedents of the movement.

def: A warning or qualification limiting how a statement should be interpreted.
ex: These conclusions carry an important caveat about sample size.

def: A condition or stipulation attached to an agreement or statement.
ex: The claim holds, with the proviso that measurement error is negligible.

def: A framework of concepts and practices that defines a discipline at a given time.
ex: The discovery precipitated a shift in the dominant scientific paradigm.

def: A division into two sharply opposed or contrasted parts.
ex: The author challenges the tired dichotomy between nature and culture.

def: A connection or central link between things, or the point where they converge.
ex: The study examines the nexus of trade, migration and identity.

def: The decisive or most important point at issue.
ex: The crux of the debate is whether intention can be measured at all.

def: A gap or missing part, especially in an argument, text or body of knowledge.
ex: This paper addresses a notable lacuna in the empirical literature.

def: A heading or set of criteria under which something is classified or assessed.
ex: These disparate practices are gathered under the rubric of 'soft power'.

def: An ostensible reason offered to conceal the true motive for an action.
ex: National security served as a pretext for tightening censorship.

def: Explaining phenomena by reference to the purpose or end they serve.
ex: Historians warn against a teleological narrative that reads the past as inevitable progress.

def: Relating to the dominance of one group, ideology or state over others.
ex: The text interrogates the hegemonic assumptions of Western scholarship.

def: To spoil or weaken the effectiveness or validity of something.
ex: Selection bias vitiates any inference drawn from the sample.

def: In spite of the thing just mentioned, used in formal writing to concede a point without abandoning the argument.
ex: Notwithstanding these limitations, the findings offer a useful starting point for further enquiry.

def: Although, used to introduce a concise concessive qualification within a sentence.
ex: The intervention produced a positive effect, albeit a modest one, across all three cohorts.

def: The use of cautious language such as modal verbs and qualifiers to soften claims and signal appropriate uncertainty.
ex: Effective hedging allows a writer to present findings confidently while acknowledging their provisional nature.

def: The process of turning a verb or adjective into a noun to create a denser, more objective academic style.
ex: Through nominalisation, 'the government decided quickly' becomes 'the government's rapid decision'.

def: To guide the reader through a text using words and phrases that indicate its structure and direction.
ex: The introduction signposts the three arguments that the essay will develop in turn.

def: A pair of expressions used to refer back economically to the first and second of two previously mentioned items respectively.
ex: Both qualitative and quantitative methods were considered; the former was ultimately chosen for its depth.

def: An impersonal signposting phrase used to draw the reader's attention to an important qualification or observation.
ex: It should be noted that these results apply only to participants over the age of sixty.

def: A formal connective meaning concerning or in relation to, used to specify the topic under discussion.
ex: With respect to reliability, the instrument performed consistently across repeated trials.

def: On the whole, used to make a cautious generalisation that admits minor exceptions.
ex: By and large, the literature supports a positive link between exercise and cognitive function.

def: To provide the theoretical or evidential foundation on which something rests.
ex: A constructivist view of learning underpins the whole of the study's design.

def: In a cautious, provisional way that leaves room for revision as more evidence emerges.
ex: We tentatively conclude that the correlation reflects a causal link, pending replication.

def: A hedging construction used to advance a claim while distancing the writer from full commitment to it.
ex: It could be argued that economic factors, rather than cultural ones, drove the decline.

def: A hedging phrase indicating that a statement is only partly true or applicable.
ex: To a certain extent, the model accounts for the anomalies, but several remain unexplained.

def: A hedging verb used to report an apparent pattern without asserting it as established fact.
ex: The data appear to suggest a seasonal fluctuation in reported cases.

def: To the extent that, used to limit the scope within which a statement holds true.
ex: The framework is useful insofar as it captures the interaction between the two variables.

def: Taking into consideration, used to signal that a conclusion follows from newly presented evidence.
ex: In light of these findings, existing guidelines may need to be revised.

def: A relevant example that clearly illustrates the general point just made.
ex: Renewable energy policy is a case in point: incentives shifted investment within a decade.

def: A signposting adverb introducing a statement that is the opposite of the one just made.
ex: Urban participants favoured public transport; conversely, rural respondents relied on cars.

def: Until the present time, used to describe the state of knowledge before a new contribution.
ex: The study documents a phenomenon that had hitherto received little scholarly attention.

def: The presence of something in insufficient quantity, often used to justify new research.
ex: There is a marked paucity of longitudinal data on the condition in adolescents.

def: A scarcity or lack of something, frequently cited when identifying a gap in the literature.
ex: Despite widespread interest, there remains a dearth of empirical work on the topic.

def: Directly relevant to the matter under discussion.
ex: The review is confined to studies pertinent to the central research question.

def: Founded or based on a particular assumption or condition.
ex: The argument is predicated on the assumption that markets tend towards equilibrium.

def: A concept or idea, often one being critically examined rather than endorsed.
ex: This paper interrogates the notion that intelligence can be captured by a single measure.

def: The range of subject matter that a piece of work addresses or deliberately excludes.
ex: A detailed treatment of pricing lies beyond the scope of the present essay.

def: To show clearly through evidence or reasoning that something is the case.
ex: The experiment demonstrates that priming significantly alters response times.

def: To regard something as being caused by or belonging to a particular source.
ex: The researchers attribute the improvement to increased engagement rather than the new curriculum.

def: To prevent something from happening or make it impossible.
ex: The cross-sectional design precludes any firm claims about causation.

def: To justify or provide sufficient grounds for a particular course of action or conclusion.
ex: The inconsistency in these results warrants further investigation.

def: A signposting phrase used to introduce a point or source that continues the same line of thought.
ex: In a similar vein, Roberts argues that institutional trust shapes compliance.

def: A signposting phrase meaning in order to achieve that aim, linking a purpose to the method that serves it.
ex: The study sought to isolate the effect of feedback; to that end, a control group was used.

def: A framing phrase used to pose or discuss a question of degree rather than a simple yes-or-no.
ex: This essay examines the extent to which social media has reshaped political discourse.

def: A hedging phrase used to introduce a general statement while conceding that finer distinctions exist.
ex: Broadly speaking, the two schools of thought differ over the role of the state.

def: To make use of a source of information, theory, or experience in developing an argument.
ex: The analysis draws on both economic theory and archival records.

def: Able to be defended successfully against criticism or objection.
ex: Once the confounding variable is accounted for, the original hypothesis is no longer tenable.

def: A hedging construction used to attach an explicit limiting condition to a claim.
ex: The model can be applied elsewhere, with the caveat that local conditions may vary considerably.

def: Pleasant and attractive in appearance, in a wholesome, slightly old-fashioned way.
ex: She had grown into a comely young woman with an easy, unaffected smile.

def: A brilliant radiance or the quality of shining out brightly.
ex: At dawn the sea took on a soft effulgence that made the whole bay glow.

def: Having a soft, radiant sheen; glossy in an attractive way.
ex: Years of careful brushing had left her hair thick and lustrous.

def: Sparkling or shining with flashes of light.
ex: Frost lay over the meadow in a scintillating sheet of tiny crystals.

def: Allowing light to pass through diffusely, so that objects behind appear blurred.
ex: Her skin was so pale as to seem translucent in the winter light.

def: Splendid and costly-looking, giving an impression of rich luxury.
ex: The suite was decorated in sumptuous velvets and gilded mouldings.

def: Giving rich, sensual pleasure through curves, fullness or luxuriousness.
ex: The perfume had a voluptuous warmth of amber and ripe fruit.

def: Extremely beautiful and delicate, showing fine, refined craftsmanship.
ex: Each petal of the enamel brooch was rendered with exquisite precision.

def: Attractive or appealing in a fresh, innocent and charming way.
ex: The child gave a winsome grin that disarmed even the sternest of the guests.

def: So beautiful as to be utterly delightful and captivating.
ex: She looked ravishing in the emerald gown, and the room turned as she entered.

def: Tall, slim and gracefully supple in figure.
ex: The willowy dancer seemed to bend with the music like a reed in water.

def: Slender and elegant in an attractive, well-proportioned way.
ex: The tailored coat gave him a svelte, unmistakably continental silhouette.

def: Thin, supple and able to move easily and gracefully.
ex: With one lithe movement the cat slipped through the narrow gap in the fence.

def: Tall, dignified and gracefully proportioned, like a classical statue.
ex: A statuesque woman in black stood motionless at the head of the staircase.

def: Attractive or appealing in appearance, so as to create a favourable impression.
ex: He was not a prepossessing figure, yet his voice held the room at once.

def: Attractive and pleasing to look at, especially of clothes or appearance.
ex: She wore a fetching straw hat tilted just over one eye.

def: Flattering to the wearer's appearance; suiting them well.
ex: The deep blue was extraordinarily becoming and brought out the colour of her eyes.

def: A harsh, discordant mixture of sounds.
ex: A cacophony of horns and sirens greeted us the moment we left the station.

def: Deep, clear and continuing to sound or echo richly.
ex: The bell gave a resonant peal that hung in the air long after it struck.

def: Having a pleasant, distinctive and usually spicy or fragrant smell.
ex: She crushed the aromatic leaves between her fingers to release their scent.

def: Having a warm, heavy, earthy scent like that of musk.
ex: A musky trace of his cologne lingered in the hallway after he had gone.

def: Relating to the sense of smell.
ex: A great perfumer relies on an olfactory memory stretching back decades.

def: An unpleasant or noxious smell or vapour given off by something.
ex: A sour effluvium rose from the neglected drains along the alley.

def: A thick, unpleasant or unhealthy vapour, atmosphere or smell.
ex: A miasma of stale smoke and spilt beer hung over the empty bar.

def: Having a very unpleasant smell.
ex: A malodorous heap of refuse had been left festering by the gate.

def: Having a rich, sweet and highly pleasing taste, smell or appearance.
ex: The market stalls were piled high with luscious peaches and figs.

def: Excessively or cloyingly sweet, often unpleasantly so.
ex: The dessert was so saccharine that a single spoonful was enough.

def: Relating to the sense of touch, or pleasing to touch.
ex: The book was a tactile pleasure, bound in soft, grained leather.

def: Pleasantly soft and smooth to the touch, taste or hearing, like velvet.
ex: The wine had a velvety texture that lingered on the palate.

def: Giving or appealing to keen pleasure through the physical senses.
ex: The poem revels in the sensuous detail of colour, scent and sound.

def: A blending of the senses in which one kind of stimulus involuntarily evokes another, such as seeing colours in sounds.
ex: Through her synaesthesia, each note of the sonata appeared as a shade of blue.

def: Polished to a warm, smooth shine, especially of metal.
ex: The burnished copper pans hung in a gleaming row above the range.

def: To make a bad or unsatisfactory situation better.
ex: The new subsidies did little to ameliorate the plight of the poorest households.

def: To place two or more things side by side, especially to invite comparison or contrast.
ex: The exhibition juxtaposes medieval icons with contemporary street art to striking effect.

def: A natural tendency or inclination to behave in a particular way.
ex: Investors underestimated the market's propensity for sudden, irrational swings.

def: A remark or statement that is dull and obvious, used as though it were fresh or profound.
ex: The minister's speech offered nothing but platitudes about hard work and hope.

def: Using inflated, pompous language with little real substance.
ex: His bombastic rhetoric impressed the crowd but crumbled under close questioning.

def: To express one's opinions in a pompous and dogmatic way.
ex: He loves to pontificate about economics despite never having run a business.

def: Vague, ill-defined or lacking clear form and content.
ex: The strategy remained nebulous, full of aspirations but short on specifics.

def: Directly opposed to or incompatible with something.
ex: Such heavy-handed censorship is antithetical to the very idea of a free press.

def: A deep-seated feeling of dislike or aversion.
ex: There was a barely concealed antipathy between the two rival directors.

def: To cease resisting and give in to demands or pressure.
ex: After weeks of strikes, management finally capitulated to the union's demands.

def: To shock or stimulate someone into taking sudden, energetic action.
ex: The scandal galvanised ordinary citizens into demanding reform.

def: A tendency or inclination towards a particular kind of behaviour, often an undesirable one.
ex: His proclivity for gambling eventually cost him his home.

def: A state of uncertainty or perplexity over a difficult decision.
ex: She was in a quandary about whether to accept the promotion and relocate.

def: Using or containing far more words than are needed.
ex: The report was so verbose that its main findings were nearly lost.

def: Angry and bitter in tone or manner, especially in a dispute.
ex: The negotiations collapsed into an acrimonious exchange of accusations.

def: A person or thing regarded as a perfect model of a particular quality.
ex: He was held up as a paragon of integrity, which made his downfall all the more shocking.

def: Something or someone that one strongly dislikes or finds utterly unacceptable.
ex: Any compromise on safety standards was anathema to the chief engineer.

def: Providing psychological relief through the open expression of strong emotions.
ex: Writing about the loss proved unexpectedly cathartic for her.

def: A strong liking or habitual fondness for something.
ex: She has a penchant for dramatic entrances and expensive shoes.

def: To combine two or more distinct ideas or things into one, often mistakenly.
ex: Critics accused him of conflating patriotism with blind obedience.

def: Unusually or disproportionately large; excessive.
ex: The project consumed an inordinate amount of time for such a modest result.

def: Proceeding gradually and subtly, with harmful effects that are not immediately apparent.
ex: The insidious spread of misinformation eroded trust before anyone noticed.

def: At the point of death, or in terminal decline and lacking vitality.
ex: Fresh investment revived what had been a moribund shipbuilding industry.

def: To discard or abandon something as no longer wanted or useful.
ex: The party quietly jettisoned the pledge once the election was won.

def: Essentially different in kind and not able to be compared readily.
ex: The festival somehow united disparate genres into a coherent whole.

def: Acting or done quickly and rashly, without careful thought.
ex: His impetuous decision to resign left the department in disarray.

def: Inclined to assert opinions as if they were unquestionable facts.
ex: He was too dogmatic to concede that his rivals might have a point.

def: To make a problem, situation or feeling worse.
ex: Cutting the support staff only exacerbated the backlog of cases.

def: Hasty and superficial, done without attention to detail.
ex: A cursory inspection missed the cracks that later caused the collapse.

def: To revoke, cancel or repeal a law, order or agreement.
ex: The board voted to rescind the controversial bonus scheme.

def: Not harmful or offensive; unlikely to provoke a strong reaction.
ex: What began as an innocuous remark somehow escalated into a full-blown argument.

def: Truthful and straightforward, even about difficult matters.
ex: In a rare candid moment, the director admitted the launch had been rushed.

def: Severe or plain in appearance or manner; without comfort or luxury.
ex: The monastery's austere rooms held nothing but a bed, a chair and a small window.

def: Requiring great and sustained effort; strenuous and tiring.
ex: The final ascent proved so arduous that two climbers turned back.

def: Expressed clearly and easy to understand; mentally clear.
ex: His lucid explanation made a notoriously difficult topic seem almost simple.

def: Expressed clearly and in very few words.
ex: Keep the summary succinct; the board wants one page, not ten.

def: More than is needed or wanted; unnecessary.
ex: The editor cut every superfluous adjective until the prose felt taut.

def: Designed to impress or attract notice in a showy, vulgar way.
ex: He arrived in an ostentatious sports car that seemed calculated to make everyone stare.

def: Having or showing an ability to assess situations shrewdly and act to advantage.
ex: An astute investor, she sold the shares just before the market collapsed.

def: Having or showing no skill; clumsy and incompetent.
ex: The rescue was hampered by an inept response from the local authorities.

def: So lacking in originality as to be boring and predictable.
ex: The film's dialogue was so banal that the audience began to laugh in the wrong places.

def: Overused to the point of being unoriginal and stale.
ex: He fell back on the hackneyed metaphor of life as a journey.

def: Ordinary and unimaginative; lacking poetic beauty.
ex: The reason for the delay was disappointingly prosaic: a missing signature.

def: Impossible to understand or interpret; giving nothing away.
ex: The judge listened with an inscrutable expression that betrayed no opinion.

def: Hard to control, manage or solve.
ex: Youth unemployment remained an intractable problem no policy seemed to shift.

def: A confusing and difficult problem or question.
ex: How to cut emissions without harming jobs remains a genuine conundrum.

def: A perfect example or embodiment of a particular quality or type.
ex: With her calm precision, she was the epitome of professionalism.

def: A close and harmonious relationship marked by mutual understanding.
ex: The teacher quickly built a rapport with even the most reluctant pupils.

def: A particular point in time, especially a critical one in a sequence of events.
ex: At this juncture, withdrawing from the deal would cost us our credibility.

def: A situation in which no progress is possible; a deadlock.
ex: After hours of fruitless talks, the negotiations reached an impasse.

def: A difficult, unpleasant or embarrassing situation.
ex: Losing his passport abroad left him in a genuine predicament.

def: To praise something or someone enthusiastically and highly.
ex: Critics extolled the novel as the finest work of the decade.

def: To make an unpleasant feeling less intense; to soothe or relieve.
ex: A full apology did little to assuage the family's anger.

def: To make someone less angry or hostile by doing or saying something.
ex: The airline offered vouchers to placate the stranded passengers.

def: To support, strengthen or reinforce something.
ex: New figures on exports helped bolster confidence in the recovery.

def: To reduce, restrict or cut short something.
ex: Budget cuts forced the museum to curtail its opening hours.

def: To voluntarily give up a possession, right or position.
ex: She reluctantly relinquished control of the company she had founded.

def: To gradually weaken or damage something, often secretly.
ex: Constant public criticism began to undermine the coach's authority.

def: To make two apparently conflicting things compatible, or to restore friendly relations.
ex: It is hard to reconcile his generous public image with his private meanness.

def: To spread throughout something, reaching every part.
ex: A sense of unease seemed to permeate the entire building.

def: To criticise unfairly in order to belittle or disparage.
ex: It is easy to denigrate the work of others without offering anything better.

def: To be a typical example of something, or to illustrate it clearly.
ex: This building exemplifies the elegant restraint of the period.

def: Without intention; by accident or oversight.
ex: She inadvertently copied the whole department into the confidential email.

def: In a way that shows strong, forceful feeling or conviction.
ex: He vehemently denied any involvement in the leak.

def: In a way that is understood or implied without being stated openly.
ex: By saying nothing, the committee tacitly approved the change.

def: In a way that leaves no doubt; clearly and without ambiguity.
ex: The minister stated unequivocally that no further cuts were planned.

def: To gradually accept a difficult or unwelcome situation.
ex: It took her a long time to come to terms with the loss of her job.

def: Not certain or fixed; done cautiously or provisionally.
ex: We reached a tentative agreement, subject to approval by the board.

def: Showing great attention to detail and care over accuracy.
ex: Her meticulous record-keeping made the audit remarkably straightforward.

def: Dealing with problems in a sensible, practical way rather than by theory.
ex: We need a pragmatic solution that we can actually implement this quarter.

def: Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something.
ex: She felt ambivalent about the promotion, torn between the salary and the extra hours.

def: No longer needed or useful; also, having lost one's job because the position is no longer required.
ex: Several roles were made redundant when the two departments merged.

def: To have a serious, gradual negative effect on someone or something.
ex: The long commute began to take its toll on his health and family life.

def: To become involved in an activity only because it is currently popular or successful.
ex: Once the trend took off, every retailer jumped on the bandwagon.

def: At the most advanced or innovative stage of development.
ex: The lab uses cutting-edge technology to sequence genomes in hours.

def: With the benefit of understanding a situation only after it has happened.
ex: In hindsight, we should have signed the contract before the price rose.

def: To remember and take a fact or consideration into account.
ex: Bear in mind that the deadline falls during the public holiday.

def: Likely to suffer from or do something, usually something undesirable.
ex: New employees are prone to underestimating how long the training takes.

def: So convincing or interesting that it holds one's attention or forces agreement.
ex: She made a compelling case for relocating the head office.

def: Tending to cause harm or damage.
ex: Skipping the pilot phase could be detrimental to the whole project.

def: Capable of working successfully or being done in a practical way.
ex: Solar power is now a commercially viable alternative for the plant.

def: In disagreement or conflict with someone or something.
ex: His account of events was at odds with the official report.

def: To examine and thoroughly repair or improve a system, machine, or method.
ex: The company plans to overhaul its outdated booking system next year.

def: To make something bad less severe, serious, or painful.
ex: The insurance was designed to mitigate the financial risk of a bad harvest.

def: To make it more difficult for someone to do something or for something to progress.
ex: Poor communication between teams hindered the launch.

def: To control or limit something, especially something harmful.
ex: New regulations aim to curb excessive spending on advertising.

def: For a limited period, until a situation changes.

def: Something that seems bad at first but eventually has good results.

ex: Every proof in the system rests ultimately on a handful of unproven axioms.

def: A philosophy emphasising individual freedom, choice and the creation of meaning in an indifferent universe.
ex: Sartre's existentialism insists that we are condemned to be free and wholly responsible.

def: The ethical theory that right action is that which maximises overall happiness or well-being.
ex: Utilitarianism judges a policy solely by whether it produces the greatest good for the greatest number.

def: The ethical theory that the morality of an action depends on duty and rules, not consequences.
ex: Kantian deontology forbids lying even when a lie would produce a better outcome.

def: The view that genuine knowledge is confined to what can be verified by observation and science.
ex: Logical positivism dismissed metaphysical claims as literally meaningless.

def: A philosophical stance questioning whether certain or any knowledge is genuinely attainable.
ex: Ancient scepticism recommended suspending judgement whenever the evidence remained balanced.

def: The doctrine that everything, including mind, is ultimately composed of physical matter.
ex: Strict materialism holds that thoughts are nothing over and above brain processes.

def: The philosophical view that reality is fundamentally mental or dependent on mind.
ex: Berkeley's idealism denied that matter exists independently of being perceived.

def: The doctrine that mind and body are two distinct kinds of substance.
ex: Cartesian dualism struggles to explain how an immaterial mind moves a physical body.

def: The view that things possess a fixed set of properties defining what they necessarily are.
